papers.abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.
bullets: Zero-shot skill specialization can be brittle because it may misjudge runtime bindings, making recovery costly.
SkillCache uses one completed trace to create a parameterized capsule combining programs and natural-language steps.
A plan executor replays capsules and returns control to the model only when needed, while retaining the original skill for recovery.
Across 87 SkillsBench tasks, warm execution reduced token use by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward.
Capsules remained effective under controlled request changes and transferred across models, improving mean reward while reducing token use.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SkillCache, an execution-grounded specialization method for LLM agents to compile skill orchestration into token-efficient capsules. This addresses memory and efficiency in agent execution.
papers.title: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
papers.tldr: SkillCache compiles one successful LLM-agent skill execution into a reusable executable capsule, substantially reducing tokens while preserving performance and enabling cross-model transfer.

papers.abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.
bullets: Studies when and why models benefit from outputting coordinate-based visual grounding in chain-of-thought reasoning.
Introduces an analysis method to measure whether models actually use their predicted grounding in reasoning traces, plus an ablation of the training recipe.
Finds improvements for counting but no significant gains over non-grounded baselines across broad spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks.
Synthetic tasks show grounding is most useful for undescribable visual references that are difficult to express in language.
Introduces BrickVision, a benchmark designed to require such undescribable visual references.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Decode Grounding Corruption. We introduce a CoT analysis technique to analyze whether a model uses its grounding. Instead of editing CoT after generation, we randomize the model’s outputted points during decoding and reset the KV-cache.

Figure 4: Synthetic Probe Tasks. We use three synthetic tasks to study where grounded reasoning improves over pure text reasoning. We find that grounding performs significantly better than text reasoning when no text-labels are available, but worse when given text labels. Zoom in for detail.

Figure 5: BrickVision. Samples from each task distribution of our BrickVision evaluation set. BrickVision tasks involve iterative comparison across objects difficult to describe in language, and require precise answers in the form of a point or integer.

Figure 3: Training Coordinate Randomization. We randomize varying percentages of coordinates in the SFT set and report task performance and grounding usage. While grounding usage decreases with more randomization, task performance remains relatively flat, except on counting.
Figure 6: SFT format ablation. We compare the appended and reflection SFT formats. We find that the reflection format generally leads to better grounding usage, and use this format in our SFT data.

Figure 10: Restyling drift. Without locking the aspect ratio or prompting Nano-Banana with bounding boxes, we find that the restyled image drifts from the original, making the segmentation map ground truth (visualized as an overlay) incorrect.
Figure 9: Benchmark construction. Our benchmark combines procedural generation with conditional image generation to produce realistic images aligned with the original synthetic ground truth.
Figure 7: Incorrect TreeVGR samples. Selected samples from the TreeVGR dataset illustrating errors in data such as incorrect box labeling or uninformative boxes.
Figure 8: Probe reasoning traces. We provide examples of our reasoning data used in our “Arrow Following” task to illustrate the difference between text traces and grounded traces.

Table 3: Training recipe comparison. We report the performance of grounded reasoning and textonly reasoning training recipes after SFT and RL training phases. Deltas that exclude 0 from the confidence interval are highlighted. We find that grounding provides a statistically significant benefit on counting, but not on spatial reasoning or perception.

Table 4: VLM performance on BrickVision. Many frontier models struggle on BrickVision, suggesting limited ability to maintain undescribable visual references. Models trained with in-domain grounding data perform better than text reasoning, demonstrating the benefit of grounded reasoning.

Table 1: Grounding usage experiments. We report change in mean performance (% acc) for our coordinate corruption experiments. Many open models don’t rely on their grounding for spatial reasoning and perception. Our retrained models (below) are more reliant on their grounding outputs.
Table 6: Point versus box grounding after SFT. We report the box minus point accuracy delta with 95% confidence intervals computed as in Appendix A. Bold deltas exclude 0.
Table 2: Appended vs reflection performance. The reflection reasoning style yields significantly better performance on counting.
Table 5: Training hyperparameters.

papers.selection_reason: Studies coordinate-grounded reasoning for spatial and visual reasoning tasks, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: Where and Why is Grounded Reasoning Useful?
papers.tldr: Grounded reasoning mainly helps visual tasks requiring hard-to-describe references, offering limited benefits on existing spatial reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
bullets: Targets the high latency and cost of maintaining diverse populations in iterative LLM-based program evolution.
Uses hundreds of low-cost agents organized into swarms, with each swarm exploring a different perspective.
Promotes diversity through hidden-state distance filtering and combines ideas by aggregating agents’ KV caches for a summarizer.
Across 21 mathematical discovery and scientific computing problems, it reaches benchmark best scores in a median of 3–8 minutes versus 60 minutes for other frameworks.
Qwen3 8B sometimes improves solutions initially found by AlphaEvolve using frontier LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Minutes that SwarmEvolve needs to reach the best score that OpenEvolve (left), ShinkaEvolve (middle), and CodeEvolve (right) reach in 60 minutes. All frameworks use Qwen3 8B and run for three seeds. Hollow circles mark problems where SwarmEvolve does not reach the target within 60 minutes. On most problems, SwarmEvolve reaches in a few minutes what the baselines reach in one hour.

Figure 2: Workflow of SwarmEvolve. In each round, SwarmEvolve launches 10 swarms of 45 latent agents. Each swarm draws parent programs from the archive and gets a focus prompt to refine, hybridize, explore, or start fresh. In each swarm, the agents take 40 latent reasoning steps, a novelty filter removes the 15 most similar agents (hollow circles), and the summarizer reads the KV caches of the rest to write one new program. The new programs are evaluated and added to the archive. A parameter tuning agent tunes the hyperparameters of the best program.

Figure 5: Mean hidden states of the latent agents for a circle packing problem with Qwen3 8B, projected onto their first two principal components: the 450 latent agents of all 10 swarms with the swarm centers (left), and the 45 latent agents of one exploration-focused swarm, each reading different parent programs (right). The swarms occupy distinct regions, and the novelty filter keeps latent agents from every cluster.

Figure 3: Latent reasoning and communication in a swarm. Each latent agent reasons recursively in the embedding space without decoding to text. Its latent reasoning steps are stored as KV cache. The summarizer then reads the concatenated KV caches from all agents and writes a new program in text.

Table 1: Best score within 60 minutes, averaged over three seeds (scores defined in Section 4 and Appendix D). For each model, bold marks the best score and underline marks the second best. SwarmEvolve (ours) has the highest average score with every model.

papers.selection_reason: Latent-space agent communication via shared KV caches is a technically meaningful efficiency contribution for LLM-based search.
papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
papers.tldr: SwarmEvolve accelerates LLM-guided evolutionary program search by using large latent-space agent swarms that share KV caches instead of repeatedly generating long text.

papers.abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native metric-3D human-action representations in modern video models.
Supports action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation.
Uses a role-adaptive action renderer and cross-stream action-video coupling to align motion with visual dynamics.
Covers six action-video tasks and generalizes from narrow-domain data to unseen scenes and interactions.
Provides effective action control and visual quality while preserving pretrained visual knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of EgoGeneralist. Role-adaptive rendering (Sec. 3.2) tailors the visual representation of metric 3D action to its task role: an ego-view map with a fixed 3D anchor for conditioning, or a multiview Posegrid for generation and metric readout. A shared frozen video VAE encodes rendered action and video into two latent streams. Cross-stream coupling (Sec. 3.3) uses joint self-attention and attention LoRAs activated only for generation targets, retaining the backbone weights and per-stream input structure. The bottom panel illustrates condition–target assignments for the three prediction directions defined in Sec. 3.1.

Adapted only on EgoDex, EgoGeneralist generalizes to in-the-wild scenes. The generated videos follow the prescribed motion with physically coherent interactions, correctly removing the purple block (left) and tilting the bucket (right).

All methods receive an initial observation and instruction. VITRA and EgoGeneralist also receive initial action states. †Being-H0 uses a single wrist-anchored rigid alignment to the GT initial hand.

Table 2. Action-conditioned text-to-video generation on 100 action–prompt instances per dataset. Since the varied prompts have no corresponding ground-truth videos, we evaluate motion control and video–text semantic alignment. Our method maintains competitive action adherence across text-specified visual contexts.

Table 1. Action-conditioned image-to-video generation on EgoDex and Xperience-10M. EgoGeneralist achieves strong visual fidelity and action control in both datasets. PCK, IoU, and Failure are in percentages; best and second-best are bold and underlined. EgoSimO/EgoSimQ use dataset-provided/Qwen-generated prompts.

Table 5. Hand, upper-limb, and camera readout on EgoDex. Multiview Posegrid gives lower reconstruction errors, indicating that its VAE latents better preserve metric action information for readout.

Table 6. Ablations of two design components for action-conditioned video generation. papers.selection_reason: Unified egocentric action-video generation and understanding; fits human-video learning and video understanding.
papers.title: EgoGeneralist: Unifying Egocentric Action-Video Tasks through Video-Native Modeling
papers.tldr: EgoGeneralist adapts pretrained video generators to unify egocentric action understanding and generation in metric 3D space.

papers.abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
bullets: Corpus-based activation search is limited to concepts present in the scanned text.
MAEMs are metamodels trained with a label-free reinforcement-learning objective to maximize cosine similarity between a target direction and generated-text activations.
A Qwen3.6-27B MAEM outperforms corpus search and a natural-language autoencoder on held-out activation inversion, covering most tested languages/domains and 89% of held-out SAE features.
The method also interprets steering vectors, recovers LoRA backdoor payloads, and verbalizes some model-workspace inner monologue.
Generated exemplars are directly verifiable with a forward pass through the subject model, though the abstract does not establish universal interpretability.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/oopsierecover for videos.
bullets: Targets the need for large amounts of corrective data and poor generalization in deployed VLA models.
Uses abduction to infer the intent behind corrective demonstrations.
Represents inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs that steer actions away from undesirable regions.
Evaluated across 6 tasks with variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks.
Reports successful recovery across broad novel situations without new corrective data for each variation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: OOPSIERECOVER: From semantic interventions to reusable VLA corrections. In OOPSIERECOVER, a human monitors VLA execution and intervenes to provide semantic corrections: a corrective trajectory and a language description for some type of correction, ci, (orange). We then synthesize the collected set of interventions for each correction type into a Semantically Grounded Gated Cost by i) parsing the sensorimotor demonstration as temporal point sets tracked on semantic scene entities, ii) generating gated costs from the motion of the point sets, and iii) verifying these costs by evaluating their capability to explain all human corrections of the same type (blue). During deployment (green), these costs determine when steering is needed and rank candidate actions using the learned corrective programs. This separates the intended correction from its demonstrated trajectory, allowing correction programs to be used in the environment where they are collected and to generalize to new situations, while the base VLA remains frozen.

Fig. 3: Simulation and real-world tasks. We evaluate a diverse set of tasks that elicit different types of corrections; avoiding collisions, improving placement precision, and correctly articulating objects.

Fig. 1: Learning reusable corrections from human interventions with OOPSIERECOVER. A human corrects a lid-closure failure and describes the intended behavior. OOPSIERECOVER grounds this feedback in semantic point sets, and uses abduction – finding a simple explanation consistent with the observed intervention – to synthesize a gated correction cost that steers a frozen VLA. (Right) The synthesized correction programs generalize: they can be reused under changed object poses and scene layouts, broadening the successful applicability of the VLA.

Fig. 5: Scaling with number of corrections. On CoffeeMug, OOPSIERECOVER rapidly reaches an 84% success rate with as few as 8 corrections, while HG-DAgger∗ achieves only 28% despite using three times as many corrections.

papers.selection_reason: VLA failure recovery from few corrective demonstrations; directly fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
papers.tldr: OopsieRecover uses semantic reasoning from a few corrective demonstrations to help VLA robots recover from failures and generalize across novel objects, scenes, and task variations.

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. We introduce \textbf{Latent RL Prior}, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using $10\times$ and $5\times$ fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge. Project website: https://yixiaowang7.github.io/latent-rl-prior-page/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly learning visual grounding and precise dexterous control with scarce demonstrations.
Pretrains a flow-matching action decoder on privileged RL rollouts, then learns a visual-to-latent interface using action supervision alone.
The decoder can be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation.
Across three simulated tasks, it outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning baselines in low-data settings, using 10× and 5× fewer demonstrations on two tasks.
Direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation and stability; robustness to mass changes suggests retained RL control knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Latent RL Prior. (a) Privileged pretraining: a state tokenizer and Q-Former supply task context to an action decoder conditioned on flow time and single-arm proprioception. (b) Visual adaptation: an image encoder and Q-Former learn context tokens while the decoder remains frozen. For bimanual assembly, left- and right-arm queries interact within the same Q-Former; each output group conditions the shared decoder with its corresponding arm’s proprioception.

Figure 5: Target pose-alignment ablations with the action decoder frozen for both latent-transfer variants. Results show mean success rates and standard deviations over three random seeds, except for explicit transfer, which uses five seeds.

Figure 8: Generalization to increased object mass. (a) Target pose alignment at a relaxed (ϵ = 0.05 m) thresholds. (b) Door lift. The leftmost point in each plot corresponds to the reference mass used for downstream visual training, e.g., for Dvis.

Figure 7: Learning-rate ablations for (a) the image encoder with the action decoder frozen and (b) the action decoder with the image encoder frozen. Panels report strict (ϵ = 0.015 m) and relaxed (ϵ = 0.05 m) pose-alignment success. We report average success rate and standard deviation across three random seeds. Each scale multiplies the tested module’s original learning rate; zero freezes it.

Figure 9: Linear contact-force probes of the visual policies. Panels predict (a) total grasp normal force, (b) per-finger normal forces, (c) per-finger tangential forces, and (d) per-finger Cartesian force vectors from each layer of the action decoder. Colors denote visual-demonstration budgets; solid and dashed curves denote the frozen pretrained and trainable scratch action decoders. Both policies fine-tune the image encoder at 0.2× its base learning rate for 100k steps. Curves average three policy seeds on the same IID probe test episodes.

Figure 6: Training stability on target pose alignment at a relaxed (ϵ = 0.05 m) threshold. Dotted curves show individual runs for latent transfer, explicit transfer, and scratch training; shaded regions show the mean ± one standard deviation. Explicit transfer uses five random seeds, while latent transfer and scratch training use three seeds each.

Figure 2: Pretraining and downstream tasks. Left: the pretraining task of target pose alignment with varied procedural objects; the inset shows example object templates. Right: the downstream tasks of target pose alignment with a held-out brush, door lifting, and bimanual assembly (left to right). The same pretrained action decoder is reused for visual adaptation across all three downstream tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Data-efficient dexterous manipulation via latent RL priors; directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Latent RL Priors for Data-Efficient Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Latent RL Prior transfers privileged RL control knowledge into a frozen action decoder, enabling data-efficient visual dexterous manipulation from limited demonstrations.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
bullets: Compares reverse-KL on-policy distillation (OPD) with GRPO by held-out accuracy versus training FLOPs across tasks, models, domains, and optimization settings.
With external post-trained teachers, OPD generally achieves lower accuracy per training FLOP than GRPO and can inflate response lengths.
Using the student’s own GRPO checkpoint as teacher, OPD recovers math accuracy with 50× fewer distillation FLOPs, with similar findings for larger students, code, and another model family.
Multi-teacher OPD consolidates domain-specific GRPO experts while matching their accuracies; distillation costs 5.2% of specialist training FLOPs across two domains and 8.0% across four.
Including specialist training, the two-domain pipeline matches joint GRPO performance with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

Both OPD runs drop to about 36% OOD macro and remain 8–15 points below the starting student through 120EFLOP. The QwQ-32B teacher only delays the drop.

Figure 19: Code domain training: in-domain collapse, out-of-domain math transfer. Qwen3-4B-Base student trained on LiveCodeBench-v1–v5 (top row) and strict CodeForces (bottom row) with GRPO or external OPD-32B, lr 2× 10−6, 16 384-token response maximum; x-axis is cumulative training compute (EFLOPs). Left column: LCBv6 mean@16 (in-domain code). OPD (Qwen3-32B) loses to GRPO at every evaluated compute budget on both training sets. Right column: math OOD macro mean@16 on AIME24 + AIME25 + AMC23. Despite training only on code, OPD-32B reaches ≈31%–34% math OOD, beating the code-trained GRPO by roughly 10 points on both training sets — an additional evidence for OPD’s cross-domain transfer (Appendix F).

Figure 29: Per-domain breakdown of the 4-domain mix. Qwen3-4B-Base student trained on math, code, IFBench, and MMLU-Pro; mean@16 on each domain against the training FLOPs spent on that domain. Dashed lines mark the self-GRPO teacher (green) and the external Qwen3-8B teacher (purple; math and code values lie above the plotted range). All OPD runs use G=1. Self-GRPO OPD, with one or multiple teachers, reaches or comes within one point of the specialists on every domain within about 1EFLOP. Joint GRPO trails the specialists on math and code but exceeds them on IFBench. OPD with an external teacher stays well below the specialists on code and IFBench.

Figure 25: The self-GRPO teacher result holds for an 8B student (companion to Figure 3). Qwen3-8B-Base student on DAPO-Math-17k; mean@16 against training FLOPs. Dotted lines mark each teacher’s accuracy, and the y-axis is broken to show the external teachers. OPD with the self-GRPO teacher reaches the teacher’s 40.1% OOD macro within about 3EFLOP (group size G=8) or 1EFLOP (G=1), against 27.9EFLOP for GRPO. With the external Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B teachers, OPD ends at 37%–38% after 65–100EFLOP, far below those teachers’ own 76.9% and 81.3%.

Figure 6: No paper in our audit reports a FLOPsbased OPD compute win over GRPO. We filter 406 OPD papers posted after October 2025. Each bar is the number of papers that pass the criterion above it, and the italic text below each bar names what the next filter removes. 170 papers use a teacher that is distinct from the student and at least as large; 70 of these compare against GRPO as a baseline; 3 of those claim that OPD is cheaper than GRPO; and none of the three measures compute in FLOPs.

Figure 26: On math, G=1 makes OPD with an external teacher more compute-efficient, but the self-GRPO teacher is still far cheaper. OOD macro mean@16 on DAPO-Math-17k for Qwen3-4B-Base (left) and Qwen3-8B-Base (right) students. Colour marks the teacher (blue: self-GRPO; green: external Qwen3-8B thinking); marker shape marks the rollout setting. With the external teacher, G=1 beats G=8 at every compute budget and reaches 47.7% (4B) and 50.6% (8B), above GRPO. The self-GRPO teacher at G=1 reaches its teacher’s accuracy within about 1EFLOP, an order of magnitude less compute.

Figure 18: Switching the training set from DAPO-Math-17k to DeepMath-103k does not change the ordering. Qwen3-1.7B-Base student after OpenThoughts-3 SFT, thinking mode; OPD uses the Qwen3-4B teacher. OOD macro mean@16 against cumulative training FLOPs; solid lines train on DeepMath-103k and dashed lines on DAPO-Math-17k. On both training sets, OPD first rises, then drops to 2.5%–4.3%, and recovers only to 7.5%–9.1% by about 17EFLOP. GRPO reaches 19.0% (DeepMath) and 17.4% (DAPO) within 8EFLOP.

Figure 28: On code, G=1 does not rescue OPD with an external teacher. Qwen3-4B-Base student trained on LiveCodeBench v1–v5; LCBv6 mean@16 against training FLOPs (log scale). Solid lines use G=8 and dashed lines G=1; the external teacher is Qwen3-8B (thinking). The self-GRPO teacher reaches 47.3% within 0.25EFLOP, above GRPO (46.4%). With the external teacher, G=1 improves on G=8 at the default batch size but not with an 8× batch, and both G=1 runs stop at 32%–36%, more than 10 points below GRPO.

Figure 32: Group-size ablation for multi-teacher OPD on the 2-domain math and code mix. Same setup as Figure 31, with an added G=4 run. Smaller groups reach the specialists’ accuracy with less compute: on math, G=1, G=4, and G=8 need about 0.2, 0.8, and 1.6EFLOP, against 10EFLOP for the GRPO specialist; on code, about 0.17, 0.3, and 0.9EFLOP.

Figure 17: External thinking teachers, 4B and 8B students. Two panels, one per student size. Curves are training trajectories on DAPO-Math-17K for GRPO and for OPD against external Qwen3-{4B, 8B, 32B} thinking teachers; x is cumulative training FLOPs, y is OOD macro mean@16 (AIME24 + AIME25 + AMC23). GRPO curves: solid up to optimizer step 200, dotted for steps 200–400 (the OPD runs trained for at most 200 steps, so the solid segments are the matched-step comparison). No OPD run reaches its teacher’s accuracy within the compute budget, and a larger external teacher does not close the gap.

Figure 15: With thinking enabled, GRPO still leads OPD after an SFT cold start (Qwen3-1.7B-Base). OOD macro mean@16 (AIME24, AIME25, AMC23) against cumulative training FLOPs, with OPD using Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-8B as the teacher. Both panels use thinking mode, DAPO-Math-17k, batch size 64, 8 rollouts per prompt, a 7168-token training limit, and a 30 720-token evaluation limit. The vertical dashed line marks the compute at which GRPO finishes. Left: SFT initialization at the best SFT learning rate (1× 10−4). Right: SFT initialization at a lower SFT learning rate (1× 10−5). GRPO reaches 24.5% (left) and 18.7% (right). On the left, OPD with the 4B teacher comes within 0.3 points of GRPO after about 1.7× the compute. On the right, no OPD run reaches GRPO.

Figure 13: Thinking mode hurts OPD much more than GRPO. Qwen3-1.7B-Base student initialized from OpenThoughts-3 SFT, DAPO-Math-17k; OOD macro mean@16 against cumulative training FLOPs. Left: student and teachers in no-think mode. Right: student and teachers in thinking mode. The vertical dashed line marks the compute at which GRPO finishes. Switching from no-think to thinking lowers the final accuracy of GRPO by 2.1 points (18.9% to 16.8%) and of OPD with the 8B teacher by 2.1 points (17.5% to 15.4%). OPD with the 4B and 32B teachers loses 8.2 and 7.7 points, ending at 9.1% and 9.0%.

Figure 24: Multi-teacher OPD with self-GRPO teachers keeps the specialists’ response length, while an external teacher drives responses to the generation limit. Evaluation response length of Qwen3-4B-Base students trained on (a) the 2-domain mix (math, code) and (b) the 4-domain mix (math, code, IFBench, MMLU-Pro). Lengths are shown as a ratio to the single-task GRPO specialist for each domain (Table 9). The dashed line marks a ratio of 1, and the y-axis is logarithmic. Hatched bars reach the generation limit. Multi-teacher OPD stays within 0.93–1.19× of the specialists on every domain except IFBench (1.65–2.25×). Joint GRPO produces 0.87–5.31× the specialist length, and OPD with the external Qwen3-8B teacher produces 3.98–37.05×.

Figure 23: External thinking teachers make OPD students two to three times as long as the teacher. Qwen3-4B-Base student; mean response length on the OOD math evaluation (16 samples per problem) over training steps. Teachers at 4B, 8B, and 14B are of three types: GRPO-trained base models (left), external thinking models (centre), and external thinking models further trained with GRPO (right). Dotted horizontal lines mark each teacher’s own response length on the same prompts, and the grey dashed curve is GRPO. With both kinds of thinking teacher, the student’s responses grow to 2–3× the teacher’s length, close to the 30 720-token evaluation limit. With GRPO-trained base teachers the gap is much smaller: the student matches the 4B teacher’s length and is 1.4× and 1.9× as long as the 8B and 14B teachers.

papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
bullets: Targets the high cost of autoregressively generating coordinates for visual plans such as points, boxes, and trajectories.
Uses a lightweight drafter to predict each primitive in one forward pass, adapting to its type, dimensionality, and length.
Trains on annotated primitives and accepts structurally valid predictions without requiring exact autoregressive token matching.
Reduces prediction errors across evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks and reports approximately 25× faster 3D point-motion generation.
A world action model using VFlash plans reaches 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces suites, versus 62.6% for the baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: FPD design. A primitive-start token triggers a prediction block layout determined by the primitive type and the preceding tool calling. By adapting the prediction block to each primitive’s structure, VFlash supports different spatial formats and lengths without requiring token-level agreement with the VLM.

papers.selection_reason: Visual planning for robotics via faster primitive decoding; directly relevant to embodied navigation and efficiency.
papers.title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
papers.tldr: VFlash speeds up visual planning by jointly decoding structured primitives while maintaining or improving spatial accuracy.

papers.abstract: We introduce SM4RT, a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction from RGB videos. While existing feed-forward approaches typically address geometry reconstruction and motion estimation separately--and often predict motions in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement--SM4RT solves these tasks sequentially by first reconstructing 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion estimation from the predicted structure. By expressing each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame, SM4RT reduces ambiguity arising from camera motion. To address the sparsity of real-world motion labels, SM4RT further incorporates a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step. We evaluate motion estimation on three dynamic-scene datasets--Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey--and SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines. We additionally benchmark geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets and show that SM4RT achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our unified framework demonstrates that combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade not only avoids performance trade-offs but also enhances motion estimation through improved geometric reasoning.
bullets: Targets joint geometry reconstruction and motion estimation for dynamic scenes.
Sequentially reconstructs 3D structure first, then bootstraps motion estimation from it.
Represents per-pixel 3D motion in the corresponding camera frame to reduce camera-motion ambiguity.
Uses a weakly supervised loss to regularize unlabeled point motions from labeled positions at another time step.
Shows best motion-estimation performance on most metrics across Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey, with competitive geometry results on five datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the framework. SM4RT is a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction. It first performs geometry reconstruction using a DUSt3R backbone (blue modules), then feeds the predicted 3D geometry into a transformer-based decoder followed by a DPT head to estimate motion (red modules). SM4RT trains the network with a fully-supervised regression loss Lconf based on ground-truth dynamic point maps and object flow; at the same time, it incorporates a weakly-supervised Chamfer loss LCD that regularizes unlabeled point motion based on labeled point positions from the other time step, to handle the sparsity of motion labels.

Figure 5. Visual results of motion estimation. From left to right, we present the input image, object flow predicted by MonST3R [61], DynaDUSt3R [21], SM4RT, and the ground-truth object flow. The top and bottom row show the input image pair at two time steps. The experiment is conducted on Kubric-F dataset. The output motions of MonST3R and DynaDUSt3R are noisy and incorrect. In contrast, SM4RT is the best among all models for dynamic scene reconstruction.
Figure 9. Visualizations of predicted point clouds and object flow from SM4RT.

Figure 4. Weakly-supervised Chamfer loss with voxelization. Left: We propose a weakly-supervised Chamfer loss, LCD, to supervise a point set 𝑃1 using another point set ?̃?2 without requiring point correspondences. By voxelizing the 3D Euclidean space, we compute the Chamfer loss within each voxel, approximating nearest-neighbor search while filtering invalid matches. Right: The top row shows outputs from a model trained without the Chamfer loss, while the bottom row shows outputs when it is used. The proposed weakly-supervised loss significantly improves dynamic scene reconstruction.

Figure 2. Visualization of object flow and scene flow. Given two video frames 𝐼1 and 𝐼2, we compare two motion representations: object flow and scene flow. The bottom-left panel shows the object flow of frame 𝐼1, where blue arrows indicate object motion. The bottomright panel shows the scene flow of 𝐼1, which additionally includes camera motion, indicated by green arrows. Object flow is less ambiguous than scene flow.

Figure 6. Visualization on TUM RGB-D SLAM Benchmark. The top image shows the first frame with object flow, while the bottom image shows the point map obtained by moving the first point map with the predicted object flow 𝑃1 (𝑡2, 𝜋1).

Figure 7. Visualizations on scale of pixel-wise scene flow and static confidence map. Left: Input images. Middle: Visualization of the predicted object flow’s 𝐿2 norm. This heatmap highlights motion magnitude, allowing for a clear distinction between dynamic and static regions. Right: Confidence maps generated by the flow prediction head. As static areas exhibit significantly higher confidence scores compared to dynamic ones, we further leverage this property to identify stable regions for relative pose estimation.
Figure 8. Visualization of the flow magnitude. The second row shows the predicted flow with the ground-truth in the third row.
Table 4. Training dataset overview. We utilize various ground truth annotations to derive both ground truth and pseudo-ground truth object flow, enabling the training of our dynamic model.

Table 3. Ablation studies on model components. We train and evaluate each component of our model on the Waymo dataset. Both the proposed weakly-supervised Chamfer loss and the injection of predicted 3D point positions into the motion estimator using RoPE [40] are essential for strong performance.

Table 2. Depth Evaluation from 2-View Input. We test on 5 established datasets: Sintel [4], Point Odyssey [62], Bonn [34], Kubric [14], and KITTI [12]. Our method maintains comparable performance on depth estimation meanwhile excels on dynamic motion estimation.

Table 1. Evaluation of motion estimation. We test on 3 dynamic scene datasets: Kubric-F [14], Waymo [42] and Point Odyssey [62]. We adopt three metrics: end-point error of object flow, relative point cloud err Lrel, and relative pose transformation. SM4RT matches top performance in dynamic point map estimation, and outperforms state of the art methods in other metrics.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a feed-forward cascade for 4D dynamic scene reconstruction, combining 3D geometry and motion estimation from RGB video.
papers.title: SM4RT: Cascaded Feed-forward Model for 4D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: SM4RT cascades 3D geometry reconstruction and camera-frame motion estimation, using weak supervision to improve dynamic-scene reconstruction from RGB videos.

papers.abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.
bullets: Existing memory failures stem from outdated evidence, mixing patients’ facts, and missing safety-critical information.
MedGraph extracts dated facts, assigns them to the correct person, and links diagnoses, medications, and measurements into state chains.
Retrieval selects the relevant patient chains at the time asked about, supplements them with original dialogue, and checks recorded safety facts.
On MedMemoryBench, it achieved the highest accuracy with both GPT and Qwen backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 10.5 and 10.4 points.
The study focuses on longitudinal medical dialogue and reports efficient construction and answering in the GPT setting.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MedGraph overview. (a) Construction: clinical facts are extracted from each session and linked to the person they describe in the fact graph (L2). Medication, condition, lab, and vital facts form chains by entity, subject, and type, following insertion order, with the patient’s and other people’s facts kept separate. (b) Retrieval: the system ranks the patient’s records, treating each chain as one unit and each fact outside a chain as an individual unit. For selected chains, it includes the matched fact, the state at the requested time, and the preceding record. It also adds causally linked facts, records from any explicitly requested date window, and original dialogue excerpts. The answer model receives the question, the assembled evidence, and the patient profile (L3), then generates an answer in one LLM call.

Figure 5: Accuracy against cost (GPT backbone): (a, b) LLM calls and input tokens spent constructing memory; (c) seconds per question, the wall-clock time from the question to the answer string, including the method’s retrieval and the reader’s generation and excluding judging. papers.tldr: MedGraph improves longitudinal medical dialogue by preserving patient-specific, time-aware clinical state and safety facts in graph memory.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.
bullets: Targets brittle VLA behavior in shifted, safety-critical real-world settings.
Probes latent layers of a VLA backbone with minimal inference overhead and supervises pre-failure trajectory segments.
Improves early detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline.
Maintains valid missed-detection and false-alarm bounds in up to 86% of unseen-task runs, versus at most 21% for baselines.
Predicts failure modes, improving unseen-task top-3 accuracy by up to 44% over a majority baseline; includes 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Steering demonstrations showing failure scores and corrections for simulated and real-world tasks. When the probe’s predicted failure score rises above the threshold, the VLA policy is automatically paused. papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses runtime failure prediction and classification for Vision-Language-Action models in embodied deployment.
papers.title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
papers.tldr: VLA-Tug is a lightweight, calibrated latent probe that detects and classifies impending VLA failures early under distribution shift, enabling real-time corrective steering.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.
bullets: Targets high VLA inference cost and distraction from redundant visual tokens, especially across multiple cameras and under distribution shift.
Uses segmentation-guided pruning to remove irrelevant patches, followed by saliency-guided attention biasing over retained visual tokens and language instructions.
On LIBERO-Spatial, removes 85% of scene-camera tokens while essentially matching unpruned success and improves OOD success by up to 7 percentage points.
Adds 7.8 ms per inference call for refinement and achieves up to 3.3× LLM-forward speedup at higher input resolutions.
Across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones, benefits are strongest in multi-camera settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-stage T3R pipeline. Stage 1 (pruning): POS-weighted SigLIP text–patch similarity localizes the target; the topscoring patch positions (with SigLIP/DINOv2 features) prompt EfficientTAM to produce an object mask, which is converted to a patch-level pruning decision while preserving original RoPE positions, so only the “interested tokens” enter the LLM. Stage 2 (biasing): Integrated Gradients over the instruction identifies salient words; an additive attention bias (𝛽=2.0) is injected into the middle decoder layers for action-token queries, steering attention toward salient text tokens and retained visual patches before the action chunk is decoded.

Figure 4: OOD robustness under object-placement perturbation (21 noise levels, 10 episodes/task). T3R (Full Pipeline) tracks the unpruned baseline for small shifts and pulls ahead beyond ∼2 cm, leading by up to 7 pp at 4 cm, while TeamVLA degrades fastest. The crossover is consistent with pruning reducing misleading background context.

Figure 3: Most visual tokens are near-inert. (a) Across all 32 decoder layers, 93.9% of visual tokens receive <0.2% of the action queries’ attention each. (b) Per-patch action-query attention concentrates on a few task-relevant patches (here the gripper and target bowls), while the background receives negligible weight.

Figure 2: Qualitative pruning on a sparse LIBERO-Spatial scene (“pick up the bowl between the plate and the ramekin”). Top: input, POS-weighted SigLIP similarity, and the EfficientTAMmask with its point prompts. Middle: T3R keeps only 13/256 patches (95% pruned), tightly localized on the target. Bottom: TeamVLA’s similarity+expansion+merge retains 226/256 (12% pruned), leaving most of the background in the sequence through the early decoder layers.

Table 2: Cross-backbone generalization. Left: CogACT on SIMPLER (single camera), average SR (%); each keep ratio corresponds to the respective method’s native operating point. Right: 𝜋0.5 on RoboTwin (three cameras), SR (%) vs. per-camera token budget (base = 33.3). Best per column/row in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token pruning and attention biasing for efficient, robust VLA robot inference; directly fits VLA and token pruning topics.
papers.title: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
papers.tldr: T3R enables faster and more robust VLA inference by pruning irrelevant visual tokens and biasing attention toward action-critical regions without training.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical coordination in humanoid robots trained as solitary agents.
Uses a hierarchical system with shared-token sequence modeling for reactive and anticipatory human–robot motion generation.
Combines high-level motion generation with a low-level whole-body tracking controller for robot execution.
Introduces adaptive retargeting that preserves contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale.
Builds a 260-hour Human-Humanoid Interaction benchmark from five motion-capture datasets and demonstrates coordinated behavior in simulation and the real world.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Social Humanoid Architecture. From RGB-D observations of a human partner (red), we reconstruct the human pose and localize the body in 3D using depth and estimated gravity. Relative human and humanoid states are encoded through the VQ-VAE encoders Eh and Er. The resulting latent motion tokens z∗, relative pose transforms T ∗, and canonical motion transforms ∆T ∗ are concatenated and processed by the DFoT policy, then decoded via Dh and Dr to future human behavior (blue) and socially coordinated humanoid motion (purple). SONIC executes the motion in sim or the real-world, and the robot state is updated for closed-loop interaction.

Figure 5: Retargeting Qualitative Results. Each panel shows a ground-truth human–human interaction (ego in orange, partner in dark blue) next to its retargeted counterpart. The ego is retargeted to the humanoid (tan), and the partner’s pose is morphed to preserve interaction (light blue). Across diverse interactions our Adaptive-HHI Retargeting method preserves the contacts and relative positioning between the two agents.

Figure 6: Real-world deployment. Frames run left to right in time. Top two rows: separate highfive and hand-wave trials. Bottom: a single continuous take in which the humanoid transitions directly from a handshake into a bend

Figure 7: Shadow teleoperation. The G1 shadows a human operator performing arm movements (top) and sitting down on a couch (bottom). The operator’s motion is encoded with Eh, quantized against the shared codebook C, and decoded with Dr into humanoid motion. Frames run left to right in time.

Figure 3: Shared-Codebook VQ-VAE. Human and humanoid motion sequences are independently encoded into latent features and mapped to a shared vector-quantized codebook that learns a common motion vocabulary across embodiments. Embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct the respective motions, enabling aligned, transferable motion representations between humans and humanoids.

Figure 4: Adaptive-HHI Retargeting. Our retargeting pipeline starts from two ground truth humans. In the first pass, we retarget the ego human (orange) to the humanoid using a contact-adaptive weight matrix to encourage body pose in regions close to the physical interaction to be preserved. In a second pass, we co-morph the partner’s pose towards more plausible interaction via a contactgated morphing strategy driven by the amount of physical contact present in the interaction.

Figure A.1: Cross-embodiment motion translation with a shared-codebook VQ-VAE. Human motion (red) is encoded into a discrete latent space shared between the human and humanoid embodiments, then decoded into humanoid motion (purple). Each example shows three frames of the input human motion alongside the translated humanoid motion in simulation (top row), and the same frames executed on the physical humanoid robot (bottom row).
Table 3: Retargeting comparison across three interaction datasets. Best per column in bold; ↑/↓ indicate higher/lower is better.

Table A.2: Comparison of retargeting methods. Adaptive-HHI extends OmniRetarget’s interaction-mesh SOCP base with partner co-morphing (joint optimization over the partner SMPLX) and distance-weighted, wrist-boosted adaptive Laplacian weighting for interaction and humanscale preservation.

Table A.4: Retargeting hyperparameters. Values are shared across all datasets without per-clip tuning.
Table A.3: Adaptive retargeting ablation on CHI3D. Mean ± std over clips. Best per column in bold.

Table A.5: Shared-codebook design ablation on HHI. H and R denote human and robot motion; H→R and R→H denote encoding in one embodiment and decoding in the other. FD is Fréchet distance. MPJPE is the root-relative mean per-joint position error of the decoded pose against ground truth (cm; 21 SMPL-X body joints for H, 29 actuated joints of the G1 for R, hands excluded). Code Agree. is the fraction of paired H/R frames assigned the same code. Best per column in bold.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
bullets: GDN-2’s erasure updates are less sensitive than value writes, motivating lower-rank, sensitivity-allocated gating.
Muir fuses gates into a low-rank projection and re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout to reduce interference from high-norm, slow-decaying rows.
A numerically stable parallel update enables efficient training with the large chunks needed for wide matrix units.
Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir reduces perplexity versus GDN-2 and Transformer, improves commonsense accuracy and extractive recall, and matches GDN-2 throughput.
At 1.34B, it supports long-context extrapolation to 10M tokens and near-perfect passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Muir outperforms GDN-2 and Transformer on language modeling and long-context throughput while improving recall over GDN-2. (a) Sensitivity-allocated low-rank gates with FFN expansion drive the bulk of the validation NLL gain over GDN-2, while dynamic matched-filter readout drives the gain on extractive recall. (b) Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir lowers validation NLL by 18.0–20.4 millinats over GDN-2 and 25.0–36.2 millinats over Transformer. (c) On 8 TPU7x chips (0.5M tokens/step) at 1.34B with our chunkwise kernel, Muir matches GDN-2 throughput despite an additional readout gate and a 30.4% wider FFN, and trains 1.64× and 2.74× faster than Transformer at 16K and 32K, respectively.

Figure 6 |Muir improves synthetic single-needle, multi-hop, multi-needle, and real-world retrieval over GDN-2. (a) Averaged across the three single-needle tasks, all Muir variants mitigate the 4K degradation of GDN-2 and extrapolate to 8K, where unextended RoPE Transformer degrades beyond its 4K training window. (b) On 5-hop variable-binding chains, static 𝛾 fails to match the varying hop lags, whereas dynamic 𝛾𝑡 leads all models at every context length. (c, d) When retrieving four values bound to a single key or four distinct keys queried jointly, dynamic 𝛾𝑡 matches or outperforms both GDN-2 and Transformer across 1K–4K. (e) Averaged across the RULER tasks (a–d) by needle depth and context length, Muir achieves the largest gains over GDN-2 on early needles (0–40% depth) at 4K–8K. (f) On real-world document extraction at 2K, Muir improves over GDN-2 on all six tasks, with dynamic 𝛾𝑡 driving 69% of the gain.

Figure 4 | Boundary-pivoted chunkwise kernel eliminates 3D decay tensors, division overflow, and VPU bottlenecks. (a) Memory hierarchy of a TPU7x chip. (b) On the 256× 256 MXU, an unfused 256 × 128 right-hand side 𝑉 achieves only 50% utilization due to zero-padded lanes, whereas the fused solve [︀ 𝑈 𝑌 ]︀ = 𝑇−1 [︀𝑉 ?̂?⊙𝜋 ]︀ achieves 100% utilization. (c) At chunk size 𝐶 = 256, leaf size 8, and 𝑑𝑘 = 𝑑𝑣 = 128, replacing naive 𝐶 × 𝐶 × 𝑑𝑘 3D VPU decay and sequential VPU triangular solves with boundary-pivoted MXU matrix multiplications, recursive block inversion, and a custom backward pass cuts forward-and-backward VPU compute by 24× and total kernel FLOPs by 12%, routing 98% of chunkwise arithmetic onto the MXU. (d) Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution combines pre-permutation VREG fusion for 𝑞𝑡 and 𝑣𝑡, MXU cumulative log-decay, numerically stable VPU decay splitting, recursive block inversion of 𝑇 on the MXU, and a packed MXU scan carrying 𝑆0 → 𝑆𝐶 in VMEM (saving 𝑆0 only for backward).

Figure 3 | Muir co-designs asymmetric low-rank gate parameterization and matched-filter query readout with MXU tile alignment and iso-parameter FFN reallocation. (a) Standard residual block with a Muir token mixer. (b) Within the Muir block, 𝑥𝑡 feeds linear-Conv-SiLU pathways for (𝑞𝑡,𝑘𝑡,𝑣𝑡) alongside a single fused low-rank gate projection that produces all five gates (log𝛼𝑡, 𝑏𝑡, 𝑔𝑡,𝑤𝑡,𝛾𝑡). (c) Asymmetric gate ranks (𝑟𝑓 , 𝑟𝑏, 𝑟𝑔, 𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (64, 64, 128, 128, 128) sum to 𝑅tot = 512 = 2 × 256, which fills two 256-column MXU tiles in the fused down-projection and aligns (𝑓, 𝑏) and (𝑔, 𝑤, 𝑞) on 128-lane VMEM tile boundaries for batched up-projections. (d) At 𝑑 = 2,048, replacing the dense (𝑏, 𝑤) gate matrices in GDN-2 cuts gate-projection parameters by 4.5×; this either reduces per-layer parameters and FLOPs by 14.6% at fixed FFN width, or frees +7.3M parameters per layer to widen the FFN under an iso-parameter budget.

Figure 2 |Matched-filter readout and low-rank erase gates improve synthetic associative retrieval and lower optimal erase strength. (a) Full whitening worsens retrieval error relative to unit gain (GDN-2), whereas half-power scaling and the Corollary 3.8 filter reduce error and shift 𝜇* from 0.60 to 0.50, with the Corollary 3.8 filter matching the static oracle. (b) On a 50/50 mixture of lags ℓ ∈ {2, 80} at 𝜇 = 0.60, the lag-matched oracle outperforms the static oracle across all horizons, while the Proposition 3.6 filter matches the lag-matched oracle at ℓ = 80 and beats the static oracle on long and mixed horizons. (c) Low-rank erase gates 𝑟𝑏 outperform dense gates at every bottleneck rank on long-lag recall, whereas low-rank write gates 𝑟𝑤 degrade below dense at 𝑟𝑤 ≤ 8 and recover once 𝑟𝑤 ≥ 16.

Figure 13 | Muir preserves early variable bindings and routes readout to the target hop at each answer step. (a) On 4-value MV-NIAH, Transformer drops on the final write 𝑉4 and unit-readout recurrences degrade after 𝑉1, whereas Muir remains accurate across 𝑉1–𝑉4. (b) On 5-hop RULER VT, Transformer recalls only the root assignment 𝐻1, whereas Muir maintains accuracy across all five hops 𝐻1–𝐻5. (c) Within-model root-needle (𝐻1) retention in 𝑆𝑡 from write milestone 𝑠1 (100%) to query milestone 𝑡q across 16 held-out prompts (interquartile bands across prompts). (d) Within-model retention of written needles 𝐻1–𝐻5 from each write (100%) across sequence milestones 𝑠1–𝑠5 to 𝑡q. (e) Share of readout weight 𝑞𝑡𝑆𝑡 (over the haystack) on each needle 𝐻1–𝐻5 across the four answer-generation steps 𝐴1–𝐴4 that chain 𝐻1 → · · · → 𝐻5.

Figure 10 | Trained models exhibit the predicted write-erase sensitivity asymmetry under both SVD rank truncation and causal gate freezing. (a) Truncating each rank-128 gate projection of the uniform-rank Muir checkpoint via SVD (one gate at a time across all layers) shows that the decay (𝑓) and erase (𝑏) gates saturate by rank 64, whereas the output (𝑔), write (𝑤), and readout gain (𝑞) gates require rank 128. (b) Replacing the dynamic write gate with its token-averaged channel mean (𝑤𝑡 ← ?̄?) across all layers degrades validation NLL 14.5× more than freezing the erase gate (𝑏𝑡 ← ?̄?) in both GDN-2 and Muir.

Figure 5 |Muir consistently lowers validation NLL relative to GDN-2 and Transformer throughout 100B-token pretraining. Held-out FineWeb-Edu validation token NLL difference relative to GDN-2 across 166M–1.34B parameters as a function of training tokens. All three Muir variants improve over GDN-2 within the first 10B tokens and reach a 12–20 mnat reduction by 100B tokens, while static and dynamic matched-filter readout provide additional reductions over Muir (no 𝛾).

Figure 7 | Muir extrapolates to 128K-token documents and 10M-token streams with the lowest perplexity at a constant 25 MB state. (a, c) Zero-shot from 4K pretraining, Dynamic YaRN Transformer diverges past 8K and unchunked evaluation exceeds HBM at ≥128K, while Muir (static 𝛾) drifts upward past 32K; dynamic 𝛾𝑡 avoids this static-gain drift and outperforms GDN-2 across 128K documents and 10M-token streams (2,560× training length). (b, d) After a 64K cooldown (0.3% of pretraining), Transformer improves through 64K before unchunked evaluation exceeds HBM at ≥ 128K, static-𝛾 drift vanishes, and all Muir variants improve monotonically below GDN-2 through 10M tokens (160× beyond cooldown).

Figure 8 | Static matched-filter readout extends passkey retrieval to 1M tokens both zero-shot and after a 64K cooldown. S-NIAH-1 accuracy across 10 needle-depth bins and context lengths 1K–1M (256× pretraining length) at 1.34B scale under (top) zero-shot evaluation from 4K pretraining and (bottom) pure-text continual cooldown at 64K. Cooldown extends Dynamic YaRN Transformer from 8K to 32K before early-depth accuracy drops at 64K and unchunked prefill exceeds HBM at ≥128K, whereas recurrent horizons change little under pure-text cooldown: GDN-2 collapses past 4K–8K, Muir (no 𝛾) fades past 32K, Muir (dynamic 𝛾𝑡, splitting (𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (128, 128) for multi-lag recall) holds through 32K before tapering at ≥64K, and Muir (static 𝛾, keeping 𝑟𝑤 = 256 for single-lag lookup) maintains near-perfect recall to 1M tokens in both regimes.

Figure 9 | Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution eliminates decay overflow and maintains wellconditioned forward and backward passes. (a) Against an exact float64 sequential reference, naive unpivoted float32 decay factorization overflows and produces NaN on 25% of heads, whereas the boundarypivoted bfloat16 and float32 kernels match the reference to machine precision on both chunk outputs and final state. (b) Across synthetic stress regimes spanning 𝜅2(𝑇 ) ∈ [1, 104], the bfloat16 block-Neumann inverse stays near its precision floor throughout the well-conditioned regime (𝜅2(𝑇 ) < 40, shaded), which contains the sampled 100B-token checkpoints of GDN-2 and Muir (markers show medians). (c) Single-layer backward gradients (𝑇 =128, 𝐶=64, 𝑑𝑘=16) match the float64 reference across all six inputs without log-decay drift.

Figure 11 | Stationary state row energies obey the closed-form law and are balanced by fractional power-law readout gains. (a) Across state channels, the analytical fixed point 𝑚* 𝑗 (5) closely tracks measured stationary row energy 𝑚𝑗 = E[‖𝑆𝑡,𝑗,:‖22] in both GDN-2 and Muir. (b) Across all heads, weighting state rows by the learned readout gain compresses the within-head p90/p10 energy spread by 35% relative to GDN-2. (c) Within each head, learned static gains |𝛾𝑗 | follow a fractional power law 𝛾𝑗 ∝ 𝜌−𝑝 𝑗 (𝑝 = 0.35) of stationary row RMS 𝜌𝑗 , intermediate between unit readout (𝑝 = 0) and full whitening (𝑝 = 1).

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 2D vision-language pre-training and reliable 3D robotic manipulation.
Jointly trains action prediction with alignment between VLA visual features and a frozen 3D perception model.
Unifies heterogeneous robot datasets across embodiments, tasks, scenes, and geometric annotations.
Uses feature-dependent layer aggregation, partial depth/calibration, and probabilistic state dropout to improve spatial supervision and visual reliance.
Training-only auxiliary components enable direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights without changing inference.
