papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.
bullets: Addresses the sensitivity of imitation-learned visuomotor policies to camera and robot-base viewpoint changes in mobile manipulation.
Separately reconstructs static scenes and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting and feed-forward 3D foundation models.
Uses kinematics-based action retargeting to render novel viewpoints and pair them with geometrically consistent transformed actions.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, plus simulation-based fidelity validation.
More than doubles average success over the strongest baseline and retains non-trivial success at large base displacements where baselines fail.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MOMASPLAT. 3D Reconstruction: We build 3D models of the environment from the navigation and manipulation data. For the dynamic objects, we segment each manipulated object and estimate its per-frame pose trajectory with a feed-forward 3D foundation model; since the scene and object poses lie in separate reference frames, we align them with a Sim(3) transformation and fit a separate object model Gobj. Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses: Given a robot base pose, T̃ , sampled around the original demonstration poses (left), we render the scene and object from the new viewpoint, transform the source end-effector trajectory into the new base frame to render the robot from a simulator, and composite the three streams into a photorealistic novel observation. Paired with the transformed actions ã1:Lj , this forms a synthetic demonstration; repeating across sampled poses yields the generated dataset. Imitation Learning: the policy is trained on the union of source and generated demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.
bullets: Supports cameras, event cameras, SPAD/LiDAR, iToF/dToF, and thermal sensors in a unified framework.
Models raw physical measurement processes with fine-grained sensor-parameter control.
Reproduces modality-specific effects such as pileup, glare, phase wrapping, saturation, motion artifacts, refractory drops, and history-dependent emission.
Enables controlled cross-modality comparisons on shared scenes and trajectories.
Provides a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Multi-modal, high-fidelity and controllable sensor emulation. Robotic simulation pipelines often focus on scene content, overlooking physically accurate sensor modeling. VisionSIM aims to bridge this gap by emulating diverse sensor types and their failure modes. (Top) A single scene is rendered once with dense ground truth — color, depth, optical flow, surface normals, segmentation, point map, direct and indirect illumination, and a temperature map. (Middle) The same scene is then replayed through a breadth of sensor models. (Bottom) Each model exposes and enables sweeping across the sensor’s physical parameters (e.g., thermal time constant, correlation function, event thresholds), thereby reproducing modality-specific failure modes.

papers.abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.
bullets: Targets online 3D bin packing with unknown arrivals, jointly selecting boxes, orientations, and placements while avoiding stack collapse.
Uses a 3D U-Net to predict placement stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives.
Integrates stability estimates into a discrete actor–critic’s action values and policy prior, with gates for unreliable or changing predictions.
Reaches 73% utilization in 0.4M Isaac Gym steps versus about 1M without stability modeling; on 60 boxes, achieves 0.734 utilization versus 0.588 for GOPT.
Shows higher placement-failure frequency than GOPT (1.03% vs. 0.63%), and is demonstrated on a real robot without added deployment search or simulation overhead.

papers.abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–memory/bandwidth tradeoff in 2–4-bit weights and 2–3-bit KV-cache quantization.
Co-designs precision representation, selection, and delivery, overlapping transfers with computation and reusing fetched precision across decoding steps.
On 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while retaining 95.4% of quantized-base throughput on an RTX 5090.
With 2-bit weights and KV cache, improves Qwen3-8B AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use.
At 128K context, 3-bit weights plus 2-bit KV matches the reported perplexity and speed of 4-bit AWQ plus 8-bit KV while using approximately half the GPU memory.

papers.selection_reason: Low-bit LLM inference with selective precision streaming and KV-cache quantization; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
papers.tldr: StrataFlux recovers much of the accuracy lost by ultra-low-bit LLM quantization by streaming selective higher-precision data from host memory and storage without sacrificing most inference speed or GPU-memory savings.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc
bullets: Addresses the sequential evaluation bottleneck in exact continuous-time sampling, where independent parallel token sampling can disrupt dependencies.
Uses previously computed model predictions to propose successive updates, evaluates intermediate states in parallel, and applies exact acceptance-and-correction.
Requires no separate draft model and no training.
Theoretical analysis shows preservation of event times, generation order, and token values, avoiding discretization and added factorization errors.
Experiments on two diffusion language models and five benchmarks reduce sequential model evaluations by 1.73–4.38× while preserving the reference sampling distribution.

papers.abstract: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team's estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift. In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across $1000$ simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from $0.542$m to $0.140$m in a $50\times50$m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.
bullets: Addresses drift in team position and orientation that relative odometry and inter-robot measurements cannot resolve.
Converts radio attenuation residuals into Gaussian information matrices and vectors for integration with pose estimation.
Models detectable shared motions and preserves robot–time correlations when the map is uncertain.
Matches joint-estimation results across 1,000 simulated Gaussian trials.
In 32 paired registered-map trials, reduced common-position RMSE from 0.542 m to 0.140 m versus a radio-weighted relative-measurement baseline.

papers.abstract: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough. Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory. Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress). Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.
bullets: Built a Gymnasium testbed that simulates ultrasound from public patient CT data.
Provides replaceable slots for organ segmentation, control, and reward methods.
Evaluated 20 published methods across 60 episodes from six held-out patients.
Only an SSIM-based reward improved the guide detectably; the final baseline reached 13.7 mm error versus 1.5 mm for a pose oracle.
Results are exploratory, simulation-only, and no guide was tested on hardware.

papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop ultrasound probe guidance testbed with replaceable controller/reward components; relevant to visuomotor control and robot learning.
papers.title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
papers.tldr: USB Gym shows that combining existing ultrasound guidance methods does not yet reliably move a simulated probe close to a target view.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave radar resolves the micrometer displacements of a moving body as micro-Doppler, enabling gait, gesture, activity, pose and vital-sign sensing. Each task relies on a downstream model trained on real data, yet radar datasets lag orders of magnitude behind vision and language. Brute-force collection will not close that gap, and existing synthesis methods (forward-only simulators, learned generators and static-scene inverse renderers) cannot fit a real capture of a moving body, leaving a sim2real gap. We present 4D Point Splatting (4DPS), a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture. Using the synchronized camera to initialize the room and body, we represent the scene as oriented points carrying material, normal and velocity, and splat each point into range and Doppler bins. Our output is the raw complex return a real radar records, so we apply the same signal processing on the rendered data to obtain any representation for training any SOTA downstream model. We fit 235 sequences on HuPR and 100 on RT-Pose, two datasets with different radars. Our reconstructions set the state of the art, with median correlations of 0.940 and 0.830 on range-azimuth, 0.829 and 0.695 on range-Doppler, and 0.988 and 0.966 on micro-Doppler. Our renders also set the state of the art in downstream sim2real gap. On RT-Pose, a pose model trained on them reaches 21.9 cm MPJPE on real data, against 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the RF-Genesis baseline, where both the rendered- and real-trained models learn nearly the same features. Our custom CUDA kernels fit a sequence in 5.7 minutes on HuPR and 12.9 on RT-Pose on one H100, making dataset-scale inverse rendering of mmWave radar possible for the first time. This work can enable synthetic data generation for any human-centered downstream task and model, and scene editing for data augmentation.
bullets: Addresses the shortage of mmWave radar datasets and the sim2real gap for moving-body sensing.
Represents scenes with oriented points carrying material, surface normal, and velocity, then splats them into range–Doppler bins.
Renders raw complex radar returns, allowing standard signal processing and training for diverse downstream models.
Achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction correlations on HuPR and RT-Pose across range-azimuth, range-Doppler, and micro-Doppler representations.
Enables dataset-scale inverse rendering, fitting sequences in minutes on a single H100 and improving real-data pose performance over a prior rendering baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable 4D point-splatting renderer for mmWave radar; transferable to 3D scene representation and synthetic data generation.
papers.title: 4D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Micro-Doppler Differentiable Rendering
papers.tldr: 4D Point Splatting is a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits moving human scenes to real mmWave radar captures, enabling realistic synthetic data generation and improved sim2real performance.

papers.abstract: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-ν_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
bullets: Nearest-neighbor preservation alone can miss large-scale structural errors: high local fidelity may still move many passages between themes.
The study evaluates local fidelity at 10 neighbors and global fidelity across 30–50% of the memory.
A bound links global fidelity to near–far rank violations, which closely track compression distance noise.
Locality-aware quantization (LAQ) adds a far-end hinge objective to OPQ codebooks while preserving bytes, rotation, and search.
LAQ improved global fidelity in all 52 held-out runs, led seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scaled to one million passages, and preserved evidence recall.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. At the same bytes, a compression that keeps more nearest neighbors can displace more of the overall memory, because retrieval follows L whereas themes and deletion follow G (local and global fidelity). (a) 27 compressions of FinQA (BGE-base) alongside four nonlinear maps (rings: Isomap [56], NPCA [57], PHATE [55], t-SNE); triangle: PCA to 16 dimensions. Rescored binary codes lie 0.32 below the diagonal G = L, while t-SNE, PHATE, and UMAP keep G at 0.22 or less. (b, c) Two 96-byte compressions plotted on the uncompressed memory layout; colored points mark passages moved to another theme: 1.7 percent for PCA with 8-bit codes versus 10.1 percent for rescored binary codes. (d, e) Across every compression and run, retrieval follows L (median Spearman ρ 0.99; partial 0.97 given G), whereas themes and deletion follow G (ρ 0.95; partial 0.79 given L). (f, g) Rescoring the 40 nearest binary codes raises L and top-10 agreement while leaving G, themes, and deletion unchanged at the binary values (black ticks). All runs: Appendix C.

Fig. 1. At the same bytes and search, locality-aware quantization (LAQ) keeps the near end of an optimized product quantizer (OPQ) and moves fewer passages to another theme. L: local fidelity (chance-corrected recall@10); G: global fidelity (the profile averaged over 30 to 50 percent of the memory). (a) Multi-Doc-2025 [11], BGE-large [12]: 2,688 held-out passages of 22 companies, each joined to its 10 nearest neighbors and colored by theme (t-SNE layout [13]); companies form islands, and banks share themes. (b, c) At 128 bytes, both keep L at 0.85; OPQ moves 8.3 percent of the passages to another theme (red) and LAQ 3.5 percent, on the split where OPQ has its lowest theme agreement; over 16 runs the mean falls from 2.8 to 2.1 percent. (d, e) Locality profiles (Definition 1) of five compressions of FinQA [14] and LoCoMo [15]: compressions of equal size agree near k = 10 and part by up to 0.30 in the G band (gray). (f) Every lost–gained neighbor pair is a violated cross pair, which bounds the profile (Theorem 1). (g) LAQ in four steps; gray: cost of each step (Section 4). (h) LAQ minus OPQ on all 52 held-out runs: G rises in all 52 and L in 46.

Fig. 5. Compressions of one memory spread off a single curve, and rescored binary codes lie furthest below the diagonal, by 0.21 to 0.41. L and G of 27 compressions of the two agent memories, three retrieval-tuned encoders; Figure 6 gives the other three. Dashed line: G = L; shaded: less of the far end kept than of the near end.

Fig. 12. The normal model of Proposition 4 holds in the G band and predicts its violations and its loss of profile. All 52 held-out runs; open markers, OPQ start; filled, LAQ. (a) Median error of each anchor’s standardized distance quantile against the normal quantile, in standard deviations, at the near end and in the G band. (b) The full integral (8) against the measured violation rate at k = 0.4n. (c) The leading term at k = 10 against the measured rate. (d) Measured 1− νk at k = 0.4n against the mean relative distance noise ω; solid line, Corollary 2; dashed line, its leading term 0.64ω (Appendix A).

Fig. 3. At the same bytes, OPQ keeps the far end best, and LAQ raises it further on every held-out memory by lowering rank violations (L, G: local and global fidelity). (a, b) Seven compressions at d/8 bytes on FinQA and LoCoMo with the retrieval-tuned encoders: OPQ has the highest G (0.82 to 0.91), whereas rescoring (arrows to open markers) raises L and top-10 agreement but leaves G and the far-end operations unchanged. (c–f) Held-out Multi-Doc-2025 across four splits: LAQ lies above OPQ at every scale, most notably in the G band (gray) and with Titan V2; the bound of Theorem 1 holds at all 160 points, with 1− νk at 0.49 to 0.60 of it; and LAQ lowers the violation rate at k ≈ 0.4n by 12 to 18 percent on average (10 to 20 percent per run). (g) Change in each operation across all 40 held-out runs; right: runs in which LAQ is higher. (h) LAQ (black) has the highest G among seven quantizers in each of nine runs with the retrieval-tuned encoders. (i) The lowest theme agreement rises from 0.80 to 0.89.

Fig. 4. The far hinge carries the gain in G, and LAQ is better than OPQ and the other quantizers in paired tests. (a) Change in G from the OPQ start for each training objective on all 52 held-out runs; bars are means. (b) LAQ against reconstruction with Lfar alone, run by run. (c) Mean change in νk by scale with the retrieval-tuned encoders; shading, interquartile range; gray, the G band. (d) Reduction of the violation rate p̄k at k ≈ 0.4n relative to OPQ. (e) Change in L against change in G; large markers are means. (f) One-sided Wilcoxon tests of LAQ against OPQ over runs, Holm-corrected, with the runs in which LAQ is higher; evidence recall@10 is tested two-sided. (g) G of LAQ minus that of each quantizer on Multi-Doc-2025, 12 runs. (h) Paired company-bootstrap 95 percent intervals for G, LAQ minus OPQ.

Fig. 10. On the topic corpora, PCA and product quantization lie on or above the diagonal (a–f). On FinQA, rescored binary codes keep neighbors yet move up to 39 percent of a company’s passages to another theme (g). (a–f) L and G of 27 compressions, three encoders of other kinds; dotted line: G = L. (g) The two 96-byte compressions of FinQA (BGE-base) by company; diamonds: means; dotted line: 20 percent moved.

Fig. 11. At d/8 bytes, OPQ keeps the highest G of seven compressions, and rescored binary codes keep a high L with a lower G. Fidelity and agreement with the uncompressed memory, retrieval-tuned encoders; (a–c) FinQA, (d–f) LoCoMo.

papers.abstract: We introduce GPWM, a Generative Particle World Model that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction. GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments. GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average. Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains. GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties, object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint actuator-object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained actions, planning searches the model's latent noise for interactions that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model, noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific policies.
bullets: Models rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials in passive and robotic-interaction settings with one representation and architecture.
Uses an object-aware multi-resolution transformer with flow matching and diffusion forcing to generate coherent long-horizon trajectories.
Trained and evaluated on the 25.5-million-frame ParticleWorlds corpus spanning varied geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments.
Reduces prediction error by 31% on average across six physical domains versus the strongest prior learned-dynamics baseline, while generalizing beyond training conditions.
Enables noise-space planning for pushing and picking, outperforming action-space search without reference trajectories or goal-specific policies.

figures.caption: Figure 2 GPWM architecture. Noisy per-particle tokens, which embed displacement, actuator motion, geometry, physical parameters, and material, pass through a multi-resolution DiT. PointNet++ layers pool particles into per-object anchors on the way down and interpolate back on the way up, and long skips connect matching levels. Each block (right) applies temporal attention, 3D relative spatial attention, and pointwise feed-forward layers, modulated by AdaLN-Zero from the per-frame noise level τ , and the network outputs clean future displacements.

Figure 1 GPWM learns 3D particle dynamics across six physical domains. Top: samples from the six domains of ParticleWorlds. Middle: given the observed frames and a noisy future, a U-shaped multi-resolution spatio-temporal transformer denoises the future motion of every particle. Bottom: GPWM (the better of its specialist and unified models in each domain) lowers prediction error relative to the strongest baseline in every domain, by 31% on average, rolls out 55× past its 16-frame training window, simulates 3D dynamics from images, and plans via guided diffusion, succeeding at picking where action-space search fails.

papers.abstract: Much of human culture is tacit and is typically learned through situated social interaction. As LLMs are deployed as interactive agents across diverse communities, assessing their cultural competence demands moving beyond existing question-answering approaches, shifting from what they know to how they adapt. In this work, we broaden the scope of cultural adaptation in NLP by investigating whether LLMs can adapt through repeated interactions via a sandbox environment. By reframing cultural adaptation as a continuous process of norm assimilation through social interaction, our work demonstrates that memory mechanisms foster longitudinal learning across repeated interactions, facilitate transfer to different social settings, and enable multilingual norm assimilation across five languages. Together, our findings lay the groundwork for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.
bullets: Frames cultural adaptation as continuous norm assimilation through situated interaction.
Uses a sandbox environment to study adaptation over repeated interactions.
Finds that memory mechanisms support longitudinal learning and transfer across social settings.
Demonstrates multilingual norm assimilation across five languages.
Establishes a foundation for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.

papers.abstract: Hand avatar reconstruction typically relies on multi-view capture or per-subject optimization, limiting its scalability. We introduce InstantHand, a feed-forward framework that constructs an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from a single image using off-the-shelf MANO, camera, and mask estimates, without test-time optimization. Image-averaged losses provide insufficient supervision for alpha leakage, which thickens thin finger contours. To address this issue, we propose a Soft Alpha Band regularizer that concentrates supervision on silhouette boundaries. Furthermore, colors regressed from image features can drift toward a learned prior even in observed regions. Our Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer preserves observed appearance by transferring source colors according to each Gaussian's rendering contribution, while completing unobserved regions using the learned prior conditioned on global source identity. InstantHand constructs an avatar in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matching per-subject-optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M and remaining competitive in zero-shot evaluation on HanCo.
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of multi-view capture and per-subject optimization.
Uses feed-forward reconstruction with off-the-shelf MANO, camera, and mask estimates.
Introduces Soft Alpha Band regularization to sharpen thin finger boundaries and reduce alpha leakage.
Uses Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer to preserve visible colors and complete unseen regions with a learned prior.
Builds avatars in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matching optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M and remaining competitive zero-shot on HanCo.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Avatars reconstructed from fully estimated inputs (SAM 3 mask, WiLoR MANO and camera) for original and edited source images. Top: an unseen InterHand2.6M test subject, with hand-drawn tattoos composited onto the source image. Bottom: an in-the-wild image released with OHTA [23], with its skin tone darkened by an image generation model. Edited rows reuse the mask, MANO, and camera of the original row, and each column shows the same pose and view.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison with prior methods on InterHand2.6M [48] (top three rows) and HanCo [55] (bottom two rows). Columns: GT, HandAvatar, OHTA, BIGS∗, Ours; the black box marks the input image.

Figure 2: Overview of InstantHand. A frozen DINOv3 encoder provides image features Fs that serve as keys and values for a conditional transformer, whose query tokens are point-embedded MANO-surface anchors obtained from the MANO layer (β,θmean). The resulting geometry and appearance tokens are decoded by scale, offset, and color heads into a canonical Gaussian hand Gcan with fixed rotation r0 and opacity α0. Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer then composes local source evidence and a global source identity under the source mask Ms to update only the Gaussian colors (c0i →c∗i ), and the avatar is animated by MANO-driven deformation W and rendered by R.

Figure 3: Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer. The Stage-1 appearance prior is refined with Gaussian footprint-aligned local evidence (Prior Refinement) and conditioned on the global source identity, which also generates a source-conditioned prior bank (Identity Conditioning). The composed representation is decoded into an observed color, an appearance gate, and a source-level shift (Appearance Prediction), and Appearance Composition blends these with the base colors under the reliability γi to produce the final Gaussian colors c∗i . Dashed arrows denote conditioning. Three further inputs of Eq. 11 are omitted for clarity. The source identity also enters Prior Refinement, and the local evidence and base colors also enter Identity Conditioning.

papers.abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
bullets: Criteria Exposure (CE) gives agents access to success criteria originally designed to verify imitation-learned policies.
With CE, the self-improving agent quickly achieves higher success under the provided criteria.
This advantage disappears when criteria are slightly changed, and skills transfer poorly across tasks.
Instruction-faithful criteria better reflect whether agent-generated programs complete the instructed task.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the self-improvement loop. Left, learning: the actor (GPT-6 Astra, high reasoning effort) writes and executes Python cells that call the robot’s primitives on five development layouts, and sees the result of each cell. Between batches the learner (Claude Code with Opus 5.5, high reasoning effort) turns the evidence into one revision of the library ℒ𝑘 , whose skills are callable code that reports what it did and whose memory entries say when to apply what, with the evidence for it; a revision is usually tried first in verification rollouts, and the loop rolls back to the best revision so far when a batch falls clearly below it. Whether the learner also sees the success criteria is the one switch between the two settings, w/ CE and w/o CE (the switch under the learner). Right, evaluation: the final library ℒ𝐾 is frozen and read-only, and the same actor runs alone on layouts the loop never saw.

Figure 1 Learning the task or the verifier? (a): in press_by_number, the criteria 𝐶orig verify a button protocol that the instruction does not state (highlighted). Without Criteria Exposure (w/o CE) the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded; with it (w/ CE) it also reads the criteria code, score and stages. Right of each setting: the test successes of its library on 20 layouts, judged by 𝐶orig and by the instruction-faithful criteria 𝐶faith. (b): libraries learned under 𝐶orig on the 16 criteria-limited tasks, 320 test episodes each, with every episode judged by both criteria (section 4.2.1). The lead of w/ CE under 𝐶orig, 51.6% against 27.8%, is gone under 𝐶faith (45.0% against 47.2%).
Figure 5 Each exposed library judged by the criteria it read and by the other. Both on the ten tasks ofℒfaith CE , seed-0 test, 200 episodes per library. ℒorig

Figure 3 Development success by round, on the 16 criteria-limited and the 9 faithful tasks. Dashed: w/ CE; solid: w/o CE; round 0 is the empty library. On criteria-limited tasks both settings start at 6% and part in round 1 (40% against 28%); after that the success-only learner barely moves and ends at 31%, against 55% with exposure. On faithful tasks the success-only learner is ahead through round 4 and both end above 90% (91% and 95%); its lead, at most 16 points, is close to the 14-point gap of round 0 (66% against 52%), where both run the same empty library.

The first fixes an order of presses that the instruction does not state, with the verification order of the criteria as evidence; the second turns a verified condition (“above 90%”) into a grip-and-pull of the button cap; the third tells the actor not to use the broom the instruction names (“pick up the broom, hand it over to the right hand”), because the verifier never looks at it. papers.abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.
bullets: Addresses the need to manually engineer proposition-grounding functions for reward machines.
An LLM generates the reward machine from a natural-language task description.
A VLM grounds reward-machine propositions in image observations during policy learning.
A VLM-based value estimator provides dense rewards based on progress toward reward-machine transitions.
Across grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, it achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.
bullets: Targets inefficient parallel decoding, where tokens must be selected jointly without harmful interactions.
Measures how committing one token changes another token’s confidence, replacing mean-field similarity penalties.
Uses cheap probes within the existing forward pass, requiring no training or additional model.
Works with the same mean-field decoding rule and key-value caching across three models and four benchmarks.
Achieves far fewer decoding steps and faster decoding in most settings, with a 1.1-point average accuracy cost; shuffled or uniform couplings remove the benefit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of measured coupling. Top: mean-field decoding penalizes two positions whose predicted distributions overlap (left). papers.abstract: We study token dynamics in deep Mamba models, with a particular focus on the attracting role of the first token. Unlike attention mechanisms, where token interactions are governed by positive scalar coefficients, Mamba dynamics involve full matrix-valued interaction coefficients with no positivity or definiteness guarantees. This structural difference makes Mamba dynamics substantially harder to analyze and prevents the direct application of existing techniques for attention-based models. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new analytical framework based on a high-dimensional invariant box and a sharp exit-time argument, which together recover an effective form of sign-definiteness. Using this framework, we characterize the possible limit points of token trajectories and prove explicit exponential convergence rates. Our analysis reveals that the first token has privileged dynamics: its limiting direction attracts subsequent tokens, inducing token clustering and attention-sink phenomena in deep Mamba models. We further show that this attraction mechanism extends to broader sequence dynamics, including state-space models, causal attention, and classical time-series models. Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B validate our predictions, showing that concentration on the first token increases with depth and dominates in later layers.
bullets: Mamba’s matrix-valued token interactions lack the positivity properties that enable existing attention analyses.
The authors develop an invariant-box and exit-time framework to recover effective sign-definiteness.
They characterize token-trajectory limit points and prove explicit exponential convergence rates.
The first token’s limiting direction attracts subsequent tokens, with the mechanism extending to state-space, causal-attention, and classical time-series models.
Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B show increasing first-token concentration with depth, especially in later layers.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Attention sink score [27] analysis in the Falcon-Mamba-7B model. Subfigure (a) shows the sink score of the first token and its moving average across layers; the score steadily increases with depth and dominates in the final layers. Subfigure (b) shows the average sink scores across token positions; the first token consistently receives the largest share.

Figure 3: Attention concentration on the first token across different depths of the Falcon-Mamba-7B model [90]. Each subfigure shows the hidden attention matrix for a specific layer: (a) Layer 1, (b) Layer 15, (c) Layer 46, and (d) Layer 60. In early layers, tokens distribute attention more uniformly, but as depth increases, nearly all tokens concentrate disproportionately on the first token. This illustrates the emergence of an attention sink in state-space models.

Figure 2: Percentage of first tokens exhibiting a single non-zero element (threshold 1× 10−4) across simplified Mamba-2 blocks with shared weights, after omitting causal convolution, input/output projections, activations, and inner residuals. Most tokens converged to 1-element tokens, consistent with simulations.

papers.abstract: Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of prescribing kinematics without explicitly targeting recovery-related muscle activations.
Combines a transformer encoder-decoder with rotary positional embeddings and flow matching to generate user-specific trajectory distributions.
Evaluated on 16 healthy participants across 15 isometric tracking tasks, including held-out users, tasks, and session-timescale fine-tuning.
Achieved under 8% mean trajectory prediction error and approximately 15% accumulated error in a live neuromotor-activation test.
Provides a proof of concept; clinical-population validation remains future work.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of trajectory prescription model. Latent representation z of both target-associated information (zv) and unknown neuromotor behavior (zU ) is generated using a RoPE [22] transformer encoder (blue flow), then decoded separately to generate prescribed trajectory v̂target (green flow) and estimated activation â (turquoise flow). A flow-matching diffusion model [7] is also trained to generate a conditional distribution of zv given zU whose samples can be passed through the target trajectory decoder to generate a distribution over v̂target (orange flow).

Figure 1: End-effector robot-mediated rehabilitation platform. Users exert forces on a LBR iiwa 14 R820 7-degree-of-freedom cobot (KUKA AG, Augsburg, Germany; a) via a custom handle attached to a SensONE 6-axis force torque sensor (Bota Systems AG, Zürich, Switzerland; b). Users’ forces along each positional axis are mapped to the corresponding x/y/z velocity of an on-screen avatar ball (c), where the z axis into and out of the screen is represented by a decrease and increase in avatar size, respectively. Users are instructed to follow a target ball along a displayed trajectory. Force and game trajectory data (of both avatar and target) are collected at 1000 Hz and 60 Hz, respectively. During this process, two Trigno Quattro 4-channel sensor motes (d), controlled through a Trigno Base Station (Delsys, Inc., Natick, MA, USA) collect surface electromyography (sEMG) data at a rate of 2.22 kHz from 8 upper limb muscles (e). Electrode placements are as follows: anterior deltoid (AD), middle deltoid (MD), posterior deltoid (PD), and biceps brachii (BB), grounded at the acromion (G1); and triceps brachii (long head, TR), brachioradialis (BR), wrist flexors (FL), and wrist extensors (EX), grounded at the olecranon (G2). All data are collected and synchronized via Redis (MongoDB, Inc., New York, NY, USA). Full implementation details are included with code release.

papers.abstract: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.
bullets: Parameter count alone poorly predicts deployment performance across architectures, workloads, hardware, and serving engines.
The framework uses differentiable architecture search with serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end measurements.
It jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure, producing heterogeneous compressed architectures.
Evaluated across long-context coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive interaction workloads.

Compared with Minitron, it improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks and compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters while retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score for a specified deployment setting.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene during capture: each keyframe spawns primitives once and refines them for only a few dozen iterations, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail. Gaussians are also inherently soft, needing many overlaps for solid surfaces. We present Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting (HIBS), which brings beta kernels to incremental reconstruction. Their shape parameter interpolates between a soft, Gaussian-like profile and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel, acting as a confidence dial for geometry. Our confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize both opacity and shape, producing solid primitives where geometry is verifiable and soft, correctable primitives where it is not. As online densification, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots. Bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling and faster rasterization, and a closed-form, shape-preserving merging formulation provides a level-of-detail (LOD) hierarchy for fast optimization and real-time rendering. On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40%. Project page: https://linus-franke.com/hibs/
bullets: Addresses poor primitive initialization, missing detail, and the softness of Gaussians in short online optimization windows.
Uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to set primitive opacity and kernel shape according to geometric confidence.
Relocates stale primitives to photometric-error hotspots during online densification.
Exploits bounded beta-kernel support for exact tile culling and faster rasterization, plus closed-form merging for LOD optimization and rendering.
On Mip-NeRF 360 under the on-the-fly protocol, reports up to 0.8 dB higher PSNR and 40% lower optimization time.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our pipeline. An RGB stream is registered with camera parameters estimated online [42]. Each keyframe spawns beta primitives using geometric observability and depth agreement, keeping uncertain primitives soft. Near-dead primitives are relocated to high-error regions, followed by a short 30-iteration optimization burst with our fused rasterizer. Periodically, small-footprint primitives are merged hierarchically using closed-form moment matching that preserves their solidity.

Figure 7. Quality during reconstruction. Top: mean PSNR over test views registered so far versus reconstruction progress, for our method and i3DGS. Bottom: PSNR immediately after each view’s registration versus just before the next test view arrives. Points above the diagonal show improvement after registration.

papers.abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes only 53.5% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline replay benchmarks and real-world interaction, where assistant responses affect user behavior and task outcomes.
Provides simulators for cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface tasks, plus persona-conditioned users with execution errors and out-of-plan behavior.
Introduces IVG-Bench with 315 interaction scenarios for evaluating visual grounding, actionable guidance, latency, and task completion.
The best evaluated model completed 53.5% of tasks within the time limit; the interaction-quality metric achieved 78.5% agreement with human preferences.
A proof-of-concept GRPO experiment improved task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B in the cooking environment.

papers.abstract: 3D-aware representations can improve robotic manipulation by providing geometric information that is robust to changes in viewpoint, object position, and occlusion. However, using 3D inputs at deployment requires additional sensing and processing, making image-based policies more practical. We ask whether an image-based policy can acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment. We propose shape-teacher alignment, a training-time mechanism that uses a pretrained 3D shape representation as an alignment target for an image-based policy encoder. Specifically, we use Point-MAE features from individual objects as targets for corresponding image patches, transferring geometric structure to the policy without changing its deployment inputs or architecture. On LIBERO, shape-teacher alignment produces image representations that are more structured around object shape and corresponding parts, while substantially accelerating policy convergence and improving success rates. For pretrained policies, convergence is accelerated by 4.7x and 5.6x on the Object and Spatial suites, respectively, without requiring the shape teacher or depth input at deployment.
bullets: Motivation: Image-only policies are easier to deploy, but lack the viewpoint- and occlusion-robust geometric information provided by 3D representations.
Method: Align image patches with corresponding pretrained Point-MAE features from individual objects during training.
Contribution: Enables an image-based policy encoder to acquire object-shape and part-level structure without changing its deployment interface or architecture.

Results: On LIBERO, alignment improves shape-structured representations, policy success rates, and convergence speed; pretrained policies converge 4.7× and 5.6× faster on the Object and Spatial suites.
Scope: The 3D shape teacher and depth input are used only during training, not deployment.

papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of scaling safe reinforcement learning (safe RL) to massively parallel training regimes, where a large number of environments are exe- cuted with short rollout horizons. Although this setting improves data throughput and wall-clock efficiency, it creates a mismatch with constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), whose safety constraints are defined over full-episode cost returns. We address this mismatch by analyzing staggered environment resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments. This analysis charac- terizes the bias induced by phase coverage and motivates a phase-aggregated cost estimator that reconstructs episode-level cost estimates from short rollout batches. We further incorporate finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch into a constraint-tightening framework, yielding a scalable Safe RL method compatible with on-policy optimization. Using an MJX-based implementation of Safety Gym, our experiments show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations while substantially reducing wall-clock training time.
bullets: Massive parallelism improves throughput but conflicts with CMDP constraints defined over full episodes.
The work models staggered resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments.
A phase-aggregated cost estimator reconstructs episode-level costs from short rollout batches.
Constraint tightening accounts for finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch.
In MJX-based Safety Gym experiments, the method matches non-massively parallel performance with substantially lower wall-clock training time.

papers.abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SplatAnything
bullets: Existing methods normalize global radial distance but leave neighboring Gaussian spacing inconsistent across scene scales and camera setups.
This mismatch shifts Gaussian-scale targets and creates ambiguous supervision.
The proposed GSNorm canonicalizes a robust scene-level Gaussian-spacing statistic as a consistent spatial reference.
A benchmark evaluates diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and extrapolated viewpoints.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, with especially strong gains under large scale and viewpoint variations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models can simulate different observers, yet it remains unclear how assigned perspectives reshape their internal representations and whether these changes govern their judgements. Here, we investigate the representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, we systematically vary persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states. We observe a systematic reorganisation of representational geometry across processing depth: early layers primarily encode image identity, whereas persona-specific structures emerge in later layers. Strikingly, prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements. This dissociation is further illustrated by minimal identity statements that alter representations even without changing responses. These findings demonstrate that representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance. More broadly, they reveal how simulated perspectives emerge as distinct structures within the representational space of artificial cognitive systems, highlighting a fundamental distinction between the geometry of internal representations and their functional consequences.
bullets: Early layers mainly encode image identity, while persona-related structure emerges in later layers.
Prompt framing changes representations more strongly than persona identity.
Persona content has a greater effect on interestingness judgements than on representational geometry.
Minimal identity statements can alter representations without changing responses.
The findings caution that representational distance alone does not indicate behavioural relevance.

papers.abstract: Self-attention carries a quadratic cost in token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers can scale with input resolution. We introduce SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians spatial operator that replaces dense self-attention with a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing the per-layer cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to subquadratic in $N$. Unlike dot-product self-attention, whose Lipschitz constant is unbounded outside a compact input domain, SSoG with fixed kernels is globally Lipschitz continuous, which, via the Picard--Lindelöf theorem, guarantees that the continuous-depth variant has a unique solution on the whole integration interval, a global guarantee that dense-attention counterparts lack in general. On CIFAR-100 at $224\times224$, in a matched discrete-Transformer setting and in the continuous setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2--4.1 points across three model widths while using 8.8--16.6\% fewer parameters, with depth and training recipe held fixed. In a looped-Transformer setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.4--8.1 points. We further probe inference-time scaling by evaluating on inputs up to $1024\times1024$ at matched batch size: in the continuous-depth (Neural ODE) architecture, SSoG reaches up to 154\% higher throughput and over 60\% lower peak memory than dense attention, with the gap widening as resolution grows, consistent with the difference in asymptotic cost. In the discrete and looped settings, SSoG also achieves over 30\% higher throughput than dense attention at this resolution. Together, these results establish SSoG as a practical, parameter-efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared, and continuous-depth Transformer variants.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic token-cost bottleneck of dense self-attention at high image resolutions.
Uses a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing per-layer complexity to subquadratic in the token count.
With fixed kernels, SSoG is globally Lipschitz, supporting unique whole-interval solutions for its continuous-depth Neural ODE formulation.
On CIFAR-100, it improves Top-1 accuracy across discrete, continuous, and looped Transformer settings while using fewer parameters.
At up to 1024×1024 resolution, it delivers substantially higher throughput and lower peak memory than dense attention, especially in the continuous-depth model.

Each panel shares a log-scaled resolution axis (224-1024) with two y-axes: throughput in images/s (blue, left) and peak allocated memory in MiB (magenta, right). papers.selection_reason: Subquadratic separable Gaussian attention operator replacing dense self-attention with efficiency and throughput gains.
papers.title: Beyond Quadratic Attention: Separable Gaussian Operators for ODE Vision Transformers

papers.abstract: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.
bullets: Addresses agents’ difficulty with long-horizon workflows, heterogeneous files, and fine-grained deliverable requirements.
Synthesizes data from real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and web-sourced files rather than manually specified workflows or generated files.
Distills 10k web-corpus candidates into 4k tasks with multi-format attachments and deliverable-level rubrics.
Trains Agent-R²-4B with supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning.
The approach improves end-to-end productivity and file-grounded reasoning, while reducing shortcut behavior and encouraging sustained exploration.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Agent-R2 data synthesis pipeline. The framework extracts file-oriented workflow blueprints from real web-corpus evidence, retrieves and verifies public attachments, and synthesizes instructions, rubrics, and references in sandbox.

Figure 6: Case study of shortcut behavior in materials-test report generation. The base model and Gemini-2.5-Pro produce flawed reports from incomplete or invalid spreadsheet evidence, whereas Agent-R2-4B recovers from parsing and execution errors, computes the required values, and verifies the generated plots in the final PDF deliverable.

Figure 5: Effective Steps vs. GDPval Performance. Effective steps are computed as average tool-call steps minus tool-call errors. Models with more effective steps generally achieve higher GDPval Pass@1.
Figure 1: GDPval Pass@1 comparison. Agent-R2-4B improves the Qwen3-4B-Thinking base model by 18.6 points and surpasses several larger open-source baselines.

Figure 4: Model behavior and completion quality. Left: completion rate, average tool-call steps, and average toolcall errors across the base, SFT, and RL variants. Right: win/tie/loss outcomes of the RL-trained model against the SFT-only model after valid completion on GDPval, where green, orange, and gray segments indicate RL wins, ties, and SFT wins, respectively.

Figure 3: Rubric-based RL training. Agent-R2 samples multi-turn rollouts in sandbox, renders generated deliverables for MLLM-as-a-judge scoring against rubrics and references, and updates the policy with group advantages and KL regularization.
Figure 7: Training reward during reinforcement learning.
Figure 8: Cosine similarity across synthesis stages.

Agent-R2-4B consistently improves over its base and SFT variants and outperforms several larger open-source baselines on the full set.

papers.selection_reason: Data synthesis and training framework for LLM agents on realistic productivity work; relevant to language foundation model agentic reasoning.
papers.title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
papers.tldr: Agent-R² scales realistic productivity-agent training by synthesizing tasks from real occupational workflows and authentic files, enabling a 4B model to outperform a much larger model on GDPval and OfficeQA.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation from low-bit quantization in resource-constrained edge MLLMs, especially small models.
Uses self-relabeling to better align limited fine-tuning data with the pretrained data distribution.
Introduces progressive block activation to recover multimodal understanding before language-modeling capabilities.
Employs a vision-sensitive factor to identify layers critical to multimodal understanding.
Across 2B–8B models and multiple benchmarks, W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct gains 6.6% average accuracy and remains about 1% below full precision.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed ProQuant. Left: examples of responses from GPT-4 [Bubeck et al., 2023] and re-sampled via the SRL scheme (Section 3.1) using Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (see more details in Appendix B). Right: QAT with the PBA mechanism, where quantization is first activated for decoding layers with the larger vision-sensitivity factor τ . As training proceeds, quantization is gradually enabled for the remaining layers in descending order of τ (Section 3.2).

Figure 6: Training loss comparison of Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct between naive QAT and ProQuant under W4A8 and W4A4. PBA exhibits faster warm-up convergence toward the pre-trained level, rapid recovery during PBA, and better final convergence.

Table 1: Weight-activation quantization results for Qwen VL series. The headers represent model architectures, bitwidth, quantization methods, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, MMMU, ScienceQA, SeedBench, TextVQA, average accuracy, and MME scores, respectively. The superscript † indicates down_proj activations are quantized to 8-bit under W4A4 settings.
Figure 5: Normalized vision sensitivity τ⃗ and weight gradient norm ∥Gw∥ℓ1 across decoding layers.
Figure 3: Accuracy of Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct W4A8 checkpoints on HellaSwag [Zellers et al., 2019] (left) and AI2D [Kembhavi et al., 2016] (right) benchmarks over training iterations.

Figure 4: Loss trajectories of TSB/VSBprioritized QAT over the first 300 steps.
