papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization-aware training for edge MLLMs; fits efficient inference and multimodal LLM deployment.
papers.title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
papers.tldr: ProQuant is a progressive quantization-aware training framework that preserves multimodal understanding in low-bit edge MLLMs, achieving near-full-precision performance at W4A8.

papers.abstract: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.
bullets: Evaluates in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning across long-horizon manipulation tasks and three robot embodiments.
Uses harder initial conditions from existing benchmarks in an extensible MuJoCo-based framework with modular task, agent, and interface components.
GPT-6 Astra scores 49.8% versus Claude Fable 5.1 at 43.6%, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Most failures involve poor strategy selection or imprecise execution rather than scene misunderstanding; agents falsely claim success on 24–39% of subtasks.
A single in-context demonstration or self-revised prompt substantially improves Astra’s performance on a five-task subset.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Failure Breakdown for RoboARCade. A-C: These plots are over all rubric subtasks, including those the agent never reached, the share succeeded (A), with correct visual reasoning and approach (B), and with correct visual reasoning (C) within the first N tries at the subtask. Success requires correct visual reasoning, approach and precision. GPT-6 Astra generally performs best. More tries mainly improve approach and success. Visual reasoning changes little across agents. D: This plot breaks down agent behavior on subtasks it attempted. Stronger agents are more likely to succeed on later tries. When they get stuck, weaker agents fail more on approach, while stronger agents fail about as often on approach as on precision. Stronger models also make fewer incorrect success claims, though GPT-6 Astra still incorrectly claims success on 24% of subtasks.

Figure 1: Representative tasks from RoboARCade. The benchmark includes 22 tasks spanning single and bimanual manipulation, assembly, physical puzzles, and biolab-inspired procedures. This figure shows 20 of them. Tasks require combinations of visual understanding, precise control, memory, and multi-step planning. RoboARCade supports rendering with Blender for high-fidelity visual observations.

Figure 2: Different settings for robot control with FMs. Hierarchical VLA: a high-level VLM issues language subgoals to a VLA policy. Code-as-Policies: an FM generates a program that controls the robot through perception and action primitives. The FM is not involved during policy execution. Agentic robot control (ARC): the FM itself is the policy, observing the scene and issuing controller targets in a closed loop. This work focuses on the ARC setting.

Figure 4: Top: This plot includes all rubric subtasks, even those the agent never reached. It shows the share with correct visual reasoning, the share with both correct visual reasoning and approach, and the share succeeded (i.e. correct visual understanding + approach + precision) in at least one of the first N tries, so every level grows with N . GPT-6 Astra generally performs best. More tries mainly improve likelihood of correct approach and success. Visual reasoning changes little. Bottom: This plot breaks down agent behavior on subtasks it attempted. Stronger models succeed at more subtasks on the first try or through monotonic progress, without reverting to an incorrect approach after finding the right one. When they get stuck, visual reasoning errors are rare (2 to 6%), and approach errors are as common as or more common than precision errors for four of the six agents. Stronger models also make fewer incorrect success claims, though GPT-6 Astra still claims success on 24% of subtasks it did not succeed at.

Table 2: Autonomous improvement on RoboARCade. Top: We evaluate GPT-6-Astra where metrics are averaged over five partially successful tasks with 10 trials per task and method. ICL loads a full successful episode before the agent attempts the task and raises the mean rubric score from 53.5% to 73.0%. A text-only prompt reaches 72.0% after two rounds of revision using graded rollouts (T2). Bottom: For a task with no successful Astra episode, T1 prompt is written from the five failed baseline trials and the T2 prompt from those and the five T1 trials, evaluated on 5 fresh trials each. Although, a small sample size, T2 is able to achieve 100% performance for a task that had zero full successes. Full metrics are in Appendix Table 7.

Table 1: Benchmark on RoboARCade. All metrics are averaged over 22 tasks with 5 seeds each, over all trials. Success measures completed rubric subtasks. Turns/EEF and Calls/EEF divide a trial’s model turns (requests to the model, each of which can issue several tool calls) and tool calls by the number of distinct end-effector (EEF) commands the agent gives the simulator. GPT-6 Astra has the highest success rate even using a minimal multi-view RGBD interface. †A lower bound: two Opus trials each lost the usage record of one interrupted response. Success-only metrics, EEF command counts and wall time per command are in Appendix Table 6.

Table 4: Where a retry lands. Each retry is a try at a subtask that follows a failed try at the same subtask, grouped by why the previous try failed. For each group, the share of retries that ended done, in a precision miss, in a wrong approach or on the wrong object. Shares are computed per task, then averaged over tasks. After a wrong object, only 5 to 14 retries per model exist, so those shares are noisy.

Table 6: Zero-shot evaluation, all metrics. The agents and interfaces of Table 1 with success-only and all-trial metrics, averaged over 22 tasks with 5 seeds each. “Success only” excludes trials with any failed subtasks. EEF cmds counts the distinct end-effector commands the agent gives the simulator; Turns/EEF, Calls/EEF and Wall/EEF divide a trial’s model turns (requests to the model, each of which can issue several tool calls), tool calls and wall time (excluding offline Blender rendering) by that count. †A lower bound, as in Table 1.
Table 3: Task sources and asset credits. The benchmark, paper and repository each of the 22 tasks draws its scene and objects from, and the embodiment it runs on.

Table 7: Autonomous improvement, all metrics. The arms of Table 2 with success-only and all-trial metrics. EEF cmds counts the end-effector commands the simulator executed; Turns/EEF, Calls/EEF and Wall/EEF divide a trial’s model turns, tool calls and wall time (excluding offline Blender rendering) by that count.

Table 8: Autonomous improvement by task. Trials solved / trials that exhausted their simulationstep or wall-clock budget, out of 10 per task and 50 in total. Failures not ended by the budget were ended by the agent itself, declaring the task done: the “success claim” rows give their number and share of that arm’s failures. Gamepad, run separately with 5 trials per arm and no ICL arm, has no successful Astra episode: its prompts are written from failed attempts.

Table 5: Subtask verification. Wrong decisions over all decisions of each kind. Subtask verification accuracy is the share of right decisions over both kinds together. Budget cut-offs and episodes the agent ended saying it could not finish are left out, since they claim nothing.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-horizon agentic robot manipulation testing in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning; directly fits embodied robot learning and VLA.
papers.title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
papers.tldr: RoboARCade benchmarks long-horizon agentic robot control and shows that current agents still struggle with manipulation strategy, precision, and reliable self-assessment.

papers.abstract: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. We propose a multi-agent framework, SMART, to obtain knowledge through capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context. SMART curates the state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from these real-world verified curated premises, SMART's knowledge guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20% on complex scientific claims spanning 3 datasets. We show that grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5%.
bullets: Addresses limited-context problems where solving claims requires additional knowledge.
Uses multiple LLM agents and structured roles to capture implicit entity states.
Curates diverse, complementary, solution-relevant premises from real-world knowledge.
Knowledge-guided reasoning improves validation performance by up to 20% across three datasets.
Grounding premises in real-world knowledge improves performance by up to 5%.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Comparing SMART-NV where no verification is performed) with verification using self (SMART-PK), external knowledge with websearch (SMART-WS), and cross-model (X-SMART-PK) on SciFact claims. Verification improves performance an average by 2-7% across methods for both datasets, with a few exceptions (see SFBench in Fig. 10). See results in appendix Table 8.

Figure 3: Improving SMART performance using external premise validation with websearch (SMART-WS) and cross model generation and reasoning (X-SMART-PK). For SciFact, X-SMART-PK uses Qwen3 8b generated premises & improves performance by 6.2%; for SFBench, GPT-5.4-mini generated premises lead to 4% improvement.

Figure 1: A complex problem’s implicit state-based reasoning using a scientific claim from SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020). We identify experts knowledgeable about participating entities and explore their state and obtain contrastive premises. We curate true premises of supporting or opposing stance and reason with these to infer the solution.

Figure 2: Comparison of SMART-PK performance with CoT and RAG on SciFact & SFBench datasets, after applying the Refute Filter (rationales are required to adequately support refute labels; see §5.2). SMART-PK improves over baselines; on avg. 10% on SFBench and 5% on Scifact over CoT (details in Appendix Table 4).

Figure 4: Comparing SMART-PK performance generating a single premise Vs. contrastive premises on SFBench claims. See Fig. 13 for SciFact claims. Contrastive premises improve performance by 3% across datasets and models. See results in Table 5

Figure 8: We compare the validation performance of SMART-PK with 3 sizes of Qwen and GPT-5.4-mini on SciFact-Open claims using premises generated and curated by one model and solution reasoning with another model. These comparisons show that both Qwen3 8b and GPT-5.4-mini generate good quality premises that other models can curate and use for solution-reasoning.

Figure 5: We compare the 5 meta-reasonsers for SciFact claims: M-Majority Voting, R-Reasoning Judge, AAggregating Judge, C-Critical Judge and S-Supporting Judge. Reasoning Judge consistently improves performance across models and datasets: by 8% on SFBench and 5% on SciFact on average (See Fig. 9 for SFBench claims and results in Appendix Table 7).

Figure 14: Distribution of curated premise stances, their alignment with the claim and their confidence ratings for Qwen3 models. Correct identification of refuted claims requires opposing premises and supported claims require supporting premises. Qwen3 1.7b curation leads to few and noisy premises compared to Qwen8b. Qwen3 32 generates too many supporting premises increasing meta-reasoning difficulty. Supporting and opposing premises are required for supporting claims of support and refute labels respectively.

Figure 12: We compare various premise generation methods using the SciFact collection. We obtain premises with a single expert in one-shot (Non-Iter) Vs an iterative generation strategy (Iter). We also compare SMART’s multiple context-derived experts with the iterative strategy. Claude-Haiku-4.5 does not allow obtaining more than one generation per API call; due to this we do not have any result for the single expert in one-shot (Non-Iter) strategy.

Figure 9: We compare the 5 meta-reasonsers for SFBench claims: M-Majority Voting, R-Reasoning Judge, A-Aggregating Judge, C-Critical Judge and SSupporting Judge. Reasoning Judge metareasoner is more consistent across models and datasets and improves performance, by 8% on SFBench and 5% on SciFact (See Fig. 5 for SciFact and results in Appendix Table 8).

Figure 11: Comparing SMART-PK performance using a stronger premise Vs. both premises. Logically using a stronger premise was a good decision (performance of both both GPT-5.4-mini and Claude-Haiku-4.5 reduces due to direct conflicts), however, model reasoning is able to use the additional nuanced information provided by both premises. Larger models are better at leveraging the nuanced information in both premises (Llama70b improves by 1.3% & Qwen3 32b by 6.7%); smaller models benefit from additional premises as they do not curate as many premises (Qwen3 1b improves by 1.5%).

Figure 13: Comparing SMART-PK performance generating a single premise Vs. contrastive premises on SciFact claims. See Fig. 4 for SFBench claims. Contrastive premises improve performance by 3% across datasets and models. See results in Table 5
Figure 15: We compare various configurations we used for generating premises. The performance of these different configurations is compared in Fig. 12.

Figure 7: Distribution of GPT-5.4-mini curated stances, their alignment with the claim and their confidence ratings for the SciFact-Open dataset. Supporting and opposing premises are required for supporting claims that of the support and refute type respectively.

Figure 10: Comparing SMART-PK, where premises are verified with parametric knowledge, with SMART-NV where no verification is performed on SFBench claims, we show that verification improves performance an average of 2% with a few exceptions (also true for SciFact claims in Fig. 6). Results are in appendix Table 7.

Table 5: Comparing the balanced accuracy of using Single Vs. Contrastive premises with the SMART framework. We examine performance before and after applying the Refute Filter (refute labels that are not adequately supported are changed to ’unknown’, essentially dropping them from contributing to balanced accuracy). Single premises often lack necessary claim knowledge that models select refute labels without adequately supporting them. Correcting for this with the Refute Filter shows that contrastive knowledge improves on average across models and datasets by 3%. The smallest model Qwen3 1.7b is worse at obtaining contrastive knowledge, but leads to better performance with single premises. We discuss these results in §6.

Table 9: Comparing inference cost for SMART-PK and SMART-WS in model calls and number of input + output tokens measured in K tokens (KTok). We report % fallbacks (Fback) to the direct reasoning prompt when there are no curated premises, the quality of curated premises (Qual) and their average numbers per stance (Sup. & Opp.). Both methods require the same # calls since we verify before obtaining stance; these do not include 10 calls that iteratively obtain premises as a single call could potentially be used to obtain all premises for GPT-5.4-mini and Claude-Haiku-4.5. All values are per claim averages. We report NA-Not applicable as the premise quality (Qual) for SFbench claims due to not having textual evidence. Average premise quality by coincidence is the same for both methods, so we report in a single column.

Table 8: Comparing the balanced accuracy of SMART without verification (SMART-NV) with self-verification (SMART-PK), external verification with websearch (SMART-WS) and cross-verification (X-SMART-PK). Improvement with each method is shown in %Improve (the difference in performance between SMART-NV and the method). Verification improves performance on average across models and datasets by by 2-7%. Grounding premises with real-world knowledge provided by websearch improves on average by 4-5% with some exceptions.

Table 3: Comparing the percentage of rationales that lack support for a refute claim that are filtered by the Refute Filter for CoT reasoning, SMART-PK reasoning with contrastive premises and the single premise generation method (SMART-S). These lead to incorrect logical reasoning on 50% of SFBench claims and 40% of SciFact claims (claims with a gold refute). CoT leads to almost double the errors than SMART on smaller models. Single premise generation leads to more errors on SFBench (double the number than on SciFact) where as the reverse is true for contrastive premises. We discuss these results in §6.

However, this incorrect performance boost is worse with CoT than SMART (the %drop is higher for CoT than SMART). It is also worse for SFBench’s Material Science knowledge than SciFact’s Biological Science knowledge (the %drop is higher SFBench than SciFact, Llama3 8b model on SciFact is an exception where the model does not generate most rationales). Web search based on a claim is noisy; up to half the RAG refute labels are based on not finding the appropriate evidence. Since RAG performance is lower than CoT, we provide % SMART improvement over CoT in the last column (SMART-PK improves performance up to 20%.) We discuss these results in §6.

Table 6: Comparing performance (BAccuracy) of SMART-WS and X-SMART-PK with SMART-PK. X-SMART-PK where models use premises from a better generating model: Qwen3 8b for SciFact and GPT-5.4-mini for SFBench. Since SMART-PK does not lead to as much of an artificial performance boost, we compare results without applying the Refute Filter. Performance on SciFact collection of claims improves by a 6.5-14.1%; and up to 8.5% for SFBench claims. We discuss these results and choice of curation model in §6.

papers.abstract: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing models to capture clinically relevant anatomy across hierarchical scales in 3D scans and reports.
Routes both image and text tokens through local and global anatomy-organized Soft Mixture-of-Experts layers.
Uses anatomy-level and global contrastive alignment to learn unified vision-language representations.
Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision and evaluated on segmentation, classification, and detection across 6 datasets.
Reports consistent improvements over 11 state-of-the-art methods; the approach is scoped to 3D medical imaging and the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the MedHiVE framework. A hierarchical encoder processes a 3D CT scan and anatomy masks alongside a full report representation zTi and anatomy-specific snippet representations zTi,a, extracted through a frozen text encoder. The global vision representation zIi is contrasted with zTi , while local vision representations zIi,a are aligned with zTi,a for each anatomical structure a. This yields anatomy-aware vision-language representations that enhance downstream segmentation, classification, and detection.

Figure 4. An overview of the 2D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6]. We consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups to facilitate analysis and model training (see Table 3). These projections illustrate the spatial distribution of the anatomies across representative slices.

Figure 2. Overview of the HiVEL layer. Global and anatomylevel vision tokens and text tokens are routed to E global experts FFNG and F local experts FFNL via first-level routers. The resulting slots are concatenated and processed by a second-level router. Global vision and text tokens are fused with H shared experts FFNS outputs via residual connection, yielding enhanced vision tokens x̂ and text tokens t̂. Vision tokens are used at all stages s ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, while text tokens are enabled at s ∈ {3, 4}.
Figure 6. Text preprocessing pipeline.

Figure 10. Qualitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. We benchmark MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE exhibits superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging its ability to capture long-range dependencies for large-scale dental arches while preserving high-fidelity boundaries in smaller, individual tooth structures. While competing methods frequently suffer from topological discontinuities (e.g., fragmented roots) or oversegmentation in high-density regions, our approach maintains global structural integrity and local connectivity. The zoomed-in regions (red boxes) highlight MedHiVE’s robustness in resolving ambiguous inter-proximal boundaries where baseline models typically fail to maintain clear separation.

Figure 9. Qualitative multi-class segmentation results on the KiTS 2023 internal test set. We evaluate the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth annotations and four state-of-the-art baselines for the joint segmentation of the kidney parenchyma, cysts, and tumor masses. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency by effectively modeling the hierarchical dependencies between nested structures; it captures the global morphology of the kidney while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for small, low-contrast cysts and heterogeneous tumor regions. Unlike competing methods, which frequently exhibit topological fragmentation or semantic leakage (e.g., misclassifying tumor voxels as healthy tissue), our approach preserves structural integrity across varying object scales. The zoomed-in insets highlight MedHiVE’s ability to resolve ambiguous boundaries in complex cases of multi-focal cystic disease, where baseline models suffer from oversegmentation and loss of connectivity.

Figure 8. Qualitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT validation set. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines across 15 abdominal organs. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging long-range dependency modeling to maintain the global anatomical context of large-scale organs (e.g., liver, stomach) while ensuring high-fidelity boundary localization for small, low-contrast structures (e.g., adrenal glands, gallbladder). While competing methods frequently suffer from inter-class leakage and topological discontinuities in anatomically crowded regions, our approach preserves structural integrity and inter-organ spatial relationships. The highlighted regions (red boxes) illustrate MedHiVE’s robustness against oversegmentation at organ interfaces, where baseline models often fail to resolve clear semantic boundaries due to similar intensity profiles in non-contrast CT.

Figure 7. Qualitative segmentation results on the PANORAMA test sets. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against the ground truth and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, accurately capturing long-range dependencies in large-scale structures (e.g., the pancreas parenchyma) while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for fine-grained objects like PDAC lesions and pancreatic ducts. Unlike competing methods that suffer from topological discontinuities or oversegmentation, our approach consistently preserves structural integrity across varying object scales.

Figure 3. Qualitative segmentation results on four datasets, from top to bottom: PANORAMA, AMOS, KiTS and GEPAR3D. Comparison of MedHiVE with the top five baselines. Red boxes highlight significant artifacts or missing components in baseline predictions. MedHiVE shows superior consistency with the ground truth in these challenging regions.

Figure 11. Qualitative comparison of visual grounding performance on external in-house abdominal CT scans with kidney lesions. Each row displays a representative abdominal CT slice paired with its corresponding part of radiology report describing kidney tumors or cysts; in the absence of voxel-wise annotations, the report serves as the reference. Grounding predictions are shown for MedHiVE (left), Merlin (center), and fVLM (right). All models are fine-tuned on KiTS 2023. MedHiVE segments lesions consistent with the radiology reports, whereas Merlin and fVLM overshoot the lesion extent or place predictions in a kidney the report leaves unremarkable (red boxes).

Figure 5. Visualization of the 3D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6], shown from the front, left, right, and back views. These projections highlight the global structural consistency and anatomical coherence of the segmented structures. Consistent with the 2D setting, we consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups for clarity and downstream processing (see Table 3). The multi-view renderings provide a qualitative assessment of segmentation quality across the full 3D volume.

Table 4. Quantitative segmentation and detection performance on the PANORAMA test sets (NIH, MSD, and In-house). Evaluation metrics include mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm), while PDAC detection efficacy is measured via Sensitivity and Specificity (%). The best results are highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, particularly in the challenging task of PDAC segmentation, where it significantly outperforms existing Transformer and Mamba-based architectures. Notably, our method achieves a substantial boost in mDSC for the In-house PDAC dataset (65.8%) and the Overall PDAC average (54.2%), representing a major improvement over the second-best performing models. Additionally, MedHiVE exhibits the lowest mHD95 and the highest sensitivity for patient-level detection, underscoring its clinical utility in identifying low-contrast ductal adenocarcinomas across diverse multi-center cohorts.

Table 5. Quantitative segmentation results on the KiTS dataset. Performance is evaluated across three distinct labels: Kidneys, Tumor, and Cyst. Results are reported in DSC (%) for individual classes, with mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) representing the overall average performance. MedHiVE achieves the highest performance in mDSC and mHD95, consistently outperforming both CNN-based and advanced sequence-modeling baselines. Specifically, the model shows a marked improvement in the segmentation of small, irregular structures compared to pure Mamba or Transformer architectures. The achievement of the lowest mHD95 further validates our method’s precision in boundary localization, demonstrating its robustness in handling the high anatomical variability and complex pathologies inherent in kidney tumor imaging. The best results are bolded.

Table 6. Quantitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT dataset. The evaluation encompasses 15 distinct anatomical structures across a wide range of scales and morphologies. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves superior overall performance, demonstrating a high degree of robustness across both large, high-contrast organs (e.g., Liver, Spleen) and smaller, more complex structures (e.g., Adrenal Glands, Duodenum). Notably, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art for the Pancreas and Duodenum, which are traditionally challenging due to their low-contrast boundaries and proximity to the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, the significant reduction in mHD95 compared to both Transformer-based and pure Mamba-based baselines indicates a superior ability to preserve global topological consistency while maintaining fine-grained local details. MedHiVE exhibits competitive or superior Dice scores across the majority of classes, underscoring the generalizability of our proposed architecture.

Table 7. Detailed quantitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. Results are categorized by individual teeth following the FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall segmentation accuracy and the lowest mHD95 among all compared methods. The performance is notably consistent across different tooth types, effectively bridging the gap between large molars and smaller incisors. In particular, our model demonstrates superior precision in the upper and lower left quadrants, where it maintains high fidelity for complex occlusal surfaces and inter-proximal spaces. The significant reduction in the average Hausdorff distance suggests that MedHiVE is less prone to the isolated voxel noise and topological errors that often degrade the clinical utility of baseline segmentation outputs.

Table 1. Comprehensive performance comparison across segmentation, classification, and detection tasks. Segmentation performance is reported in mDSC (%), while PDAC classification and detection are reported via Sensitivity (%), Specificity (%), and mAP (%). VRAM is measured in gigabytes (GB) (↓), and speed in million voxels per second (MV/s) (↑). The best results are bolded.

Table 8. Quantitative segmentation performance on the ToothFairy2 dataset subset. Evaluation follows the FDI World Dental Federation notation across the upper and lower dental arches. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates a clear state-of-the-art advantage, particularly in maintaining structural continuity across the most challenging anatomical sites. Our method significantly outperforms all baselines in the posterior extremities, specifically the third molars (FDI 18, 28, 38, 48), where standard models typically struggle with severe under-segmentation or total loss of connectivity. Furthermore, MedHiVE attains the second-best mHD95 among all methods. These results validate the robustness of our approach in handling the high morphological variability and lower image quality characteristic of the ToothFairy2 benchmarks, ensuring precise tooth-by-tooth delineation across the entire oral cavity.

Table 12. Ablation study on the AMOS-CT validation set across 15 organ classes. We evaluate the impact of the Text (T) supervision and Contrastive Loss (CL) components on segmentation accuracy (mDSC) and boundary precision (mHD95). The results demonstrate that incorporating textual representations (Config #2) consistently improves performance for anatomically complex organs, while the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest overall accuracy and a significant reduction in Hausdorff Distance (mHD95 from 5.0 to 3.6 mm). This suggests that the joint contrastive objective effectively regularizes the latent space, particularly benefiting small-scale structures such as the adrenal glands and duodenum. B, T, and CL indicate baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 10. Ablation study on the PANORAMA and in-house datasets demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate our proposed method across three diverse test sets: NIH (public), MSD (public), and a multi-institutional In-house dataset. Segmentation quality is measured through mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm). Additionally, we report patient-level PDAC detection performance using Sensitivity/Specificity (%). The results indicate that while text guidance (T) significantly improves tumor localization, the addition of contrastive learning (CL) is crucial for refining boundary transitions, as evidenced by the reduction in mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 11. Ablation study on the KiTS dataset demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate the incremental contribution of text-based prompts (T) and contrastive learning (CL) over the baseline (B) architecture. Segmentation performance is reported via class-specific DSC (%) for Kidneys, Tumors, and Cysts, alongside aggregate mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) metrics. The results indicate that text guidance (T) primarily benefits cyst segmentation, while the addition of contrastive learning (CL) yields the largest gain for tumors and further reduces mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 14. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D dataset, including ToothFairy2 subset across 32 individual tooth classes (FDI notation). We evaluate the contribution of Text (T) conditioning and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained dental segmentation. While the baseline (Config #1) performs adequately on centralized teeth, the integration of textual representations (Config #2) provides a significant performance boost in boundary precision, reducing mHD95 from 6.5 to 2.0 mm. Notably, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) demonstrates superior robustness in segmenting distal molars (e.g., FDI 18, 28, 38), which are typically prone to severe imaging artifacts and morphological variation. This confirms that the contrastive objective effectively regularizes the feature space for anatomically rare or obscured structures. This indicates that the benefit of the anatomy-level contrastive objective can depend on overlap between the pre-training anatomy inventory and the target structures. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 13. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D test set, excluding ToothFairy2 subset across 32 dental classes (FDI notation). We quantify the influence of Textual Supervision (T) and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained segmentation. The inclusion of text-conditioned representations (Config #2) yields substantial gains in semantic recognition across the dental arch. Crucially, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest boundary fidelity, reaching sub-millimeter precision (mHD95: 0.5 mm). This indicates that the contrastive objective mitigates surface errors effectively in anatomically complex regions, such as the lingual surfaces of incisors (FDI 11, 21) and the occlusal pits of molars (FDI 36, 46), where baselines exhibit higher spatial variance. As this dataset covers dental anatomy absent from our pre-training inventory, the anatomy-level contrastive objective is expected to contribute less here. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.
Table 3. List of selected anatomies.

Table 9. Comparative quantitative analysis of tooth segmentation on the full dataset, including GEPAR3D [42] and ToothFairy2 [8, 9, 31] subsets. Evaluation is conducted for individual teeth using FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results bolded. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall mDSC, particularly in the segmentation of molars and premolars. MedHiVE achieves the second-best mHD95, indicating precise boundary localization. Notably, the performance gap is most pronounced in the posterior regions, where complex root morphologies and proximity to distal anatomical landmarks typically challenge standard segmentation models. These results underscore the effectiveness of our architectural design in maintaining local precision while capturing the global context of the complete dental arch.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.
bullets: OPSD can suffer from Teacher Drift, where the teacher adopts the student’s incorrect intermediate reasoning.
Drift tends to begin earlier in lower-resource languages, making uniform supervision unreliable.
TOPSD uses teacher–student likelihoods to locate drift and select a supervision prefix.
It verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix before distillation.
Across mathematical reasoning in ten languages and three model scales, TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, especially for low- and medium-resource languages.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of TOPSD. The student generates a reasoning trajectory in the target language, while the privileged teacher additionally observes the English problem and reference solution. Step 1 (Teachable Prefix Selection) uses the cumulative teacher-student likelihood ratio to select a candidate teachable prefix, determining where teacher supervision may be applied. Step 2 (Teacher Recoverability Verification) checks whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from the selected prefix, determining whether supervision should be applied. Only prefixes that pass verification receive distillation on the corresponding states of the original student trajectory. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on a high-resource Spanish problem. Both the base model and COPSD omit the cross-term 3a21 and incorrectly use 3a2 = 19, producing the answer 22. TOPSD correctly matches the coefficient using 3a21 + 3a2 = 19 and obtains the correct answer 352. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 8: Qualitative comparison on a low-resource Telugu problem. The base model forms an incorrect determinant-area expression, and COPSD produces repetitive reasoning without a valid area derivation or boxed answer. TOPSD correctly derives the triangle area as 1012(i+ j), computes S(n) = 1012n(n+ 1)2, and obtains the correct limiting value 1012. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison on a medium-resource Thai problem. The base model uses an incorrect asymmetric parameter range, while COPSD reports only an incomplete enumeration of five solutions. TOPSD factorizes the equation as (4x− 3y)(3x+ 2y) = 0, counts both parameterized solution families over their complete ranges, and obtains the correct answer 117. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of COPSD and TOPSD on Bengali mathematical reasoning. Starting from similar correct formulations, COPSD becomes stuck in repeated divisibility statements, while TOPSD continues the derivation to b = 21 and b = 49 and obtains the correct answer 70. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 2: Teacher Drift in multilingual reasoning. (a) Student accuracy across languages. (b) Cumulative teacher-student likelihood ratio Ci,t indicates earlier alignment in low-resource languages. (c) Teacher recoverability Rec(m) decreases with longer student prefixes. Colors indicate language-resource groups.

Figure 1: Teacher Drift in a Korean reasoning example. The teacher’s next-token predictions are evaluated on prefixes of one student trajectory. At t = 36 and 180, it predicts 2 instead of the student’s 0, correcting a dodecagon’s side count from 10 to 12; at t = 314, it predicts 0, following the repeated error. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 6: Completion-based illustration of Teacher Drift. The same privileged teacher is greedily continued from three progressively longer prefixes of a single student completion. It recovers the correct answer 78 at t = 600 and t = 700, but follows the student’s incorrect reasoning and returns 6 at t = 768. This provides an outcome-level view of how prefix accumulation affects teacher recovery. English translations are shown in gray.

The fixed-prefix baseline retains the first 10% of each student trajectory, while TOPSD adaptively selects teachable prefixes. Both methods use the same Teacher Recoverability Verification procedure. Bold indicates the best result for each metric.
Table 5: Training hyperparameters used for TOPSD. Unless otherwise specified, the same configuration is used across all model scales.

Relative Cutoff Position reports the cutoff as a percentage of trajectory length, averaged over trajectories with detected cutoffs. Overall is the mean relative cutoff position over all trajectories with detected cutoffs across the ten languages.

papers.abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is observational theory learning: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.
bullets: Generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs.
Learners receive only observed transitions—without program labels, task identities, or support examples.
Controls program complexity, curriculum progression, recurring subprograms, and continual evaluation with level skipping.
Seven representative baselines plateau below ceiling, with larger gaps at higher curriculum levels.
Targets observational theory learning, beyond solving isolated few-shot visual reasoning puzzles.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of continual observational theory learning. A useful theory system should continually evolve as a learner receives a stream of observations. During theory acquisition (blue arrows), the learner discovers new theories when existing ones cannot explain an observation (Mirror) and abstracts recurring compositions into reusable units (Up + Rotate). Theory application combines them to explain new observations.

Figure 6: SCORE and highest curriculum level attempted in each benchmark mode. No baseline progresses beyond Lv2. SCORE sums 100× accuracy over attempted levels, so only models that reach Lv2 can exceed 100. Trained baselines show the mean ± one population standard deviation over three seeds; LLMs are evaluated once with greedy decoding on the first 100 tasks at each attempted level. Cont-Mono-OC is evaluated only on Multi-A and Multi-B. Labels above the bars give the highest level attempted.

Figure 4: Observations across modes and levels. Each pair shows one before–after observation from Levels 1, 2, and 8 of each mode. Observations become more complex through longer hidden programs, more objects, relational structure, and primitive expansion.

Figure 7: Transfer failures despite exact support fit. Five failure patterns on Lv1 tasks: (a) incorrect displacement (AR), (b) incorrect flip axis (Cont-Mono), (c) two color shifts instead of one (Cont-Mono), (d) a rotation-only output when rotation followed by a flip is required (Disc-Mono), and (e) the correct color change applied to the wrong object (NEO; dashed boxes mark the changed object). Rows show Input, Target, and Prediction. Both supports are predicted correctly (one shown), but the query is incorrect; green/red borders mark correct/incorrect predictions. Examples (a–d) use Single-A/B and (e) uses Multi-A.

Figure 3: BabyTheorist program language and task generation. (a) Each program step pairs a selector, which identifies the objects to transform, with a primitive, which specifies the transformation. (b) The illustrated depth-6 program combines frequently recurring subprograms of depths 1, 3, and 2. Learners that discover such subprograms can reuse them to efficiently explain more complex phenomena.

Figure 9: Selector types. Each row shows a source scene and the objects selected by different selector types. Global selection applies to all objects; attribute-based selectors choose objects by properties such as color or hollowness; spatial selectors choose objects by position; and index-based selectors use a fixed raster-scan ordering.

Figure 10: Footprint-preserving transformation primitives. Representative before-after examples for primitives that transform selected objects while preserving their footprint, including rotation, reflection, and color change.

Figure 11: Footprint-changing transformation primitives. Representative before-after examples for objectshape primitives that change the interior or boundary of selected objects, including fill_interior, hollow, and add_border.
Figure 12: Movement primitives. Representative before-after examples for primitives that translate selected objects up, down, left, or right.
Figure 13: Relational primitives. Representative before-after examples for primitives that use a target object, including color swapping and row or column alignment.

Figure 15: AR: support fit without query transfer. Each column shows a different depth-one Single-B task from this 256-task subset (seed 42). The adapted model fits both supports but fails on the query.

Figure 8: Step-wise inference succeeds where joint inference fails. Joint predictions are wrong despite exact support fit. Given ground-truth intermediate supports, inferring a theory for each program step separately (Separate) yields correct intermediate and final outputs. Each step’s theory is inferred from its first support pair. This diagnostic adds supervision and changes inference, so it is not a baseline comparison.

Figure 16: Transfer errors on depth-1 programs. Cont-Mono (a–c) and Disc-Mono (d–f) fit both supports but make reflection-axis, color-change, and translation-distance errors, respectively (seed 42). papers.abstract: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.
bullets: Targets PCB routing, which requires coordinating connectivity strategy, geometry, and strict design rules.
Uses board images plus electrical and geometric data to plan topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions.
Executes plans through KiCad’s native router with bounded local recovery and structured feedback for guide revision.
Achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% across four PCBWorld-Bench splits.
Outperforms the evaluated baseline on three real-world subsets, while performance drops substantially on D3-C.

papers.abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $π_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
bullets: Motivation: Existing world-action and vision-language-action policies inherit costly architectures designed for video or language generation rather than control.
Method: Train a policy transformer from scratch in pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 feature space; use action-conditioned future-feature prediction during training, but generate only actions at inference.
Results: La-JEPA attains state-of-the-art average performance among policies without embodied pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0 and corrected-instruction LIBERO-Plus benchmarks.
Efficiency: Its S and B variants run 2–5× faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming them on the reported benchmarks.
Design insight: JEPA features outperform video-VAE latents, and training-time future prediction helps even when omitted during inference; real-robot performance is comparable to π0.5 on four tasks.

papers.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling

papers.abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.
bullets: Targets dense optical flow on MCUs, where limited on-chip SRAM restricts input resolution.
PACE-NAS separates macro design for peak SRAM from micro search over operators and depths for accuracy–latency trade-offs.
Replacing transposed convolutions and adding lightweight context modules reduces memory use and endpoint error without increasing peak SRAM.
MCUFlowNet-S runs 1.76× faster than retrained EdgeFlowNet with 1.6% higher EPE, and avoids collisions more often in simulated forest flights.
The framework also speeds up a PIDNet-S semantic-segmentation variant by 1.17× at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire protocol and ask what notices a fault in it. On Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher), we injected up to 23 faults into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, from one value to every value. Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten, and a comparison with ten fault-free seeds at most 21%. A clean evaluation of all 1,060 final policies agreed with the curves: of the 728 boundary-fault runs both curve checks passed, 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds, though nearly all ended on other weights and, for reward faults, logged other returns. Checks of the run itself, not of its outcome, saw every fault. A step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed, on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two, with no fault-free run and, on Pendulum, a median 3% more training time. An episode record kept at the environment caught the faults in the trainer's log. We list such faults found in practice, in Gymnasium 1.3 and our own code and, reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries, and recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment.
bullets: The study examines silent faults in wire-protocol communication between distributed RL environments and trainers.
Across four tasks, learning-curve and fault-free-seed comparisons detected few faults unless nearly every value was corrupted.
A clean evaluation of 1,060 final policies confirmed that most faulty runs appeared normal by outcome, despite using different weights or logging different returns.
A step ledger maintained on both sides caught and located every tested boundary fault, with a reported median 3% training-time increase on Pendulum.
Environment-side episode records detected faults introduced in the trainer's log; the authors recommend both mechanisms.

papers.title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Outcome-based checks often miss silent reinforcement-learning faults, while step-by-step boundary ledgers and environment-side episode records detect them reliably.

papers.abstract: Frontier-based exploration systems repeatedly evaluate geodesic travel costs between robot poses and candidate viewpoints, and tour-based planners consume the full pairwise distance matrix built from them. Recomputing these matrices with one graph search per source scales with the explored map size, whereas distance caches that refresh only locally affected or newly created frontiers can retain stale costs between surviving pairs when newly discovered free space creates a global shortcut. We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring for monotonically growing occupancy grids. H-TRIP partitions the known map into a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports. Each unknown-to-free revelation is decomposed into efficient rank-one min-plus edge insertions at the affected leaf, and only decreased port-to-port summaries are propagated along its ancestor chain. A shared hierarchical lift evaluates the dense many-to-many matrix of shortest distances for all active query points on the occupancy map. We prove that sequential insertions preserve exact shortest-path distances on the grid. Benchmark experiments confirm exact agreement with reference searches on fully built maps and show that dense many-to-many queries at a few dozen viewpoints are up to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential k x BFS. On exploration runs with sixteen robots, in-loop queries on the growing occupancy graph are 2.21x-8.59x faster than co-scheduled k x BFS on maps with side 256, 512, and 1024 cells.
bullets: Addresses stale distance caches and the high cost of recomputing pairwise geodesic distances as maps expand.
Uses a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports and rank-one min-plus updates for each newly revealed free-space region.
Propagates only decreased port-to-port summaries through affected ancestor nodes, then lifts them to query-point distances.
Proves exactness under sequential occupancy-grid insertions and matches reference graph searches on completed maps.
Achieves up to two orders of magnitude faster dense queries than sequential k×BFS; sixteen-robot runs are 2.21×–8.59× faster on tested map sizes.

(b) Super-tile U1 receives that summary through φT2→U1 together with a newly passable seam, after which RepairClosure writes ∆SU1 on BU1 . (c) Super-tile U5 applies the same interface step to its 10×10 children U1, . . . , U4, where φU1→U5 plants ∆SU1 and RepairClosure writes ∆SU5 on BU5 .

papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel task of describing human facial expressions of a facial image in natural language, which captures the nuances of facial actions and emotional states beyond traditional emotion categories or facial action units (AUs). To achieve the facial expression captioning model, we propose a three-stage training framework that trains a vision-to-language model using synthesized image-text pairs and the BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. To overcome the challenge of missing training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning, we propose a strategy that involves synthesizing and combining captions using GPT-3.5 and existing annotations on either emotion categories or AUs. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating captions that describe details of facial actions and emotions, as well as the inferential relationship between them, even when those emotions are not present in the training data. It is also demonstrated that the vision-to-language task enhances the performance of the intermediate visual features on both AU detection and emotion classification tasks.
bullets: Addresses the lack of image-caption pairs for detailed facial expression description.
Synthesizes image-text training pairs by combining GPT-3.5 captions with emotion-category and facial-action-unit annotations.
Uses BLIP-2 pre-training techniques to link image encoders with large language models.
Generates descriptions capturing facial actions, emotional states, and their inferred relationships, including unseen emotions.
The learned visual features also improve facial action-unit detection and emotion classification.

papers.selection_reason: Vision-to-language model for facial expression captioning; fits multimodal LLM training and alignment.
papers.title: Describe Your Facial Expressions by Linking Image Encoders and Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A three-stage vision-language framework generates nuanced natural-language descriptions of facial actions and emotions from face images while improving related AU detection and emotion classification.

papers.abstract: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.
bullets: Model switching in long conversations normally repeats context prefill, while hybrid models additionally maintain recurrent and convolution histories.
HST transfers all three state types using structured recurrent-state maps and order-preserving convolution-history alignment.
Adapters are calibrated against the frozen target model’s continuation outputs; full-attention cache updates are merged offline.
Across five benchmarks, reported task retention is 89.88% for 4B→27B and 94.11% for 9B→27B transfers.
On synthetic 16K inputs with source caches available, handoff body speedups are 21.66× and 21.91×.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-model state handoff for hybrid linear-attention LLMs; directly targets KV cache and recurrent-state transfer efficiency.
papers.title: Beyond K/V Caches: Cross-Model State Handoff in Hybrid Linear-Attention LLMs
papers.tldr: Hybrid State Transfer enables efficient cross-model handoff by transferring full-attention, recurrent, and convolutional states, preserving up to 94.11% task performance with over 21× handoff speedups in tested settings.

papers.abstract: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of disentangling ego-motion from scene dynamics in 4D occupancy world models.
Uses explicit SE(2) geometric decoupling to create a purely dynamic feature space with attention-free temporal fusion.
Applies physics-constrained ODEs only to residual agent motion and ambiguous, high-uncertainty voxels.
The 28.3M-parameter FreeOcc-E runs at 27 FPS and reports 0.47 m NFCD and 32.1% mIoU on nuScenes.
Transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI and retains 92.8% of ideal mIoU under sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

figures.caption: Figure 16: Rain scene overview (nuScenes scene-0441). Left: front camera image showing wet road, reflections, and rain droplets. Right: LiDAR BEV coloured by height; the intersection geometry and parked vehicles are clearly visible despite rain-induced noise in the point cloud.

Figure 1: Overview of FreeOcc. Previous sweeps are encoded into BEV, fused by a continuoustime temporal aggregator, propagated to future ego frames by SE(2) warping, and decoded by the Discriminative Occupancy Decoder plus the Physics-Aware Continuous Flow Matching. The final prediction blends both paths using decoder uncertainty.

Figure 3: 4D occupancy forecasting on nuScenes(sample 1720) in BEV and 3D views across six horizons. FreeOcc-E is compared against OccWorld and ViDAR; more qualitative examples are given in Section D.

Figure 2: Ego-aware future propagator. At each horizon, the warped BEV—obtained via SE(2) ego-motion alignment—is explicitly added to the residual scene dynamics predicted by a ConvGRU and a residual projector.

Figure 10: Zero-shot SemanticKITTI predictions (sample 2070). BEV and 3D occupancy predictions from a nuScenes-trained model evaluated on SemanticKITTI, comparing FreeOcc-E against OccWorld and ViDAR. Despite domain differences (64-beam LiDAR, different driving context, no fine-tuning), FreeOcc-E preserves road-level structure and major obstacles. The denser 64-beam input provides richer geometric detail than nuScenes’s 32-beam data, and FreeOcc adapts without retraining, an advantage of operating on raw 3D geometry rather than appearance-dependent features.

Figure 6: Long-horizon comparison at τ=6 (3.0 s, nuScenes sample 3380). Ground Truth, OccWorld, FreeOcc-D, and FreeOcc-E are shown in paired BEV and 3D views. At 3.0 s, OccWorld exhibits boundary blur and noise around moving objects. FreeOcc-D slightly over-predicts occupancy, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves sharper boundaries and cleaner free space.

Figure 5: Temporal evolution of GT vs. FreeOcc-E (nuScenes sample 1730). Top row: groundtruth occupancy at τ=2 (1.0 s), τ=4 (2.0 s), and τ=6 (3.0 s), each shown as BEV (left) and 3D voxel rendering (right). Bottom row: corresponding FreeOcc-E predictions. Agreement is strongest at short horizons. By τ=6, the main discrepancies appear in the far field and around dynamic actors, while large static structures remain well preserved.

Figure 11: Additional zero-shot SemanticKITTI scene (sample 1080) and noise suppression analysis. Top: 3D occupancy predictions at the maximum forecasting horizon (τ = 6, 3.0s), comparing our model variants (FreeOcc-D, -G, -E) against Ground Truth. Bottom: BEV temporal evolution at τ = 3 and τ = 6. Road geometry, vegetation boundaries, and building walls are consistently captured, reinforcing the cross-domain robustness reported in Table 4.

Figure 7: 3D voxel-level uncertainty across prediction horizons (scene-0274, τ=1 to τ=6). Each panel renders occupied voxels coloured by the decoder’s predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv; cool tones indicate low uncertainty and warm tones indicate high. At short horizons, uncertainty is concentrated near dynamic actors and occupancy boundaries. As the horizon increases, uncertainty expands into the far field and intensifies around moving objects. By τ=6 (3.0 s), most remaining structures are assigned substantially higher uncertainty. This behaviour is consistent with the ensemble design in Section 3.7, which assigns more weight to the ODE path where decoder confidence weakens.

Figure 4: BEV visualization of 4D occupancy forecasting (additional scene, sample 0970). Columns span τ=1 to τ=6, comparing FreeOcc against OccWorld and ViDAR on a dense urban scene with multiple interacting vehicles. FreeOcc-E preserves scene layout and object extent more faithfully over the full 3.0 s horizon, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR drift more noticeably after τ=3.

Figure 8: Noise suppression analysis (nuScenes sample 1290). Paired BEV and 3D views highlighting hallucinated occupancy at long prediction horizons between FreeOcc-D and FreeOcc-E. FreeOcc-E clears vacated space more effectively while preserving plausible future object positions.

Figure 12: Robustness on nuScenes (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2500). Occupancy predictions under ideal and imperfect sensor conditions. FreeOcc-E retains its predictions under severe temporal perturbations, while OccWorld and ViDAR break into fragments and hallucinated clusters when temporal input is degraded.

Figure 13: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2090). Zero-shot predictions under ideal (top two rows) and imperfect (bottom two rows) sensor conditions. The cross-domain robustness gap compounds both the sensor-domain shift (nuScenes→SemanticKITTI) and the temporal perturbation, yet FreeOcc-E retains recognisable road and object geometry in both cases, while OccWorld and ViDAR suffer severe structural collapse.

Figure 14: Robustness on nuScenes at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 1600). Long-horizon predictions under ideal (top) and imperfect (bottom) sensor conditions. At the maximum forecasting horizon, OccWorld and ViDAR dissolve into discontiguous fragments, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves the road layout and principal object silhouettes. The gap between ideal and imperfect rows is noticeably smaller for FreeOcc-E than for OccWorld or ViDAR, consistent with the quantitative retention rate in Table 5.

Figure 15: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 2090). The most challenging evaluation setting: simultaneous cross-domain transfer, long-horizon prediction, and degraded sensor input. FreeOcc-E still recovers the overall road layout and major object boundaries, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR suffer near-complete structural collapse.

Figure 9: BEV uncertainty evolution (nuScenes scene-0220, τ=1 to τ=6). Each panel shows the BEV occupancy coloured by the predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv at horizon τ . Cool colours (cyan/green) indicate low uncertainty; warm colours (orange/red) indicate high uncertainty. Uncertainty increases with horizon and concentrates on dynamic objects and far-field voxels. Similar behaviour appears in Figure 7.
Table 1: 3D Geometry Forecasting on nuScenes. Evaluated via Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD, m) ↓, L1 Depth Error (m) ↓, and Absolute Relative Error (AbsRel, %) ↓.
Table 5: Robustness to sensor temporal imperfections on nuScenes. The imperfect setting adds severe timestamp jitter and 30% history-frame dropout. All metrics are voxel-based.

Table 6: Ablation study on nuScenes validation. Metrics are voxel-based. The results demonstrate that explicit geometric decoupling and physics-aware regularization are the primary drivers of forecasting quality.
Table 2: 4D Occupancy Forecasting on nuScenes. Evaluated via Class-Agnostic 3D Voxel mIoU (%) ↑.
Table 4: Zero-shot transfer from nuScenes to SemanticKITTI (no fine-tuning). We report metrics across short-term and long-term horizons to assess structural preservation under distribution shift.

Table 3: Efficiency comparison on nuScenes. We evaluate the parameter count and inference speed of our three variants: D (Decoder-only), G (Generation-only), and E (Ensemble) against representative baselines. All measurements are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090.
Table 10: Information-matched warp baselines versus FreeOcc on nuScenes.
Table 11: Static and dynamic mIoU on nuScenes.

Table 7: Inference latency on rain sequence (nuScenes scene-0441, 40 keyframes). Both FreeOcc variants maintain stable latency indistinguishable from dry-weather conditions. FreeOcc-E’s worstcase is still 1.4× faster than our OccWorld run under ideal conditions.
Table 13: Isolating the modality from the forecasting modules (6-horizon average on nuScenes).
Table 12: Comparison with SparseWorld-TC on our metrics ({1, 2, 3} s horizons).
Table 9: FreeOcc-E with a self-predicted trajectory (no future information).
Table 8: FreeOcc-E mIoU under injected future-trajectory error on nuScenes.

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned 4D occupancy forecasting world model with ego-motion decoupling; directly relevant to interactive/video world models and embodied navigation.
papers.title: FreeOcc: Decoupling Ego-Motion for Efficient 4D Occupancy Forecasting via Continuous Flow Matching
papers.tldr: FreeOcc is a lightweight 4D occupancy forecasting model that explicitly removes ego-motion and uses uncertainty-aware flow matching for efficient, robust prediction.

papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
bullets: Addresses the non-identifiability of latent states from observational data alone.
Proves affine identifiability with general injective emissions and Gaussian transitions.
Shows intervention-based identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift for general nonlinear latent dynamics.
Validates the theory on FitzHugh–Nagumo simulations and applies it to decision-making models and neural stimulation responses.
Provides simulation-based guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Nonlinear iSSM identifies a broader class of decision-making dynamics. Latent flow fields and trajectories for linear (left, blue) and nonlinear (right, magenta) iSSMs trained on interventional data from point-, line-, and bistable-well systems. Ground truth: gray arrows and black lines. Panels show best seed by Jacobian similarity; check marks indicate correct qualitative recovery.
