(a) iSSM leverages do-interventions to identify latent dynamics up to permutation, coordinate-wise scaling, and shift. (b) Two independent failure modes prevent SSMs from identifying the true dynamics g∗: identification error ϵ1, resolved by interventions, and hypothesis class mismatch ϵ2, resolved by a nonlinear model class. (c) Latent trajectory recovery across model class (rows) and data regime (columns): only a nonlinear model trained on interventional data recovers the true trajectory (gray).

Figure 2: Nonlinear iSSM identifies FitzHugh-Nagumo latent dynamics. (a,b) Open-loop rollout and aligned latent trajectories on a test trial: true (black), linear iSSM (blue), nonlinear iSSM (magenta); mean ± s.d. across 10 seeds. Gray lines mark interventions. (c) Latent flow fields from the seed with highest Jacobian similarity to ground truth. Gray/black: true flow (arrows) and trajectory (line); blue/magenta: inferred linear/nonlinear flow and trajectories. (d) Median inferred input map B after permutation-scale alignment. (e) Latent-dimension sweep over D ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} shows that model selection picks out the true dimension (D = 2).

Figure 4: Nonlinear iSSM outperforms linear iSSM on macaque prefrontal cortex recordings. (a,b) Example reconstructions and rollouts: observations (black), linear iSSM (blue), nonlinear iSSM (magenta); mean ± s.d. across seeds. Gray lines mark interventions. (c,d) Reconstruction and rollout accuracy on held-out control and stimulation trials. Asterisks: p < 0.05.

Figure 5: Nonlinear iSSM predicts human iEEG stimulation responses more accurately, including at a held-out site. (a) Axial view: recording contacts, stimulation sites, annotated epileptogenic contacts, and the held-out site. (b) Rollouts for the held-out site trial: observations (black), linear iSSM (blue), nonlinear iSSM (magenta); mean ± s.d. across seeds. Grey line: stimulation pulse. (c,d) Reconstruction and rollout accuracy on held-in and held-out site trials. Asterisks: p < 0.05.

Figure 7: Nonlinear iSSM identifies Van Der Pol oscillator latent dynamics. (a,b) Open-loop rollout and aligned latent trajectories on a test trial: true (black), linear iSSM (blue), nonlinear iSSM (magenta); mean ± s.d. across 10 seeds. Gray lines mark interventions. (c) Latent flow fields from the seed with highest Jacobian similarity to ground truth. Gray/black: true flow (arrows) and trajectory (line); blue/magenta: inferred linear/nonlinear flow and trajectories. (d) Median inferred input map B after permutation-scale alignment. (e) Latent-dimension sweep over D ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} shows that model selection picks out the true dimension (D = 2).

Figure 6: Numerous and diverse interventions improve latent recovery. (a) Latent accuracy improves with more training interventions. (b) Diverse amplitudes and irregular timing yield higher latent accuracy; boxes: 10 seeds, ***p < 0.001 main effect. (c) Latent accuracy versus rollout (black) and reconstruction (gray) accuracy; gray dashed line: identity.

Figure 11: Intervention-design trends replicate on point and line attractors. Top row (a-c): point attractor; bottom row (d-f): line attractor. Panel layout matches Fig. 6: (a,d) latent accuracy versus intervention count; (b,e) amplitude-timing factorial (10 seeds); (c,f) latent accuracy versus rollout (black) and reconstruction (gray); dashed line: identity.

Figure 12: Latent accuracy under softened interventions and model comparison. Sweep over the intervention hardness parameter α of the data-generating process, from a purely additive drive (α = 0) to a hard clamp (α = 1), comparing nonlinear iSSM to two baselines. (a) Bistable well (App. J.1). (b) FitzHugh-Nagumo replication (App. J.2). Asterisks indicate α-regimes where iSSM significantly outperforms both baselines (p < 0.05).

Figure 10: Virtual stimulation of clinically annotated sites. (a) Peak and (b) sustained networkwide response ∥∆y∥ to virtual stimulation of healthy (n = 51) and epileptogenic (n = 26) bipolar pairs, under the linear and the nonlinear iSSM. Mann-Whitney U tests, FDR-corrected over the two readouts and two models; ∗ ∗ ∗: p < 0.001.

Figure 8: Accuracy versus latent dimension D. (a) Reconstruction and (b) rollout accuracy for linear (blue) and nonlinear (magenta) iSSMs; mean ± s.e.m. across 10 seeds. Asterisks mark significant differences (p < 0.05, FDR-corrected).

Figure 9: Accuracy versus latent dimension D. (a) Reconstruction and (b) rollout accuracy for linear (blue) and nonlinear (magenta) iSSMs; mean ± s.e.m. across 10 seeds. Asterisks mark significant differences (p < 0.05, FDR-corrected).

papers.selection_reason: Extends interventional state-space models to identify nonlinear neural dynamics, which is highly relevant to Latent Action Models and the architectural trends in Large Language Models (e.g., Mamba).
papers.title: Identifying Neural Dynamics Using Nonlinear Interventional State Space Models
papers.tldr: Interventions enable nonlinear state-space models to identify latent neural dynamics beyond the linear settings of prior work.

papers.abstract: Tensor network kernel machines (TNKMs) combine nonlinear features with low-rank tensor representations to model complex relationships efficiently. However, selecting an appropriate tensor rank remains challenging, as conventional rank-search methods require training multiple candidate models, increasing computational costs. In this work, we focus on a canonical polyadic (CP) tensor network parameterization and propose GB-CPKM, a gradient boosting framework that builds a higher-capacity predictor by sequentially adding fixed-rank learners. This approach provides a new perspective on rank selection by incrementally increasing model capacity, with ensemble size selected based on validation performance rather than through explicit rank search. Experiments on real-world regression benchmarks show that GB-CPKM trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory than a conventional rank-selection method based on cross-validation, while achieving comparable predictive performance. These results highlight the potential of gradient boosting to improve the computational efficiency and scalability of tensor-network learning.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of selecting tensor ranks in tensor network kernel machines.
Uses a canonical polyadic (CP) parameterization with gradient boosting to incrementally increase model capacity.
Selects ensemble size through validation performance instead of training many candidate ranks.
On real-world regression benchmarks, trains up to 6× faster and uses up to 2× less peak memory than cross-validation-based rank selection.
Achieves comparable predictive performance, with scope demonstrated on regression tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Ablation study of base-learner rank in GB-CPKM on four real-world datasets, with each column corresponding to a dataset. The top row shows cumulative training time (in seconds), while the bottom row reports validation MSE on a logarithmic scale. Across the evaluated datasets, higher-rank base learners achieve better predictive performance while also reducing cumulative training time. However, rank selection should also account for memory requirements, which may constrain the use of higher-rank models in practice.

Figure 1: Comparison of the training procedures for CP tensor network kernel machines (CPKMs) using gradient boosting (GB) and rank selection via validation (CV). (a) GB-CPKM incrementally builds an ensemble by training fixed-rank R̂ base learners and concatenating their factor matrices along the rank dimension to represent the combined model. The ensemble size M is selected based on validation performance. (b) In contrast, CV-CPKM independently trains candidate models with different CP ranks and selects the rank that achieves the lowest validation error. In the diagrams, each base learner model is represented by D factor matrices of size I ˆ R̂, where I is the number of rows and R̂ is the CP rank. Different colors distinguish the trainable factor matrices. Factors in gray are fixed and are not updated.

Figure 3: Comparison of GB-CPKM (red) and CV-CPKM (blue) on four real-world datasets, with each column corresponding to a dataset. From top to bottom, the rows show cumulative training time (in seconds), test MSE, and peak memory consumption (in MiB), plotted against the number of considered candidate CP ranks. Solid lines indicate the mean across 10 runs, and shaded regions represent ˘ 1 standard deviation. GB-CPKM consistently requires less training time and peak memory than CV-CPKM, while achieving comparable predictive performance. The test MSE of GB-CPKM is similar to that of CV-CPKM, with overlapping variability bands in some cases, and approaches comparable values across the evaluated datasets. These results highlight the potential of GB-CPKM to reduce computational costs without substantially compromising predictive accuracy.

Table 1: Performance comparison of GB-CPKM and CV-CPKM across regression benchmarks. We report test mean squared error (MSE), training time (seconds), and peak memory consumption (MiB). Each experiment is repeated over 10 runs, with results reported as mean ˘ 1 standard deviation. N denotes the number of samples, and D denotes the input dimensionality. Overall, GB-CPKM trains up to 6ˆ faster and uses up to 2ˆ less peak memory, on average, than CV-CPKM, while achieving comparable test MSE. The hybrid variant, GB-CPKM(H), further improves predictive performance on most datasets by performing an additional full ALS sweep on the combined model.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a gradient boosting framework to improve the computational efficiency (training speed and memory) of tensor network kernel machines, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Gradient Boosting for Efficient Rank Discovery in Tensor Network Kernel Machines
papers.tldr: GB-CPKM avoids expensive explicit tensor-rank searches by sequentially boosting fixed-rank tensor network kernel learners.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives. On layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, contribution is far more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and the overlap between dominant sets concentrates on a few expert pairs. Auto-interpreting these sets reveals a division of labor below coarse domains, with distinct experts for Java and front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials, while the coarse domains themselves take very unequal numbers of experts. Our SAEs and code are available at https://github.com/Bytedance-Seed/SAE-Interprets-MoE.
bullets: MoE expert specialization is analyzed in feature space rather than through predefined domain labels.
An SAE trained on MoE-layer outputs enables exact decomposition of each latent’s activation across experts.
Across Qwen3-30B-A3B layers 4, 30, and 46, expert contribution is more concentrated than selection, with most latents driven by only one or two experts.
Expert overlap is concentrated in a few pairs, and interpreted latent sets reveal distinctions such as Java versus front-end code and geometry versus arithmetic/polynomials.
The analysis is scoped to selected layers of Qwen3-30B-A3B; SAEs and code are released.

figures.caption: Figure 1 An MoE layer outputs a router-weighted sum of its active experts (left), and since the SAE encoder is affine, each latent’s activation decomposes exactly over these experts (middle). Thresholding the contribution fractions averaged over a corpus gives the dominance graph (right), and auto-interpreting the latents an expert dominates describes its role (bottom), such as a Java expert (E50) and a front-end web expert (E57) at layer 30 of Qwen3-30B-A3B.
Figure 2 Rank profiles of the gating weight and of the contribution. C̄r is markedly steeper than ḡr.

Figure 6 Latent-side degree distribution of the dominance graph, the share of the 220 latents that are dominated by exactly 0, . . . , 4 experts. In every layer more than half of the latents have a single dominator. Degree 4 accounts for at most 0.014% and is not visible at this scale.

Figure 8 Pairwise Jaccard similarity of the expert dominant sets at τ = 0.2, with the experts in their original index order on both axes. The three layers share one colour scale, which saturates at 0.05, and the diagonal is masked.

Figure 7 Expert-side degree of the dominance graph, the number of latents each expert dominates, with the 128 experts of each layer sorted by degree in ascending order. The horizontal axis is a rank rather than an expert identity. No expert has degree zero in any layer.
Figure 3 Explanation word clouds of three experts of layer 30. Word size is the frequency among the explanations of the latents sampled from the expert’s dominant set.

Figure 4 Word clouds of expert 72 of layer 30, built from (a) routed tokens weighted by gating mass, (b) the same tokens reweighted by their contribution to mutual information without the top five function words, and (c) latent explanations. papers.abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.
bullets: Targets mobile deployment under compute and memory constraints without additional training.
Decomposes grouped-layer weights into shared SVD-derived dictionaries and sparse, layer-specific coefficients.
Uses Hessian-aware sparsification, dictionary refinement, and factor-specific quantization.
On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, it outperforms existing post-training low-rank methods.
Compresses LLaMA-7B by 5.1× with a 2.9-point WikiText-2 perplexity increase; the abstract reports a 3.6× higher compression ratio than the prior low-rank state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 1: DictLLM: Dictionary-based compression method. DictLLM resolves the weight memory bottleneck by compressing transformer weights into a shareable dictionary. It compounds four compression steps. ➊ The first step factorizes input-scaled weight matrices of grouped layers into a shared dictionary and layer-specific coefficients. ➋ We then prune the layer-specific coefficients using a dictionary-aware Hessian. ➌ We refit the shared dictionary to the resulting sparse coefficients. ➍ We quantize both the dictionary and the coefficients into NVFP4 using input statistics for the dictionary and dictionary-aware Hessians for the coefficients. The resulting compressed representation enables efficient projections by transferring a small set of shared dictionaries.

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/racercode/Mustard
bullets: Targets dynamics-based industrial anomalies, such as irregular movements, that static visual methods may miss.
Uses optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to model local motion patterns and global temporal evolution.
Employs normal-pattern reasoning without model updates, supporting efficient adaptation across products.
Experiments show strong detection of spatiotemporal anomalies and plausible explanations.
Scope: designed for motion-related defects; the abstract does not quantify performance or specify datasets.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot. Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assumingthat the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a k-nearest neighbors (KNN)- based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal learning tool, but as an effective basis for ad hoc coordination. Website: https://proroklab.github.io/PAVE/
bullets: Addresses ad hoc cooperation between previously unpaired robots operating sequentially in the same environment.
Shares value functions to communicate each robot’s environmental preferences and support coordination.
Uses a KNN-based uncertainty filter to reduce overconfident decisions in unfamiliar states.
Improves task success by up to 48.5 percentage points over naive or selfish agents in simulated and real-world experiments.

papers.abstract: We present a progressive imitation framework that learns terrain-appropriate humanoid parkour skills and subsequently adapts their hand--knee support. Human demonstrations provide traversal behaviors, but their contact patterns need not suit a robot's proportions or the available support surfaces. Our framework changes the role of demonstrations across three stages: privileged imitation produces physically executable robot references; terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide skill acquisition; and geometric support guidance with a reduced motion-prior weight enables contact adaptation. Candidate-based precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation guide support without prescribing a contact sequence. The deployed policy selects behaviors from onboard depth, proprioception, and velocity commands without an external skill label. On the Noetix E1, the policy achieves 96.34\% hybrid success in simulation and transfers without real-world policy fine-tuning, completing 29 of 30 individual obstacle trials and four of five hybrid courses. Support-adaptation ablations show higher traversal success for the complete adaptation stage on the tested terrains, while qualitative observations show changes in contact placement. These results support acquiring skills from demonstrations before relaxing their influence to accommodate robot-specific support configurations.
bullets: Human demonstrations are converted into physically executable robot references before skill learning.
Terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide parkour acquisition, then reduced prior influence allows geometric support adaptation.
Candidate precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation guide support without prescribing a fixed contact sequence.
The onboard policy uses depth, proprioception, and velocity commands without an external skill label.
On the Noetix E1, it achieves 96.34% hybrid simulation success, completes 29/30 individual obstacle trials and 4/5 hybrid courses; results are limited to the tested terrains and tasks.

Geometric hand–knee candidates (bottom) guide precontact placement, while contact evaluation and state transitions determine support and retention terms. Task, style, and support rewards are combined with the weights in Eq. 1 for actor–critic training. The actor and critic use gated expert networks, distinct from the discriminator heads. At deployment, only the actor and its observation-processing modules are retained; privileged geometry, reference motions, discriminators, and the critic remain in training.

papers.abstract: Diet is a major determinant of health, yet accurate dietary assessment from free-living meal images remains challenging. Existing retrieval-based Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches to nutrient estimation typically rely on textual food representations, while, to our knowledge, direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated. We present NutriVisRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a vision encoder to retrieve similar meals with known nutritional annotations and provide them as multimodal in-context exemplars for VLM nutrient estimation at inference time, without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate NutriVisRAG across four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including free-living meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes, where carbohydrate estimates are compared against two dietitians' annotations. Across all 96 configurations (4 datasets x 4 VLMs x 3 retrieval encoders x 2 prompting strategies), NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, with improvements more frequent under whole-meal (35/48) than per-item prompting (21/48). Across the evaluated configurations, the lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM--dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini, under whole-meal prompting, the best-performing retrieval encoder for each dataset reduced the primary error on all four datasets relative to Vanilla, with reductions of 1.7--35.7%. Overall, our results show that grounding in multimodal exemplars comprising images and respective annotations can improve nutrient estimation at inference time without task-specific fine-tuning, although the benefits remain configuration-dependent.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating nutrients from free-living meal images, where textual retrieval may not capture visual similarity.
Uses a vision encoder to retrieve annotated meals and supplies their images and nutritional labels as inference-time exemplars.
Evaluated 96 configurations spanning four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies.
Reduced primary estimation error in 56/96 configurations, with more frequent gains for whole-meal prompting than per-item prompting.
Benefits were configuration-dependent, though the best retrieval setup improved GPT-5.4-mini results on all four datasets under whole-meal prompting.

papers.abstract: Enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to control humanoid robots requires both reliable whole-body interfaces and knowledge of how to use the body that carries over across tasks. We present HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command Humanoids), a harness in which perception returns the 3D position of any point the VLM selects in its image, and execution turns commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking, and gaze into whole-body motion with a learned tracker. We find that both measuring the scene and executing commands accurately raise task success. We then fine-tune a VLM on trajectories in which teacher policies solve five base tasks through HITCH, so that it learns how to operate the humanoid. Without task-specific trajectories, the fine-tuned model completes 51% of SIMPLE episodes and 42.5% of HumanoidArena episodes, and adding five trajectories per SIMPLE task raises its SIMPLE success to 95%. On a real G1, it carries a box and walks to a goal without real training data.
bullets: Addresses reliable perception, control interfaces, and transferable body-use knowledge for VLM-controlled humanoids.
Maps selected image points to 3D positions and converts pelvis, torso, hand, walking, and gaze commands into motion using a learned tracker.
Fine-tunes the VLM on teacher-policy trajectories covering five base tasks.
Achieves 51% success on SIMPLE and 42.5% on HumanoidArena without task-specific trajectories; five trajectories per SIMPLE task increase success to 95%.
Demonstrates real-world box carrying and goal-directed walking on a G1 without real training data.

papers.abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL
bullets: Targets privacy-preserving medical FL under long-tailed local and global data distributions.
Addresses the common assumption that test data follow a uniform, known distribution.
Uses adaptive re-sampling, expert-classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to reduce classifier and feature-space bias.
Ensembles retrained expert classifiers at inference to handle agnostic test distributions.
Experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: GTAFL framework workflow: (1) Clients receive global model and expert parameters, then perform local training with GI-GDS sampling and gradient computation. (2) Clients transmit class-wise gradients and model parameters to the server. (3) Server performs aggregation, expert retraining using optimized global federated features, and self-supervised refinement with unlabeled data. (4) The server sends the updated global model and expert classifiers parameters to clients. (5) Expert ensemble inference for test-agnostic prediction.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for language-model post-training, combining dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories. This creates a feedback loop where each update changes the student and thereby the training distribution that generates subsequent updates. Yet, how this feedback shapes learning and generalization remains poorly understood. We conduct a mechanistic analysis of OPD's learning dynamics, distinguishing the two feedback loop stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast through which these updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape the rollout distribution. This framework helps us understand both limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also increase the probability of unsuccessful continuations, exposing the student to unreliable supervision in subsequent rollouts. Finally, we show that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy. While OPD alone may degrade generation, it can yield substantial accuracy gains after sufficient offline preparation. Together, our results connect teacher supervision, student geometry, and the evolving rollout distribution in determining the learning dynamics of OPD and its effects on downstream performance.
bullets: OPD couples teacher supervision with student-generated trajectories, creating a changing training distribution.
The analysis separates learning into signal-to-update conversion and broadcast of updates across prefixes and rollouts.
Students may respond weakly despite large teacher–student disagreement because of parameter and prediction geometry.
Local improvements in teacher agreement can increase unsuccessful continuations, causing degeneration through unreliable supervision.
Offline distillation can prepare students for substantial later gains in OPD, even without immediate held-out accuracy improvements.

Figure 1: OPD’s learning dynamics, visualizing the feedback loop at the top (detailed in Section 3.1), and illustrative successful and failing processes at the bottom in reasoning settings we analyzed empirically. In principle, OPD propagates current teacher requests Γt(s)|s∼µt to motion at any future prefix x through shared parameters, captured by the Neural Tangent Kernel K(x, s). papers.abstract: Service Robots are becoming a reality and are progressing by leaps and bounds. Alongside this avenue of robotics is also the field of prosthetics, which is evolving rapidly. These topics are hot cakes in the industry and are widely developed. Some have one quality, and some have others, but are making a shoreline towards success. The development of arm and hand as individual or as a package is becoming common as more and more advanced collaborative robots come to the surface and join their human counterparts in the real world. This dissertation presents an open-source 3D-printed arm which was assembled and programmed on two fronts. The first is the control of the hand by utilising teleoperation with a camera and ML-based hand pose estimation. Secondly, it is the control via kinematics utilising the Denavit-Hartenberg method to define the motion and to find the position of the end effector in 3D space.
bullets: Targets collaborative and home-service robotics through an anthropomorphic arm and hand.
Uses camera-based teleoperation with machine-learning hand-pose estimation.
Applies Denavit–Hartenberg kinematics to define motion and determine the end-effector’s 3D position.
The arm is assembled and programmed across both teleoperation and kinematic-control approaches.

papers.abstract: We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by trans- forming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordi- nate frame. This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training. The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios. We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions. Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data. This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance. However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization. To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.
bullets: Canonicalizes obstacle configurations into a shared coordinate frame so a surrogate trained on one reference mission can support others.
The neural surrogate predicts minimum UAV–obstacle clearance and guides test generation toward critical scenarios.
On the Aerialist test bench, it achieved a 42% average critical-test-case hit rate versus about 10% for the constrained-random baseline.
The approach maintained high input diversity and competitive performance against recent UAV testing competition techniques.
Reproducibility resources include the trained surrogate and over 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.

papers.abstract: Physical human--robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.
bullets: Addresses the need for intrinsically bounded and safe physical human–robot interactions.
Introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP).
Provides an open-source deployment suite integrating ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware.
Evaluates trajectory tracking, sudden loss of wall contact, and learning-by-demonstration on a Kinova Gen3 arm.
Finds that H-PMP smoothly trades off between admittance and impedance without computational overhead, supporting unstructured-environment use.

papers.abstract: Current language-guided 3D object placement typically predicts a rigid 6-DoF pose, ignoring the physical reality that indoor placements are dictated by contact. Consequently, predicted poses often float, interpenetrate supports, or fail to deform soft surfaces. We propose Deformable Contact-Aware Placement (DCAP), a framework that reframes placement as a drop-to-equilibrium process. Rather than predicting a static pose, DCAP constructs a semantic release state that specifies the drop location, object scale, and deformable components, allowing a coupled rigid-deformable simulator to settle the object under gravity and friction. This explicitly separates semantic intent from physical realization. Evaluated on a benchmark of 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases, DCAP significantly outperforms static baselines. On standard placements, it improves VLM Physics & Naturalness by 21.2 points and human preference by 26.5 points over the strongest raw rigid baseline, while reducing mean penetration depth by 72.3%. Compared to simulated rollout baselines, DCAP reduces residual speed by 72.1%. Ultimately, our results prove that physically accurate 3D placement requires modeling semantic intent and physical realization as strictly separate processes.
bullets: Targets floating objects, support interpenetration, and failure to deform soft surfaces in rigid 6-DoF placement.
Predicts a semantic release state—drop location, object scale, and deformable components—rather than a final pose.
Uses coupled rigid-deformable simulation with gravity and friction to realize the placement through drop-to-equilibrium.
On 2,063 prompt–asset–scene cases, it improves physics/naturalness and human preference while substantially reducing penetration and residual motion.
The approach separates semantic intent from physical realization; its scope is indoor placement involving contact and deformability.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are a widely adopted starting point for remote sensing tasks. Most are pretrained on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery at a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. Many applications instead rely on very high resolution (VHR) imagery, where individual buildings, roads, and amenities are resolved. We study which pretraining regimes transfer well to this scale. We introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark suite of ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer spanning five task families, eight application domains, and both satellite and aerial platforms. We evaluate twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions. We find that both pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining transfer effectively to VHR tasks, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce; at the full label fraction the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead, with the two close together there. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. Guided by these complementary results, we continue the self-supervised pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluate the resulting encoder without changing the downstream protocol. The continued model gives a clear improvement over the released backbone when labels are scarce and a modest one at the full fraction, at no increase in inference parameters or compute. These findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: already strong, broad natural-image pretraining can be further improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.
bullets: Introduces VHR-Bench: ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer, covering five task families, eight domains, and satellite and aerial imagery.
Evaluates twelve frozen encoders across three pretraining tiers and two labeled-data fractions.
SkySense performs best with scarce labels; at the full label fraction, DINOv3 ViT-L is slightly ahead, with both closely matched.
Continuing DINOv3 ViT-L pretraining on 1.02 million VHR tiles improves performance, especially when labels are scarce, without increasing inference parameters or compute.

papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $ρ=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.
bullets: Covers theorem proving, solver engineering, mathematical constructions, and attempts on open conjectures.
TCSExam-Full has 100 expert-reviewed tasks; TCSExam-Lite has 20 tasks and reduces attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget.
Tasks are validated by the Lean kernel or executable checkers, enabling objective evaluation.
GPT-6 Astra leads Full with an index of 71.9, while Opus 5.5 leads Lite with 72.3; rankings strongly align (Spearman’s ρ=0.93).
Evaluations produced improved solver outputs, constructions, and independently verified special cases and bounds for open-conjecture attempts.

papers.abstract: Generating compositional 3D scenes from a single image requires recovering detailed object geometry and coherent spatial arrangements. Existing object-to-scene methods, including SAM3D and MIDI, extend object generation through image-context reasoning or inter-instance modeling. Coordinating objects remains challenging with limited scene-level supervision. Directly extending object-centric generators to entire scenes can degrade geometry and fail to preserve instance scale, orientation, and pose. We propose Bri3D, a framework bridging scene-level structural reasoning and object-level generative priors through instance-aware voxel scene anchors. Bri3D predicts a color-coded scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, enabling a frozen object generator to synthesize detailed textured geometry in the anchor-defined spatial reference. This coarse-to-fine design separates scene organization from object-scale detail synthesis, focusing scene-level training on spatial organization and anchor refinement while reusing pretrained object priors. Experiments demonstrate improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality, and generalization. Bri3D predicts scene layouts efficiently; full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.
bullets: Addresses poor coordination between object geometry and scene-level spatial organization in single-image 3D generation.
Predicts a color-coded voxel scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements.
Extracts each instance into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible scene anchor for refinement.
Reuses pretrained object-level generative priors while training scene components mainly for organization and anchor refinement.
Reports improved layout, geometry, visual quality, and generalization, with faster full-scene generation than SceneGen and SAM3D.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Generalization to diverse room scenes. The upper three rows compare reconstructions of a living room, a garage, and a classroom, with the input image followed by the results of DepR, PartCrafter, MIDI, SceneGen, SAM3D, and Bri3D. The lower row shows a multi-room overview and reconstructions of its bathroom, bedroom, living room, and kitchen, each generated from a separate room-level input. Together, the examples illustrate object reconstruction across varied scene configurations and room types.

The Scene Scaffold Generator and Anchored Voxel Refiner replace the voxel-generation stage of a two-stage object generator, while its detail-synthesis stage remains frozen. SC-VAE denotes the StructureColor VAE, and snowflakes indicate frozen modules. The scaffold is generated in latent space and decoded at 1283; each object is refined to a 643 voxel support. The anchor initialization follows Eq. 5, including object-wise latent normalization.

Figure 5 Comparison of 3D scene layouts and failure cases. (a) Columns show the RGB input, ground-truth layout, and predictions from MIDI [18], SceneGen [28], SAM3D [3], and Bri3D. Red wireframe boxes mark the groundtruth object extents, making displacement, missing instances, and shape deviations visible. Bri3D better follows the reference arrangements in these examples. (b) Red rectangles highlight our failures: nearby objects may merge in the cluttered seating area (Case 1), and some instances may be omitted in the densely populated classroom (Case 2).

Figure 6 Color-coded scene scaffold vs. connected component analysis. From left to right: RGB input, instance label map, geometry-only CCA result, and the predicted color-coded voxel grid. In the upper example, CCA groups the refrigerator, microwave, and table into one connected region; in the lower example, it merges the touching bed components and teddy bear. The predicted instance colors provide additional separation cues at these contacts, allowing joint position–color clustering to recover distinct object anchors. Colors indicate instance identity rather than surface texture.

The dining-area and bedroom examples include room surfaces together with foreground furniture, illustrating how structural labels can extend the scaffold beyond object instances. This extension depends on reliable labels for those regions and remains preliminary; floors, walls, and ceilings are excluded from the main Bri3D experiments and quantitative results.

Figure 8 Additional qualitative comparisons and robustness to imperfect segmentation. (a) Geometry and layout comparisons with MIDI and SAM3D on indoor and outdoor scenes; MIDI is shown with normal shading. Bri3D produces coherent layouts and faithful object geometry, while MIDI suffers from distorted shapes and implausible arrangements. (b) With an erroneous instance label map (Wrong Seg), Bri3D exhibits only local cracks, whereas SAM3D produces incorrect object partitions and collisions, including interpenetration between the teddy bear and the bed.

Figure 9 Robustness to instance segmentation granularity, label colors, and implausible partitions. From left to right: input image, input instance segmentation, predicted semantic voxel grid, and reconstructed textured meshes with bounding boxes. The first two rows show the same tabletop scene containing a bottle, a mug, a large box, a ball, and two small stacks of blocks. The segmentation changes only the grouping of these small stacks: each stack receives one label in the first row, while its individual blocks receive separate labels in the second row. The last two rows show deliberately implausible partitions of a chair, together with changes in instance label colors. Despite these inconsistent instance boundaries, Bri3D preserves the overall object geometry and spatial arrangement.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.
bullets: Addresses the blind spot where on-policy students rarely train on teacher-reached states outside their own rollout distribution.
Uses maximal coupling of speculative decoding to interpolate between student and teacher rollouts while preserving the standard on-policy loss.
Keeps the student token when distributions agree and substitutes underweighted target tokens otherwise; interventions decrease as learning progresses.
Across six students and five public math benchmarks, CoRD improves average pass@1 by 0.9–2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2–3.4 points over on-policy distillation.
On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student closes the gap in 16 steps with CoRD, versus not reaching closure in 80 steps for on-policy distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CORD. (i) Left (OPD’s blind spot): On-policy distillation trains only on student rollouts. Teacher-preferred reasoning paths that the student rarely or never visits therefore receive little or no supervision. (ii) Right (our coupled sampler): CORD keeps the same training loss and budget, but changes the rollout sampler. By coupling the student with a teacher-leaning target qα, it preserves agreeing tokens and replaces disagreements with underweighted target tokens. This maximal coupling steers rollouts into teacher-preferred states missed by OPD with the minimum possible intervention rate, minimally perturbing the student’s original trajectory.

Figure 3: Visited-state divergence and held-out accuracy. CORD maintains higher visited-state reverse KL and ends with higher held-out pass@1 for all six students in Table 1. Top: reverse KL to the teacher at states visited during training (5-step moving average). Bottom: pass@1 on about 200 held-out problems from the training distribution, evaluated at steps 0, 40 and 80.

Figure 4: Teacher-side closure and replacement rate. For the 4B-Base student and Qwen3-8B-Base teacher, CORD reaches in 16 steps the closure on teacher-reached states that OPD fails to reach in 80. Left and middle: closure of the reverse KL to the teacher on frozen teacher-reached and student-reached states, measured every 8 steps. Right: the realized replacement rate, which falls slowly as the student approaches the target.
Figure 2: One-step coupled sampling. On a threetoken vocabulary with α = 0.6, student proposals are kept whenever possible and replaced only when necessary, so the emitted token follows qα exactly.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D models use Transformers to predict camera poses, depth, and structure in one pass, avoiding iterative multi-view optimization. Long sequences and deep attention incur high compute and memory costs, motivating Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) for deployment. Existing PTQ methods mainly suppress channel-wise outliers by smoothing or orthogonal rotation. Geometry Transformers introduce a different challenge: heterogeneous token types share one activation quantization grid. A few special tokens may exert high leverage over global outputs and be updated by only a subset of blocks. Token-blind transforms, which apply the same transformation to every token, reduce overall quantization error but cannot remove differentiated degradation across token types. We propose QMapAnything, a structure-aware PTQ framework. We cast floating-point-preserving rotation and smoothing as a token-blind reparameterization group, and prove that they yield common-mode gains while leaving relative token SNR unchanged. We introduce a statistic $Γ$ that combines a special token's quantization disadvantage and output leverage to predict whether differentiated bias correction is needed beyond rotation. Experiments on geometric benchmarks show that W4A8 closely matches full-precision performance. Under W8A8, peak memory falls by $2.2$--$3.1\times$ versus FP32, with up to $3.1\times$ speedup on real hardware. These results provide a principled and efficient approach to deploying feed-forward 3D reconstruction models in resource-constrained edges.
bullets: Feed-forward geometry Transformers face high compute and memory costs, while heterogeneous tokens share a single activation quantization grid.
Token-blind reparameterizations reduce overall quantization error but cannot change relative signal-to-noise differences between token types.
The proposed statistic Γ combines special-token quantization disadvantage with output leverage to predict the need for differentiated bias correction.
Experiments report near-full-precision performance with W4A8; W8A8 reduces peak memory by 2.2–3.1× and achieves up to 3.1× hardware speedup.
The approach targets deployment of feed-forward 3D reconstruction models on resource-constrained edge devices.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of QMapAnything on a quantized Transformer block. attn.qkv, mlp.w12 and mlp.w3 apply a rotation matrix transform R to their input, the matching inverse folded offline into the weights. attn.proj needs no input-side transform, since its rotation is absorbed entirely into Wproj. R is the group element addressing S3. The standard token-uniform correction removes a shared systematic offset and can be folded into a layer bias. The group-external term bs targets the S1–S2 interaction by correcting only the special-token row.
Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on three scenes. MapAnything is the FP32 reconstruction. RTN, QuaRot, and QMapAnything are W4A4.

Figure 3: Structural properties of MapAnything that guide the PTQ recipe. (a): block-wise relative scale error. Global blocks (red) are more sensitive than frame blocks, consistent with S4. (b): histogram of flattened activation magnitudes |x| in attn.qkv. A few maxima set the per-tensor scale (S3). (c): patch vs. scale activation ranges. The type-level gap supports the shared-grid mismatch in S1. S2 follows from the multiplicative role of the scale token.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Uses pose-aligned structural tokens, read-only scene tokens, and write-once instance tokens to preserve roads, appearance, and traffic-participant identities.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.
bullets: Addresses privacy, copyright, and compliance constraints that prevent centralizing document ownership.
Uses lightweight neighbor advertisements and cached query history for semantic peer routing.
A best-first walk progressively rewires the overlay toward relevant peers, improving recall through self-organization.
Across three real-world workloads, ZeroRAG outperforms decentralized baselines on recall and network-message cost.
It approaches centralized-store recall and LLM answer accuracy, self-heals after catastrophic failures, and scales to 100,000 peers.

papers.abstract: Text-guided image editing with diffusion models struggles with spatial edits (e.g. manipulating objects, changing viewpoints, manipulating occlusions) that depend on the 3D structure understanding of a scene. Marigold and follow-up work demonstrate that a pretrained diffusion backbone already harbors strong geometric priors that can be activated for depth estimation, yet how to redirect these priors toward editing remains unresolved. Through per-layer gradient probing, we discover that the editing and depth objectives are compatible in early transformer layers but actively conflict in late layers, explaining why naive depth-conditioned editing either ignores geometry or degrades visual quality. We present StitchEdit, which first activates the backbone's geometric capability via a lightweight depth-denoising adapter, then selectively fine-tunes this adapter for editing using a probe-guided per-layer learning rate schedule that preserves depth knowledge where it helps and prunes it where it conflicts. On the proposed StitchEditBench, a benchmark of 150 geometry-dependent edits spanning spatial transformation, occlusion manipulation, and viewpoint change, StitchEdit consistently surpasses both instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines on perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.
bullets: Geometry-dependent edits such as viewpoint changes, spatial transformations, and occlusion manipulation remain challenging for text-guided diffusion editors.
Per-layer gradient probing finds that editing and depth objectives align in early layers but conflict in late layers.
A lightweight depth-denoising adapter activates geometric knowledge before probe-guided, layer-specific fine-tuning for editing.
On StitchEditBench, StitchEdit consistently outperforms instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines in perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.

papers.abstract: A child who learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace this to what learners read when deciding. A position, count or time takes new values as input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that saw no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
bullets: Coordinate-like inputs such as positions and counts can exceed training experience, while coincidence-based relations remain size-invariant.
The proposed memory uses cycles whose state grows with input size but is read through finite, symmetry-based observations, linked conceptually to grid cells, place cells, and hippocampal indexing.
Its computational power is characterized as equivalent to Turing-machine computation synchronized with input.
Trained on strings of at most 40 symbols, it solves five benchmark tasks that the abstract reports LSTMs and Transformers do not solve, including duplication and binary addition.
With larger cycles after training, it reverses a million-symbol string despite seeing no training string longer than five; performance fails beyond cycle capacity as theoretically predicted.

papers.abstract: Reasoning trajectories generated for the same problem often arrive at conflicting answers. These disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that can be reused to explore new solutions. We introduce Adaptive Semantic Branching (ASB), a training-free inference procedure that turns cross-trajectory disagreement into targeted candidate generation. ASB first groups independently sampled trajectories by extracted final answer, selects a representative from each group, and aligns their reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program. A persistent-divergence objective identifies the point at which initially similar reasoning paths develop different continuations. For each selected directed pair, ASB retains the source trajectory's textual prefix, extracts a short reasoning window from a competing donor trajectory, and generates a fresh solution conditioned on both. A diversity-aware policy allocates up to three additional generations according to the answer-cluster structure. In a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ASB increases oracle candidate coverage from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems. The method uses 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set, averaging 8.152 calls per problem. We provide a precise specification of the branching operator, alignment objective, generation policy, and experimental configuration.
bullets: Groups trajectories by final answer and selects representative paths from each answer cluster.
Aligns reasoning steps with monotonic dynamic programming to locate persistent divergences.
Combines a source trajectory prefix with a short competing reasoning window to regenerate solutions.
Allocates up to three extra generations based on answer-cluster diversity.
Recovered correct candidates for 10 of 55 initially uncovered problems using 576 additional generation calls overall.

papers.abstract: Memory summaries, prompts and steering vectors set a language model's beliefs and are judged by the prediction they produce. A prediction does not say how firmly it is held. We separate a belief's content, what it predicts now, from its weight, the number of new observations it is worth: for an ideal observer, the amount of evidence behind it. In Bernoulli inference we set beliefs in nine open-weight models of 8 to 397B parameters and follow each belief with the same new observations. We argue that these models hold an answer without its evidence and recover its weight from the text they re-read. Weight therefore follows the form of the evidence and the question asked more than its amount: matched on their current estimate, a record of observations and a summary of its counts usually move apart under the same new observations, in either direction. Scale does not close the gap. Across the nine models 64 observations are worth 20 to 53 as a record and 9 to 151 as a summary, no closer to 64 at 397B than at 8B. Where no text stands behind a belief there is little to re-read: a steering vector can install a record's answer, and sixteen observations undo it where a neutral passage leaves it in place. Where reasoning first writes the counts into the context the weight returns, and the same 64 observations are worth 58 to 67 in either form. A matched answer is not a matched belief, and methods that set beliefs should be judged by the futures they produce.
bullets: The study separates belief content—what a model predicts—from belief weight—how much new evidence should change that prediction.
Across nine open-weight models, beliefs with matched current estimates diverge under identical Bernoulli observations when represented as raw records versus summaries.
Models often recover evidential weight from text they reread, rather than retaining it intrinsically with the answer.
Steering vectors can install a belief’s answer without its supporting evidence, making it easier to overturn; reasoning that writes counts into context restores the weight.
The findings suggest belief-setting methods should be evaluated by the futures they produce, not only by immediate predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A schematic of the protocol: a belief has a content that current readouts show and a weight that only an update reveals. I. Six routes aim at the same prediction, 0.55 for heads. II. The prepared state is read as a continuation and as an estimate, and the route decides which readout shows the content. III. The same sixteen new observations follow every state, and how far each state moves gives the weight of its belief in observations (Bayes: w = n). Values are illustrative, taken from the 8 to 12B models.

Figure 4: What a belief is worth in the report channel, by route, model and question. Weight w in observations under sixteen new observations (filled: expected-count question, hollow: next-toss question). Arrows run from n = 8 to n = 64 against the Bayesian values (dashed). Top band: not revised (the interval of S includes zero, or w exceeds 1,000). Bottom band: worth less than one observation. †: some answers are counts of the new segment (Appendix J). Values in Appendix I, the largest models in Tables 2 and A10.

Figure 3: Same answer, different future. Estimate after sixteen new observations against the current estimate, under the next-toss question, for a record and a summary of 64 observations. Solid: after sixteen observations with 25% heads. Hollow: with 75% heads. The shaded gap between the two is how far a route moves. Grey: a Bayesian observer whose estimate is worth 64 observations. †: some answers after a summary are counts of the new segment, which lowers their level and leaves the gap unchanged (Appendix J, with all routes and readouts).

Retention R of the written content against the number of new observations, with the natural record of sixteen in grey. Middle: the trace miscounts a record of 64 observations with 27 heads and answers from the count it wrote, where the true count gives 42. papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.
bullets: Addresses the need to condition fixed-objective WAMs on new driving goals without retraining.
Applies model-agnostic energy guidance to intermediate clean-action estimates using only forward access to the frozen model.
Stabilizes guidance with scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded corrections.
Improves three frozen WAMs by 1.8–3.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 hard-split across three sampler seeds.
Adds less than 10% sampling time per step, supporting practical post-training control.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/
bullets: Addresses blur, stretching, geometric and texture errors, and temporal instability in monocular or image-based Gaussian avatars.
Trains on EDGAR-SET, combining real and synthetic degraded/ground-truth/reference triplets to simulate recoverable failures.
Uses identity features from Sapiens, a one-step conditional diffusion backbone, and a Mixture-of-Experts design for varied degradation types and severities.
Refined multi-view renderings supervise optimization of one Gaussian avatar, avoiding diffusion refinement at every output frame.
Across three reconstruction methods and three settings, improves perceptual, reconstruction, and cross-view consistency measures, including challenging yaw and open-mouth cases.

papers.abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.
bullets: Addresses the nonconvex challenge of jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and dynamic deformation.
Separates camera motion estimation from non-rigid reconstruction, formulating both as rotation-focused QCQPs with SDP relaxations and global-optimality certificates.
Uses depth prediction for scaled bundle adjustment and an embedded deformation graph for dynamic motion.
Solves the relaxations with a GPU-accelerated Burer–Monteiro/Riemannian optimizer, then refines geometry with dynamic Gaussian splatting.
Experiments on seven benchmarks show accurate motion estimation, scalability to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.
