papers.abstract: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/.
bullets: Infers otherwise invisible interior cavities from multiview observations of an object collision.
Replaces difficult density optimization with explicit hypotheses encoding structural assumptions.
Uses global gradient-free search with forward-only MPM simulation, followed by local gradient-based refinement with differentiable MPM.
Improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over a density-based SfC baseline on the SfC benchmark.
Stress tests and robustness analyses define the method’s scope and limitations.

papers.abstract: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent. We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost. Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.
bullets: Compares main-agent retrieval, non-persistent subagent retrieval, and persistent subagent retrieval across enterprise questions and multi-turn follow-ups.
The persistent subagent maintains retrieval state, returns evidence directly, and supports correction requests from the main agent.
Uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens, 45.0% lower estimated API cost, and 9.1% lower average response time than skill-based retrieval.
Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it responds 15.6 seconds faster per question but uses 65.1% more tokens and costs 29.1% more.
The approach shifts response synthesis to the main agent while the retrieval subagent focuses on state maintenance and evidence provision.

papers.abstract: Affordance grounding asks which visible part of an object performs a requested operation, a basic capability for embodied manipulation and human--robot interaction. Most existing methods follow a System Two paradigm: a multimodal language model first writes a chain of thought and then turns its conclusion into a box or points for a segmenter. This incurs considerable inference cost, gives the semantic decision little direct control over the extent of the final region, and makes mistakes hard to correct. Yet locating an affordance is essentially a perceptual judgment that need not be argued out in words. We therefore propose, in which frozen segmenters propose candidate regions and a System One model decides directly which of them perform the operation, generating no text and reading each decision from a single forward pass. Our contributions are twofold. (1) An inference framework that confirms candidate regions level by level, from object to part to sub-part, with evidence passed between the levels in both directions so that the levels correct one another. (2) A System One model trained for this framework: existing System One models are built for general-purpose decisions, judge one candidate per request and are ill-suited to the framework's region questions, so ours learns directly from the requests the framework itself produces and judges all candidates of a level at once. Trained only on InstructPart and evaluated with definition-aligned operation words, outperforms chain-of-thought methods in domain and in zero-shot transfer to UMD and IIT-AFF, is better overall than existing System One models run in the same framework, and needs fewer judge requests. To our knowledge, is the first approach to bring System One models to affordance grounding.
bullets: Addresses costly, error-prone System Two pipelines that reason in language before producing regions.
Uses frozen segmenters to propose candidates and a System One model to confirm regions hierarchically from object to part to sub-part.
Passes evidence between hierarchy levels in both directions so regions can be mutually corrected.
Trains the judge on framework-generated region requests and evaluates all candidates at a level in one forward pass.
Trained on InstructPart, it outperforms chain-of-thought methods in-domain and transfers zero-shot to UMD and IIT-AFF, while requiring fewer judge requests.

papers.abstract: Quantization and pruning reduce the cost of deploying language models, but their effects are usually reported as benchmark scores. Such scores record only the loss that remains at the output. Inside the model, compression damages some components more than others, and the rest of the network can partly compensate. The observed loss therefore reflects both the damage and this compensation, which benchmark scores cannot separate. How the two combine, and whether their balance changes with model size, remains unclear. We study this compensation for in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small, identifiable set of attention heads. To separate the two, the expected loss from ablating these heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, attributed to the components responsible, and the part that reaches the output. This decomposition is then compared across model sizes. For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of it as models grow. Compressing the heads produces the same pattern. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.
bullets: Benchmark loss alone conflates internal damage with the network’s ability to compensate for it.
The study examines in-context retrieval, supported by a small, identifiable set of attention heads.
It exactly decomposes ablation-induced loss into damage, compensation from other components, and output-level loss.
For comparable damage, smaller models restore most of the loss, while larger models retain most of it.
The same scaling pattern appears under head compression, making compression relatively benign in small models but costly in large ones.

papers.title: When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
papers.tldr: Compression can become disproportionately harmful as language models grow because larger models compensate less for damage to critical attention heads.

papers.abstract: Robotic simulators that represent shear within tactile sensing are becoming increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation. However, simulating contact shear with high-fidelity deformable or soft-body simulation is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large-scale reinforcement learning. Here we introduce \textit{TactileLab}, a scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework built on IsaacLab, with a particular focus on a new optical-flow-based tactile representation termed \textit{simulated tactile flow}. Instead of relying on soft-body physics to model shear deformation, TactileLab uses rigid-body simulation to efficiently estimate dense tangential motion at the contact interface, producing tactile flow fields that encode shear-relevant contact dynamics. This flow field complements geometric features from a contact depth field. We further introduce a novel policy architecture for jointly processing long-horizon proprioceptive signals and rich tactile observations. Across multiple contact-rich tasks, policies trained using simulated tactile flow learn efficiently at scale and exhibit emergent contact-aware behaviours. To facilitate sim-to-real policy deployment, we then propose a novel real-to-sim tactile translation method that maps real tactile image streams to simulated tactile flow and depth fields, together with a new tactile data collection method, and validate it across diverse tactile sensor designs. Using this pipeline, we demonstrate real-world deployment on tasks encompassing dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation. Overall, TactileLab provides an end-to-end sim-to-real framework for scalable tactile policy learning, enabling diverse shear-sensitive manipulation across heterogeneous tactile robotic systems.
bullets: Uses rigid-body simulation to generate dense optical-flow-like tactile fields representing tangential contact motion, combined with contact depth features.
Introduces a policy architecture for integrating long-horizon proprioception with rich tactile observations.
Provides real-to-sim translation from real tactile images to simulated tactile flow and depth fields across diverse sensor designs.
Demonstrates efficient learning and real-world deployment on contact-rich dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation tasks.
Scope: focuses on shear-sensitive tactile manipulation while avoiding computationally expensive deformable-contact simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the TactileLab simulation framework and simulated tactile-flow computation. The rigid-body simulation pipeline computes contact geometry and generates low-dimensional contact descriptors, contact-depth images, and dense tactile-flow fields for policy learning. Simulated tactile flow is obtained by projecting the three-dimensional contact patch onto the tactile image plane and calculating the image-space displacement induced by the relative motion between the tactile sensor and the contacted object.

Figure 3: (a) Overview of multimodal tactile policy learning for dexterous in-hand manipulation. During training, the predicted flow is supervised by a paired simulated tactileflow target through a reconstruction loss and by a discriminator D through an adversarial loss. The HSV flow images are used only for visualization; the network output is a two-channel flow field F̂.

papers.abstract: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions in generated playable worlds.
Uses a persistent memory with a volumetric occupancy grid for static geometry and identity-indexed 3D states for players and other entities.
Jointly learns action-conditioned dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery within a local region, while a separate renderer generates first-person views.
In Doom, it models geometry-aware movement and player–NPC interactions, with an end-to-end backend latency of about 160 ms on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro.
Demonstrates zero-shot use on unseen maps, multiplayer via composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: World-state model architecture. The Shared Context Transformer encodes geometry, entity histories, and actions. The Discovery Transformer processes Geometry Queries and Spatial Entity Queries to complete geometry and generate new entities at time t. The Transition Transformer predicts player and entity states at t+1, additionally attending to Current Entity Tokens that include newly accepted entities. papers.abstract: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.
bullets: Addresses the limits of relying on visual reconstruction or semantic feedback alone for evaluating robotic futures.
Uses diverse candidate trajectory search, pairwise multimodal semantic comparisons, and pixel/perceptual consistency signals.
Optimizes the model with group-relative advantages using fixed context and branch-specific rolling histories for long sequences.
Across RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, experiments report improved visual fidelity on RT-1 over continued supervised fine-tuning under matched protocols.
Ablations indicate benefits from diverse search, combined feedback, and rolling histories; scope covers real-world and simulated manipulation.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.
bullets: Parallel decoding introduces error because tokens revealed together are sampled independently.
For arbitrary data, this error equals the entropy production relative to the reversed masking process.
For Markov data, generation maps to random sequential adsorption with labelled gaps and is solved exactly for any number of steps.
In the many-step regime, error is governed by a thermodynamic metric derived from token mutual information; optimal unmasking schedules follow its geodesics.
Longer-range correlations concentrate error early, favoring schedules with initially smaller steps that improve path error and perplexity with fewer steps.

papers.abstract: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection
bullets: Evaluates LBP, Gabor filters, wavelets, FFT, CNN features, and gray-level run-length features with several classifiers.
LBP combined with SVC and CNN showed high specificity and accuracy; statistical tests supported LBP’s relevance.
SHAP was used to identify the most influential features for classification.
On the reported small dataset, SVC reached 98.06% accuracy and CNN 97.8%; on a larger benchmark, CNN reached 98.9% and SVC 96.7%.
The study focuses on automated MRI diagnosis and evaluates performance across datasets, but the abstract does not detail clinical deployment or broader validation.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video, but their predictions rarely show which participant, event, or interval supports an answer. Moreover, answer-level supervision alone does not teach a model to interpret structured video evidence. To systematically mitigate this issue, we present THG-Omni, a human-centric graph-supervision framework that links Segment Anything Model~3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations. Candidate semantic claims are checked against the source video and available audio before they are used to construct training questions, while track geometry provides explicit spatial and temporal supervision. The resulting questions teach an omni-modal reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, affect, interactions, and their timing from a structured graph. At inference, THG-Omni uses a predicted graph constructed from the evaluation video. Experiments on IntentBench show consistent improvements over the unadapted backbone across social reasoning, emotion understanding, and deception perception. On NExT-QA, THG-Omni achieves 89.54\% accuracy with the matched graph, compared with 85.10\% without graph input. Further validation experiments show that compact graph input achieves 78.22\% accuracy, compared with 78.02\% using the full graph and 77.58\% without graph input. A complementary diagnostic demonstrates that the predicted graph preserves evidence useful for answering questions even without the source video and audio. Together, these findings show that THG-Omni improves human-centric video reasoning while grounding its evidence in identifiable participants and events. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-n94hhfcwp5666/
bullets: Addresses the lack of evidence traceability and limitations of answer-only supervision in omni-modal video models.
Builds structured graphs from participant tracks and temporally grounded annotations, with claims checked against video and audio.
Trains models to reason about participant attributes, actions, emotions, interactions, and timing.
Improves over the unadapted backbone on IntentBench; on NExT-QA, matched graph input reaches 89.54% versus 85.10% without graph input.
Compact graphs retain comparable performance to full graphs, and predicted graphs preserve useful evidence even without the source video or audio.

papers.abstract: Head pose estimation is important for human computer interaction and driver monitoring, but many image based methods remain too costly for resource constrained deployment. We propose STAG-Net, a structure-aware attention over landmark groups for lightweight head Pose estimation that estimates head pose from facial landmarks using movement aware selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self attention, and a global geometry descriptor. We develop variants using FaceMesh and Face Alignment Network landmarks and evaluate them under cross dataset and subject independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI. STAG-Net achieves the lowest mean absolute error among all compared landmark based methods in every evaluated setting. On BIWI frames with valid detections, the FAN variant also records the lowest overall error among all compared methods, reaching $3.51^\circ$ under cross dataset evaluation and $2.39^\circ$ under subject independent evaluation. The regressors use only 0.012 to 0.043 million parameters and 24.1 to 83.6 thousand FLOPs, about three orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs than FSA-Net. Despite including landmark extraction and regression, the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 frames per second on a Tesla T4 GPU, nearly twice the 164.5 frames per second of the fastest measured image based baseline, and 111.0 frames per second on CPU. After normalization by dataset size, STAG-Net processes training samples seven to eight times faster than FSA-Net and more than one hundred times faster than HopeNet and TokenHPE, while complete training finishes within 28 minutes. These results show that STAG-Net combines leading landmark based accuracy with substantially lower training and inference cost.
bullets: Targets efficient head pose estimation for resource-constrained human–computer interaction and driver-monitoring systems.
Combines movement-aware landmark selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self-attention, and a global geometry descriptor.

Achieves the lowest mean absolute error among compared landmark-based methods in every setting, with the FAN variant reaching 3.51° and 2.39° on BIWI under the two protocols.
Uses 0.012–0.043M parameters and 24.1–83.6K FLOPs; the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 FPS on a Tesla T4 and 111.0 FPS on CPU.

papers.abstract: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.
bullets: Goal interpretation errors propagate through downstream planning and actions.
The method first fine-tunes an LLM to produce valid EAI symbolic goals.
CORE then learns to rank complete candidate outputs generated by the model.
Evaluated on household scenes from the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark with several open-source LLMs.
The approach outperformed prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge-graph baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Our two-stage generate-then-rank approach on an example record. Stage 1: given the instruction, scene objects, and task prompt, the fine-tuned LLM generates 𝐾 = 9 outputs, of which three are unique candidate goals; each is drawn as the dishwasher contents it specifies and written as node (N), edge (E), and action (A) goals. Stage 2: the candidates and their likelihoods are the input. Contrastive learning pairs the positive, the best candidate, with each negative, a lower-quality candidate; the ranking loss raises the positive’s score and lowers the negatives’, more strongly for the pair with the larger quality gap. The output is the candidate with the highest likelihood after training. Likelihood is the average per-token probability; changes are in percentage points.

papers.abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.
bullets: Frozen embeddings capture the four key memory axes poorly; changing a memory’s date or place barely changes its representation.
A projection layer on top of frozen embeddings does not recover the missing axis information, which is encoded internally in distinct attention-head patterns.
Axis-LoRA adds four per-axis LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them with a per-query gate.
Across three embedding models and four benchmarks, it raises mean R@10 by 1.28–1.56 percentage points while updating only a small fraction of parameters.
Training uses a small axis-counterfactual dataset; the method is evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (a) Failure case in personal-memory retrieval. An axis cue in the query (here, the time axis) does not separate the gold from content-similar distractors that mismatch on the axis, so the gold falls below them in the ranked list. (b) Axis-LoRA. Four axis-conditional LoRA adapters (T/S/E/Ev) attach to the last 20% of layers of the frozen embedding model and produce per-axis representations ϕA(q), ϕA(m). A per-query gate (MLP → sparsemax) outputs routing weights wA with exact zeros on inactive axes. The final score is the frozen-base similarity plus a gated per-axis term.

papers.abstract: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MRI enables non-invasive assessment of left atrial (LA) scar, an imaging marker associated with atrial fibrillation ablation outcome. However, automatic scar segmentation is hindered by low contrast, the thin atrial wall, scarce labels, and extreme class imbalance. Conditional diffusion offers iterative mask generation, but its suitability for sparse 3D LA scar segmentation remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Conditional Mask Diffusion (CMDiff), which predicts clean masks using a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet. We compared CMDiff with a deterministic baseline on identical cases in five-fold cross-validation of 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects, with 48 training and 12 held-out cases per fold. CMDiff achieved a scar DSC of 0.47 $\pm$ 0.08, HD95 of 12.89 $\pm$ 6.39 mm, and ASD of 1.91 $\pm$ 0.96 mm, compared with deterministic baseline values of 0.51 $\pm$ 0.08, 10.86 $\pm$ 5.39 mm, and 1.58 $\pm$ 1.03 mm, respectively. Under the same implementation, clean-mask prediction performed substantially better than the noise-prediction configuration evaluated in this study. Thus, CMDiff was technically feasible but did not improve segmentation performance: DSC was lower, and both HD95 and ASD were higher. Direct mask diffusion therefore provides an analytical alternative, but not a competitive performance advance for this task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jizhang02/CMDiff.
bullets: Addresses low contrast, thin atrial walls, scarce labels, and severe class imbalance in LGE MRI scar segmentation.
Uses a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet for iterative clean-mask generation.
Evaluated with five-fold cross-validation on 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects.
CMDiff achieved DSC 0.47 ± 0.08, HD95 12.89 ± 6.39 mm, and ASD 1.91 ± 0.96 mm, versus 0.51 ± 0.08, 10.86 ± 5.39 mm, and 1.58 ± 1.03 mm for the deterministic baseline.
Clean-mask prediction outperformed the evaluated noise-prediction configuration; source code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Small language models are often trained under tight data budgets, where the choice of pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe. We compare two contrasting corpora at matched 10-million- and 37-million-word budgets: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and the BabyLM 2026 strict pretraining corpus. For each corpus, we train teacher models, distilled 58-million-parameter Baby-Llama students, and no-distillation student ablations, using the same model families, training recipes, and evaluation protocol across corpora. Across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, and COMPS, the corpora produce different skill profiles rather than a single quality ranking. BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks, while Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a synthetic state-tracking task. The contrast appears across teacher and student models and at both budgets, with the cleanest cross-seed replication in the distilled student comparison. Targeted controls show that the central contrast persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context; direct teacher ensembling also does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior. Entity Tracking magnitudes nevertheless remain sensitive to training dynamics. For this corpus pair, corpus choice can therefore produce different relative skill profiles at small scale, motivating multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data.
bullets: Compares Britannica and BabyLM 2026 corpora at matched 10M- and 37M-word budgets.
Uses matched teacher, distilled 58M-parameter student, and no-distillation setups with the same evaluations.
BabyLM 2026 performs consistently better on linguistic acceptability benchmarks.
Britannica is often stronger on the synthetic Entity Tracking task, across teachers and students.
Results support multi-benchmark evaluation; Entity Tracking performance remains sensitive to training dynamics.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) commonly decode responses by proceeding autoregressively across blocks while iteratively denoising multiple tokens within each block. This structure makes block-level policy optimization a natural adaptation of autoregressive policy optimization. However, the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable because it marginalizes over the intermediate states and reveal orders of the denoising process. To realize the block-level formulation, we construct a prefix-block state and use a single model evaluation to define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood. The resulting block surrogate ratio is a product of its token surrogate ratios, allowing variation at individual positions to propagate across the entire block before clipping. We therefore introduce Prefix-Block Policy Optimization (PBPO), which preserves block-level conditioning but applies surrogate importance weighting and clipping separately to each token. PBPO further diversifies repeated updates by resampling corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix, a design motivated by masked-dLLM pre-training. Under our analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies the variance of gradient contributions relative to token-local weighting. Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods.
bullets: Addresses the intractable likelihood of fully denoised blocks in dLLMs.
Builds a prefix-block state and a single model evaluation to form a factorized one-step block surrogate.
Applies surrogate ratios and clipping separately per token, avoiding the higher gradient variance associated with block-product weighting under the paper’s assumptions.
Resamples corrupted prompt and revealed-prefix views to diversify repeated updates.
Shows competitive performance against existing dLLM reinforcement-learning methods across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides information about object properties that can improve robotic grasping and manipulation. However, accurate object recognition during the early stages of grasping remains challenging, particularly under strict real-time constraints. This study presents a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system for early-stage object recognition. The system was experimentally evaluated using six everyday objects and three recognition approaches: feature-based classification using support vector machines (SVMs), raw-signal classification using 1D convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) and convolutional recurrent neural networks (C-RNNs), and spatiotemporal heatmap classification using a 2D-CNN. The effects of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition accuracy and real-time feasibility were systematically investigated. Increasing the number of sensing elements improved recognition performance across all approaches. The best-performing method, based on spatiotemporal heatmaps and a 2D-CNN, achieved F1-scores of 0.9796, 0.9846, and 0.9903 using 16, 24, and 32 sensors, respectively. The optimal configuration, comprising 32 sensors and a 100-ms temporal window (50 samples), was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of approximately 101 ms from contact onset and an energy consumption of 63.8 microjoules per inference. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing for accurate, energy-efficient, and real-time object recognition during robotic grasping.
bullets: Evaluated six everyday objects using SVM, 1D-CNN, C-RNN, and spatiotemporal heatmap-based 2D-CNN approaches.
Recognition performance improved as the number of sensing elements increased.
The heatmap-based 2D-CNN achieved the strongest F1-scores, reaching 0.9903 with 32 sensors.
A 32-sensor, 100-ms temporal-window configuration achieved approximately 101 ms latency and 63.8 μJ per inference on an embedded platform.

papers.abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.
bullets: The study explains accuracy loss from irrelevant statements or off-distribution tokens even when they provide no competing answer.
MLPs enrich irrelevant-token representations, while parrot-like heads carry prefix content to the prediction position; relational readers mostly avoid unrelated sources.
Intrusion heads promote distractor content and provide weaker support for the correct answer, rather than directly suppressing it.
These heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely distinct from heads that use helpful context.
An oracle residual replacement recovers 97.6% of the induced drop; masking about ten heads recovers 57% with bounded impact on useful context.

papers.abstract: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.
bullets: Adds a windowed, content-dependent bias to attention scores using a causal convolution over low-dimensional hidden-state projections.
Works with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation, and supports high-dimensional position embeddings through high-dimensional convolutions.
Evaluated for language modeling, long-context extension, and vision.
In reproduction experiments, it outperformed five 1D and eight 2D baselines.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
bullets: Reactive navigation may choose locally feasible actions that cause unsafe, socially disruptive, or semantically inappropriate futures.
The method uses a discrete visual action prior and two task-aligned world models: one predicts nearby social dynamics, while the other predicts future scene semantics.
World models score candidate actions during training and guide group-relative preference distillation; they are removed at deployment for single-pass inference.
Across five held-out scenarios, the resulting policy is reported as safer, more socially and group-coherent, more goal-directed, and more human-like than reactive and learned baselines.
The approach confines the computational cost of foresight to training rather than performing online world-model rollouts.

papers.abstract: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.
bullets: Addresses limited space, clutter, and collision risks in wide dual-arm workspaces.
Finds collision-free gaps along the shared boundary for object transfer.
Uses placement followed by a push, avoiding fixed handoff poses and simultaneous arm interaction.
Coordinates buffering and transfers with a joint Monte Carlo Tree Search planner.
Experiments report shorter execution sequences and lower cost than fixed handoffs in denser scenes, while remaining competitive in lighter scenes.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses. We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical positions. Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd.
bullets: OPD feedback is disproportionately concentrated on style-related tokens, with 3.5× the mean absolute discrepancy of mathematical tokens.
SD-OPD uses centered student–base log-probability differences as update coefficients, retaining them only when aligned with centered teacher–student feedback.
The student signal is recomputed each training round to reflect evolving learned preferences.
Across five Qwen3 teacher–student configurations (1.7B–8B), SD-OPD raises six-task math average pass@1 (avg@16) by 7.76–10.37 percentage points over OPD.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. When continuous predictions are formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under a continuous reconstruction objective based on mean squared error (MSE). We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF) to apply squared supervision directly to token identities. TIBF fixes token embeddings, combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. We show that, for fixed token embeddings, the squared error in token posterior prediction controls the squared errors of the continuous denoising prediction and the flow velocity. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, TIBF achieves mean Gen.PPL values of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls. Further evaluations show improvements across multiple sampling budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF.
bullets: Continuous MSE supervision can treat distinct token distributions as identical when they produce the same embedding average.
TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model and applies squared supervision to token identities.
A theoretical analysis links token-posterior error to continuous denoising and flow-velocity errors.
The method achieves mean Gen.PPL of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls under matched budgets.
Results improve across multiple sampling budgets; the approach focuses continued training on probability prediction while retaining pretrained embeddings.

papers.abstract: Multimodal self-supervised learning is challenged by heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex information interactions across multimodal data sources such as images, text, audio, and tabular data. While contrastive methods effectively align shared semantics, they typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, overlooking modality-specific and synergistic information, thus leading to suboptimal representations. We propose the Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (MIIB), a principled framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition that explicitly encodes redundant, unique, and synergistic information within multimodal interactions. MIIB employs a dual-path model architecture for modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion, optimized using surrogate tractable entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without requiring explicit mutual information estimation. By leveraging variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, MIIB efficiently captures complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wanglingzaishi/MIIB.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex interactions among multimodal data.
Uses Partial Information Decomposition to represent redundant, modality-specific, and synergistic information.
Employs dual-path modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion with entropy-based surrogate objectives.
Uses variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation without explicit mutual-information estimation.
Experiments on diverse benchmarks report consistent improvements over existing multimodal self-supervised methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of MIIB. Given n input modalities X = (X1, . . . , Xn), we first augment them to generate two views, X′ and X′′. These views are encoded independently by modality-specific encoders and latent converters to extract latent features e′1 . . . e ′ n and e′′1 . . . e′′n, which provide unified embeddings for subsequent multimodal interaction. These features are then processed by two parallel Transformer streams. The Fusion Transformer processes concatenated multimodal features to produce fused representations Z′, Z′′ while processing individual modality features to yield modality-specific representations Z′ 1 . . . Z ′ n and Z′′ 1 . . . Z′′ n . The Synergy Transformer operates on the concatenated multimodal features to model cross-modal interactions, producing synergistic representations Z′ s and Z′′ s . Finally, these representations are used to compute the modality-specific loss (LMS), modality fusion loss (LMF), and synergistic loss (LSynergy).
Fig. 1. The process framework for multimodal representation learning organizes modality-specific learning and fusion as a sequential yet interdependent process.

papers.abstract: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.
bullets: Targets safe handling of handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, where robots must infer intent and manage physical contact.
Uses a lightweight two-camera RGB intent model to generate language prompts for a VLA policy; low-confidence predictions suppress motion.
Applies interaction-specific arm impedance profiles during contact and an independent latched voice-triggered safe-stop mechanism.
Evaluated four fine-tuned VLA models on a Unitree G1 using approximately 1,300 VR-teleoperated multimodal episodes.
Intent gating improved the best standalone model’s macro-F1 from 0.75 to 0.90, with 6.27 ms p95 intent-inference latency.

(c) During deployment, task-conditioned arm-compliance profiles and the latched safe-stop mechanism supervise the SONIC whole-body controller, enabling safe and compliant handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically using a single global scale-and-shift alignment. Crucially, we discover a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This discovery invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which warp scene geometry by enforcing a single transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Across diverse experimental settings, our sensor-free method shows strong photometric quality of Gaussian Splatting while substantially improving geometric accuracy and outperforming state-of-the art geometry-focused methods.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 3DGS’s strong visual quality and weaker geometric accuracy.
Identifies that monocular depth errors are piecewise-linear and vary across regions, making global scale-and-shift alignment inadequate.
Models depth correction with regionally smooth, edge-aware affine fields.
Uses spatial gradients in a normal-aware regularizer to align rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals.
Reports strong photometric quality alongside substantially improved geometry across diverse settings, without sensor data.

figures.caption: Figure 8: We compare the raw disparity predictions of (a) Metric3D-V2 and (b) MoGe against groundtruth sensor depth on the exact same scene. While the distinct network architectures allocate their local scale-and-shift parameters differently, both fundamentally exhibit the same region-dependent, piecewise-linear fragmentation. This confirms that spatial affine distortion is a systemic property of modern foundation depth models.

Figure 2: Method overview. (a) 3DGS renders depth D and normals n, and Depth-Anything-V2 predicts the disparity d. (b) The affine fields α and β are estimated from disparity and depth gradients and smoothed by a guided filter (Sec. 3.1). (c) They supervise the losses of Secs. 3.2 and 3.3. All fields are re-estimated at every iteration.

Figure 1: Robust 3DGS geometry via spatially varying affine rectification. (a-c) Standard 3DGS overfits appearance, producing noisy underlying geometry. In contrast, our method extracts clean, highly accurate meshes while maintaining photorealism. (d) Monocular disparity exhibits piecewise-linear distortions, proving that a single global scale-and-shift alignment is fundamentally insufficient (scatter plot). (e) We overcome this by estimating an edge-aware spatial scale field (αsmooth) to rectify the monocular depth prior, yielding geometrically consistent 3D representations.

Figure 9: Additional qualitative comparison on NeRF-LLFF dataset. Visualized across the Flower, Fern, and Horns scenes under extreme view sparsity (rendered RGB, depth, and surface normal maps). (a) Unconstrained 3DGS severely overfits to the limited training views, resulting in massive floating artifacts and chaotic underlying geometry. (b) DRGS mitigates some artifacts via global depth alignment, but still suffers from noisy surface normals and blurred geometric details. (c) DropGaussian struggles to properly initialize in this sparse setting, leading to heavily corrupted backgrounds and incomplete structures. (d) In contrast, our proposed method leverages spatially rectified monocular priors to extract clean, highly accurate geometry with sharp object boundaries, smooth backgrounds, and highly consistent surface normals, all while preserving photorealistic appearance.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative mesh comparison on ScanNet++ dataset. (a) The DN-Splatter baseline exhibits high-frequency noise and artifacts across large planar surfaces like walls and ceilings. (b) Our proposed method successfully suppresses this noise to reconstruct much smoother, flatter surfaces that better approximate (c) the ground-truth geometry.

Figure 7: Piecewise-linear disparity fragmentation across diverse indoor topologies. Across various scenes, the monocular depth prior consistently fractures into distinct, spatially coherent affine regimes (visualized in red, orange, and grey). The accompanying scatter plots demonstrate that fitting a single global scale-and-shift transform (K = 1) is mathematically ill-posed, as the optimizer would be forced to average errors across fundamentally incompatible linear clusters.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on Mushroom dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.2). (a) The globally aligned DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline suffers from degraded geometries due to structural warping. (c) By rectifying the exact same monocular prior, our method better recovers crisp planar surfaces and sharp complex object boundaries than (b) the sensor-supervised DN-Splatter.

Figure 12: Qualitative comparisons of our proposed geometric regularization on MuSHRoom dataset. Visualized via rendered normals (top row) and depth maps (bottom row). (a) The unconstrained baseline (All off) exhibits severe geometric drift, yielding highly chaotic and noisy surface normals. (b-d) Applying individual loss terms in isolation yields incomplete geometry: while Ldepth anchors global scale, it fails to resolve high-frequency structural noise, and while Lgrad or Lnormal improve local structure, they struggle without an absolute metric anchor. (h) Our full formulation combines these constraints. By anchoring the global metric scale while explicitly enforcing local spatial gradients and physical orientations, the complete approach reconstructs exceptionally clean planar surfaces (e.g.,, the walls and ceiling), sharp structural boundaries, and globally consistent depth.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on ScanNet++ dataset. We show rendered RGB and depth with red bounding boxes highlighting areas where we generate visually sharper depth, particularly along boundaries of furniture and complex geometry, compared to the DN-Splatter baseline.
Figure 6: Qualitative mesh comparison on ScanNet++ dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.3). Interestingly, we are able to recover window geometries which are absent from ground-truth mesh.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons on NeRF-LLFF dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.1).

We show that our method achieves state-of-the-art geometric accuracy among sensor-free explicit representations, completely avoiding the structural collapse observed in the directly comparable DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline. Full quantitative evaluation of the individual and combined contributions of our proposed geometric loss terms. We report photometric (novel-view synthesis), depth estimation, and 3D mesh reconstruction metrics against the unconstrained Splatfacto baseline. Our full configuration (All) provides the best overall balance, enforcing strict structural integrity (highest mesh F-score and Normal Consistency) while maintaining competitive rendering quality. Best results in each column are indicated in bold.

Table 15: Ablation of prior filtering strategies. Evaluated on the coffee_room scene using the Depth-Anything-V2 prior. Novel-view synthesis and depth metrics are reported on the right (disjoint-trajectory) split, whereas Tables 6 and 14 report the left split. Removing the filter results in severe geometric degradation due to raw monocular noise. While a standard Gaussian filter mitigates some noise, it indiscriminately blurs across physical boundaries. Our Guided Blur strategy uniquely preserves sharp structural edges, yielding the best performance across all photometric, depth, and geometric metrics.

Table 18: Comprehensive scene-wise evaluation of the DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline. Evaluated across the MuSHRoom dataset test split. Because this baseline relies on a single global scale-and-shift transform to align monocular depth, it is highly susceptible to piecewise-linear distortions. This results in severe structural collapse on complex scenes (e.g., computer and kokko), validating the necessity of our proposed spatially varying affine rectification.

Table 16: Ablation on gradient matching formulation. Evaluated on the coffee_room scene. Novelview synthesis and depth metrics are reported on the right (disjoint-trajectory) split. Relying solely on MSE fails to capture sharp orientational changes, leading to degraded Normal Consistency. While Cosine similarity provides excellent directional cues, combining both magnitude (MSE) and directional (Cosine) alignment yields the highest overall surface extraction F-score and best novel view synthesis.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn cross-modal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modality-specific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/brightest66/InfMasking.
bullets: Addresses the underuse of information available only from joint modality observations.
Randomly masks modality features before fusion to generate diverse partial combinations of cross-modal evidence.
Enforces consistency with an unmasked fused target or labeled class proxy across all masked views.
Uses Gaussian modeling and closed-form variational bounds to optimize the infinite-mask objective.
On evaluated benchmarks, improves predictive performance and synergy-related PID and InterSHAP measures.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed InfMasking framework. Given n multimodal inputs X = {X1, X2, . . . , Xn}, InfMasking uses label-proxy supervision in the supervised setting (upper) and augmented-view alignment in the unsupervised setting (lower). Both settings share the same backbone architecture. Modality-specific encoders fm, m = 1, . . . , n, extract latent features, and the infinite masking operator samples subsets of their tokens before fusion. The fusion module gϕ then produces the complete multimodal representation Z from unmasked modality features and masked fused representations Z1 mask, Z 2 mask, . . . , Z k mask from sampled combinations of retained tokens across modalities. In the unsupervised setting, the fusion module gϕ additionally produces unimodal representations Z1, Z2, . . . , Zn from individual modalities, whereas in the supervised setting the corresponding unimodal branches are obtained by projecting modality-specific latent features.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.
bullets: Introduces 358 structured tasks spanning five capability domains and 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers.
Targets four failure subtypes: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, and Context Forgetting.
Evaluates 14 frontier agents from eight vendors across 5,012 trajectories.
Agents average 0.642 overall, but Unreachable Goal tasks fall to 0.458, with only 23.2% passing.
Failure profiles vary substantially by subtype, so aggregate task success can obscure important weaknesses.

papers.abstract: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) can degrade during aerial inspection in repetitive or poorly textured environments. We propose an active environment-modification framework for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) relying on cameras and an inertial measurement unit only, without prior maps or additional localization sensors. Inspired by the fairy tale of Tom Thumb, the UAV creates visual features on demand by releasing ground markers or marking walls through physical contact. An information-based indicator triggers interventions using temporal confirmation and hysteresis. Evaluation includes three simulated environments and a 900-run factorial campaign. Lower cruise speed and active marking are associated with reduced divergence, while accuracy among non-divergent runs depends on speed-strategy interactions. Corridor experiments, with five runs per configuration, use OptiTrack for flight control while VIO-based marking decisions remain active online. The combined framework reduces the reported position root mean square error by approximately 35% relative to baseline VIO, supporting active feature creation for drift mitigation.
bullets: Addresses VIO degradation during aerial inspection without prior maps or additional localization sensors.
Uses physical ground markers or wall markings to create trackable visual features.
Triggers interventions with an information-based indicator, temporal confirmation, and hysteresis.
Simulations and corridor experiments associate active marking and lower speed with reduced divergence.
Accuracy among non-divergent runs varies with interactions between speed and intervention strategy.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed VIO-based framework. papers.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.
bullets: Addresses short, ambiguous questions whose visual referents cannot be uniquely identified.
Uses three cooperating agents to propose interpretations, ask clarifying questions, and answer using resolved intent and visual evidence.
Applies a bounded, cost-aware policy to trade off information gain against user effort and limit clarification complexity.
Learns from interactions through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization.
Evaluations report better answer accuracy and joint answer-grounding performance, plus zero-shot transfer across datasets.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion policies trained without an explicit smoothness objective tend to produce jerky, high-energy gaits that stress actuators. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer an appealing reward source: given a rendered rollout, a VLM returns an aesthetic quality score on [0,10] without task-specific feature engineering. We find, however, that aesthetic preference and physical smoothness point in opposite directions: across four production VLMs, clips with higher joint acceleration receive higher aesthetic scores (mean Pearson r=+0.66). We study PhySA (Physical Smoothness and Aesthetics), which keeps the two on separate, independently removable reward channels: a sparse, asynchronous VLM score and a phase-triggered correction channel that adjusts physical penalty weights from simulator state. Ablations attribute the smoothness gain to the correction channel. On MuJoCo Humanoid-v5 at 2.6M steps, PhySA lowers joint acceleration by 26 to 32% relative to vanilla PPO, Text2Reward, and Eureka (three seeds), at the cost of shorter episodes. In a single extended run it lowers joint acceleration by 59.5% relative to Prompt2Policy, while a three-seed replication shows a smaller, non-significant reduction (7.2%). The gain does not transfer to IsaacLab or the Unitree G1, even after rescaling the smoothness term.
bullets: VLM aesthetic preferences can conflict with physical smoothness: higher-scored clips had higher joint acceleration across four VLMs.
PhySA uses two independently removable channels: sparse asynchronous VLM aesthetics and phase-triggered simulator-state corrections to physical penalties.
On MuJoCo Humanoid-v5, it reduced joint acceleration by 26–32% versus vanilla PPO, Text2Reward, and Eureka at 2.6M steps, but produced shorter episodes.
A single extended comparison reported a 59.5% reduction versus Prompt2Policy, while a three-seed replication found a smaller, non-significant 7.2% reduction.
The smoothness improvement did not transfer to IsaacLab or the Unitree G1, even after rescaling the smoothness term.

papers.abstract: Point clouds represent 3D object geometry as sets of spatial coordinates. A fundamental task in their analysis is keypoint detection, i.e., identifying a sparse subset of points that captures the most salient features. While supervised methods rely on manual annotations, unsupervised approaches leverage intrinsic geometric properties to localize keypoints without human input. We introduce GEKey, a self-supervised framework that uses the geodesic eccentricity transform, an SE(3)-invariant geometric measure, to identify instance-specific salient points. These points serve as pseudo-labels to train a model that aligns its predictions with the object's intrinsic structure. GEKey is simple, efficient, and robust, preserving intra-class variation by balancing instance-specific and category-level structure. Extensive experiments on ShapeNetCoreV2, KeypointNet, CAPE, ITOP, and DeformingThings4D show state-of-the-art performance in both keypoint detection and alignment, with strong resilience to noise, downsampling, deformations, and real-world conditions. The code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Pierreoo/GEKey.
bullets: Targets sparse 3D keypoint detection while preserving salient geometric structure and intra-class variation.
Uses an SE(3)-invariant geodesic eccentricity transform to generate pseudo-labels.
Trains a model to align predicted keypoints with each object’s intrinsic geometry.
Reports state-of-the-art keypoint detection and alignment across five datasets.
Robust to noise, downsampling, deformations, and real-world conditions.
