papers.abstract: Legged robots equipped with manipulators have shown significant potential in the fields of daily life and industry in complex environments. However, existing methods mainly focus on global navigation or manipulation independently, while overlooking the last-mile navigation problem, where the robot must jointly determine the base placement, approach direction, and grasp execution to achieve reliable object grasping, and different manipulation stages require distinct control behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation (LMGN), a unified policy learning model for Quadruped robot loco-manipulation. An Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) representation is first introduced to explicitly represent the features of grasp-compatible base placement and approach direction. We then develop a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) policy that models stage-aware behaviors across the stages of base adjustment, pre-grasp alignment and grasp execution, and object lift. Finally, a new optimization method that jointly aligns navigation and manipulation, stage-dependent expert routing, and action-level consistency is proposed to optimize the HMoE policy. Extensive experiments on the Habitat and Isaac Gym simulators demonstrate that LMGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, denoting that integrating grasp-aware reachability with stage-aware policy learning significantly improves the success rates of last-mile navigation and target grasp for robots.
bullets: Targets the last-mile problem: jointly choosing base placement, approach direction, and grasp actions.
Uses Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) to represent grasp-compatible robot positioning and approach directions.
Employs a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts policy for stage-specific behaviors.
Jointly optimizes navigation–manipulation alignment, expert routing, and action consistency.
Experiments in Habitat and Isaac Gym report improved last-mile navigation and grasp success over existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed LMGN. The policy fuses grasp-guided reachability features, point-cloud observations, object pose, and proprioception, then uses a geometry-aligned hierarchical MoE policy to select stage-specific expert routes for base motion, end-effector adjustment, and gripper control.
Figure 3: Weight curves of the high-level expert routes in HMoE and some snapshots during a representative episode.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D. Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Concertina Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/Traly/concertina
bullets: Addresses the decoupling of cognition and manipulation in existing vision-language-action policies.
Encodes each control timestep as a continuous latent action token and generates trajectory blocks through the shared Transformer.
Applies physical-coordinate supervision and the same corrupt-and-reconstruct process used for multimodal pretraining.
Uses 0.21% active action projections in a 4.46B-parameter model, with no separate action-generator layers.
Reports 98.15% success on LIBERO, 85.9% on LIBERO-Plus, and 4.142 completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Action Interface Audit across representational, computational, and parameter coupling. (a) Physical action error span (p05–p50–p95) and structural decoding fragility under singletoken substitutions: continuous coordinates (Concertina) preserve unit error geometry (EGC = 1.0×, 0% invalid), whereas 256-bin quantization induces a 25.1× error span and compressed DCT+BPE tokenizers (FAST+, MolmoAct2-FAST) suffer 82.2% and 77.9% invalid trajectory shapes while perturbing 30/30 steps on valid decodes. (b) Normalized Jacobian singular value spectrum (σi/σ1) of Concertina’s continuous action encoder ∂Eϕ(a)/∂a ∈ R2560×20 across pretraining updates, maintaining a full-rank 20D manifold (effective rank 18.63/20, Spearman ρ = 0.86–0.93). (c) Layerwise emergence of cross-time trajectory coupling (NLR, |t− t0| ≥ 6) across the 36-layer BARD-VL-B4 backbone versus 0.0% for the position-wise interface (Dψ ◦ Eϕ) alone. (d) Action-Specific Capacity Ratio (ASCR) across VLA families, showing that Concertina uses 78×–167× fewer action-specific parameters (0.21%) than external-expert architectures (16.5%–35.1%).

Figure 2: From decoupled VLAs to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). Comparison of four architectural routes to robot manipulation: (A) OpenVLA quantizes coordinates into discrete vocabulary tokens (language-objective VLA); (B) π0 delegates continuous trajectory generation to a separate flow-matching action expert (separate-objective VLA); (C) Dream-VLA retains a shared diffusion VLM backbone but switches to a flow-matching objective for continuous control (switchedobjective VLA); (D) Concertina instantiates an eVLM that preserves both the shared diffusion VLM backbone and its native masked block reconstruction operator over continuous latent action tokens.

Figure 3: Blockwise horizon partition, physical action coherence, and cumulative recipe progression. (a) Regular-LIBERO suite-level and overall success over 200 episodes (40 tasks × 5 episodes, Wilson 95% CIs) at fixed 2,400-step finetuning budgets, showing consistent gains across all four suites (38.5% → 73.0% overall). (b) Directional cosine similarity of physical action increments across temporal lags ∆t = 1 . . . 30 over 999,830 AgiBot frames (30 Hz, 95% task-bootstrap CI); enlarging the block size from K = 5 to K = 10 more than doubles intra-block coherent action mass (9.8% → 21.3%, 2.17×). (c) Official 1,000-sequence CALVIN ABC–D chain survival curves (SR@1–5) across block partitions (K = 5 vs. K = 10) and pretraining corruption/weighting schedules (1.333 → 1.701 → 2.087 AvgLen). (d) Cumulative CALVIN ABC–D progression from uniform coordinate weights (0.41) to physical weighting, state masking, 60k multi-block pretraining, aligned single-block execution (4.135), and two-block continued pretraining (4.142).

Figure 4: Co-design of action representation and supervision objective in the shared hidden space. (a) Shared-hidden gradient cosine between the main relative-action objective and auxiliary absolute-action objective across eight fixed windows is −0.891 (99% of action slots < 0), reducing combined-vs-main alignment to +0.474 (auxiliary/main norm ratio 0.88×). (b) Layerwise parameter update divergence across all 26 active Transformer layers (L2–L27): while relative update norm ∆W/W rises from 4.6% to 9.3% with identical overall magnitude (1.003×), the parameter update direction cosine plunges from 0.604 at Layer 2 to 0.138 at Layer 22 (pooled cosine 0.225). (c) Resulting readout degradation (5.12× teacher action loss, 2.47× position error, 1.60× normalized MAE) and 92.0% closed-loop CALVIN collapse (2.970 → 0.237). (d) Complete 2× 2× 2 factorial co-design across 8,000 CALVIN chains on 4.46B BARD-VL-B4, showing consistent gains from probability-valued gripper BCE (+0.427 AvgLen) and trainable action interfaces (+0.311).

Figure 6: Validity masks separate embodiment coordinates, reconstruction selection, and time padding. The canonical 20D layout provides fixed slots for single-arm and bimanual embodiments; coordinate validity q, masking indicator m, and timestep validity v play orthogonal roles in the supervised objective.

Figure 7: Risk-guided decoding scores candidate action tokens and supports selective iterative refinement. The token-risk head predicts log reconstruction error from detached hidden states; candidate slots are committed in order of confidence, and optional refinement rounds remask and update low-scoring positions when the predicted score improves.

Table 2: Main results across regular LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC–D, grouped by architectural paradigm. Regular-LIBERO Avg. is the arithmetic mean of its four suite scores. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best result per column. The π0.5 and IMLE-VLA rows follow the comparison reported by Hosseinkhani et al. (Hosseinkhani et al., 2026). EFFVLA reports suite-level LIBERO-Plus averages, while Concertina and the remaining LIBERO-Plus rows report the official 10,030-task benchmark with Long labeled LIBERO-10. CALVIN reports average completed chain length and sequence success rates (SR@1–5) on ABC→D.

Table 1: Architectural comparison between representative VLA paradigms and our eVLM (✓: satisfied; ×: not satisfied; : partially satisfied). Columns 1–2 reflect representational coupling (whether actions enter and are supervised in physical coordinates); columns 3–4 reflect computational and parameter coupling (whether the VLM backbone directly generates trajectories without a separate action Transformer, DiT, flow expert, or post-codec generator); the remaining columns summarize training and decoding structure. Coordinate supervision marks for dual discrete-continuous objectives (HybridVLA), latent-codec policy losses (CAT), or discrete-pretrain/continuous-finetune stage switches (Dream-VLA).

Table 3: Controlled pretraining ablation evaluating physical coordinate weighting (ωd), proprioceptive state masking, early-layer freezing, and random-resized crop (RRC). Every configuration runs 4,800 pretraining updates on AgiBot followed by 2,600 CALVIN finetuning updates (global batch 1,536) and is evaluated on all 1,000 official CALVIN ABC–D chains.
Table 7: Multi-embodiment pretraining dataset mixture totaling 146,433 episodes and 80.2M frames across five robot manipulation sources.

Table 11: Closed-loop decoding budget and replanning frequency on LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks × 5 initial states = 50 episodes per arm; failed episodes capped at 280 steps). Executing a full E = 10 block before replanning outperforms step-by-step replanning (E = 1, +8.0 pp) by preserving intrablock motion coherence, whereas open-loop 50-step execution in π0.5 (E = 50) degrades success by −12.0 pp (95% paired bootstrap CI [−24.0,−2.0]).

Table 10: Offline reconstruction accuracy (32 windows, 2,880 non-gripper coordinates per arm) and 100-sequence closed-loop CALVIN ABC–D performance across decoding budgets at fixed checkpoint identity (H = 10,K = 10,M = 1). Risk-guided refinement (D ≤ 4, R = 5) reduces offline MAE on 25/32 CALVIN windows (∆ = −0.00084, 95% paired bootstrap CI [−0.00125,−0.00043]) and 25/32 LIBERO windows (∆ = −0.00840 vs. D = 1, R = 0, 95% CI [−0.01316,−0.00400]), while single-pass parallel decoding (D = 1, R = 0) already achieves 3.92 AvgLen at 65.8ms median latency (6.58ms per executed control step).

Table 12: Error-Geometry Consistency (EGC) and representation diagnostics on 512 CALVIN windows (H = 30, D = 7). Unperturbed MAE measures round-trip reconstruction error; EGC, invalid shape, and valid RMSE refer to single-token substitution.

Table 13: Expanded representation stress test across 512, 4 × 2,048, and 8,192 windows. Invalid shape is the fraction of single-token edits that fail to decode into 30× 7 coefficients. Time support counts affected steps with a coordinate change exceeding 0.01 normalized units.

Table 14: Full-path NLR stability across finite-difference step sizes ϵ ∈ {0.01, 0.02, 0.04} on the 4.46B BARD-VL-B4 checkpoints. Each cell averages 11 coordinate probes with zero repeatedforward jitter; interface-only NLR is identically zero.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses vision-language-action and robot manipulation with a unified diffusion VLM.
papers.title: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: Concertina unifies visual-language reasoning and continuous manipulation in a single diffusion backbone, achieving strong performance with minimal action-specific parameters.

papers.abstract: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zyphra/zyfa.
bullets: Targets long-context attention, where softmax limits the benefits of FP8 matrix throughput on MI355X.
Uses direct FP8 probability computation, ping-pong overlap of softmax and matrix multiplication, and power-of-two probability scaling before rounding.
Achieves 1.16–1.76× AITER throughput on inputs from three models at sustained clock speeds.
On 32K-token Gaussian benchmarks, reaches 1.26–1.37× speedup at head dimension 128 and 1.99× for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.
At head dimension 128, numerical error is within a few percent of Composable Kernel and Triton, and 62–78% lower than AITER’s.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Thread traces showing that AITER’s FP8 kernel leaves the matrix pipe idle while its waves compute exponentials and wait at barriers, and that ZYFA’s FP8 kernel keeps the matrix pipe busy most of the time. A thread trace records every instruction that a wave issues, cycle by cycle, here with the thread-trace mode of AMD’s rocprofv3 profiler. Each panel shows the two waves that share one SIMD over 2500 cycles in the middle of the loop over key blocks, where every block repeats the same work, in the FP8 kernels at dqk=128 (S=8K tokens, H=32 heads, multi-head attention). Each wave row shows the class of each instruction that the wave issues, and the matrix-pipe row below it shows when that wave’s MFMAs run. A vector instruction runs on the vector pipe during its bar in the wave row, so the wave rows already show when the vector pipe works. An MFMA keeps running on the matrix pipe for 32 to 64 cycles after its short bar in the wave row, while the wave issues other instructions, so the matrix-pipe rows show that work separately.

Fig. 16: Output error of one attention call for every layer of each model, as relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs (lower is more accurate). The inputs are the q, k, and v that each model produces on the first 4095 tokens of WikiText-2 (S=4K). The FP8 row uses a logarithmic axis.

Fig. 5: Scaling each block of probabilities before rounding keeps them in the range where FP8 is accurate, and dividing by the sum of the same rounded values keeps the attention weights summing to one. The schematic shows the probabilities p of one query row by 64-key block. (1) AITER’s FP8 kernel rounds p to e4m3 relative to the row maximum. Blocks more than 6 binades (factors of two) below the maximum become subnormal, with fewer significant bits, and values more than 10 binades below underflow to zero in the numerator. The row sum adds the unrounded p in FP32. (2) ZYFA multiplies each block by 2o so that its largest probability gets the same e4m3 value as p=1, and the scaled matrix instruction (MFMA) that computes PV divides the factor out at no cost. The numerator and the row sum use the same rounded values p̂. The P error is the relative error that rounding p adds to the attention output on Mistral-7B (Figure 20).

Fig. 1: Throughput of ZYFA and AITER’s default kernels on the queries, keys, and values captured from one layer per model at sequence length 16K, timed at sustained clocks (the steady clock after warmup launches). L20 is layer 20. The label above each pair is AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time. Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B have head dimension 128, where the FP8 kernel uses lean P, which writes each FP8 probability with one multiply-add instead of an exponential. DeepSeekV2-Lite has the MLA shape, where the FP8 kernel uses exact P, which evaluates the exponential (Section IV-B), and AITER uses Composable Kernel (CK) in FP8 and its OPUS kernel, written with AITER’s C++ template library, in BF16. Table X gives the clock of these runs.

Fig. 8: Throughput of ZYFA and AITER against sequence length on Gaussian inputs (random q, k, and v with standard deviation 0.1). Times are kernel-only, the device time of the kernel alone without the time that the host takes to launch it. AITER is AITER’s default kernel for each configuration, which at dqk=192 is its OPUS kernel in BF16 and Composable Kernel in FP8. The BF16 panels also show AITER’s Triton kernel and, at dqk=192, AITER’s assembly kernel.

Fig. 21: Error that each stage of one FP8 attention call adds to the attention output, as relative RMS error against fp64 attention, on all three models, without and with a Hadamard rotation of Q and K. The stages are quantizing Q, K, and V (input), quantizing the probabilities (P ), and the rest of the kernel’s arithmetic (Section V-E). The dashed line is the total error of ZYFA’s BF16 kernel. At dqk=192 AITER runs Composable Kernel (CK), whose P arithmetic is not emulated, so only its input term and total are shown.

Fig. 17: Kernel time against output error for each kernel on captured layers at S=4K, the q, k, and v that each model produces on WikiText-2. Output error is the relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs. Filled markers are FP8 kernels, and open markers are BF16 kernels. Each marker is one kernel on one layer, and markers toward the lower left are faster and more accurate. At the head dimensions of DeepSeek-V2-Lite, AITER’s FP8 kernel is Composable Kernel, so their FP8 markers coincide.

Fig. 28: The speedup of ZYFA over AITER barely changes between layers. Each line is the time of one attention call of ZYFA or of AITER’s default kernel in every layer, measured inside a full forward pass of each model at sequence length S=16K on two PG-19 documents. The label in each panel gives AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time, as the median and the range over layers, so a value above 1 means that ZYFA takes less time. In the shaded first layers of Qwen3-8B the running row maximum keeps growing, so ZYFA rescales its output accumulator far more often than in the other layers.

Fig. 18: KL divergence of each next-token distribution from that of the same model with attention computed in fp64, when every attention call uses the kernel under test, averaged over the tokens of eight WikiText-2 sequences of 4K tokens (lower is closer to fp64). Each marker is the mean over the sequences, and its bar spans the lowest to the highest sequence. The dashed line is attention computed in fp32. Filled markers are FP8 kernels, and open markers are BF16 kernels. Triton has no FP8 kernel at the head dimensions of DeepSeek-V2-Lite.

Fig. 15: Output error of one attention call on synthetic inputs at S=8K tokens, as each kernel’s relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs, divided by AITER’s error (below 1 is more accurate than AITER). Gaussian draws q, k, and v from N (0, 0.12), as in the timing runs. Every other input starts from standard normal q, k, and v. Logit SD 1, 4, and 16 scale q and k by 1, 2, and 4, which gives logits with these standard deviations in nats. Stepped Max raises the logits of each successive block of 64 keys by a fixed step, so the row maximum keeps growing. 4-Key Sink scales the first four keys by 8. Rising Logits adds a linear ramp along the keys to every row, and Alternating Rows adds it to every other row. Sink + Flat Tail puts the first key 12 nats above a nearly uniform rest. Full Range draws magnitudes log-uniformly between 2−6 and 28 with random signs, which spans the e4m3 range after scaling.

Fig. 9: Roofline for FP8 multi-head attention at dqk=dv=128, kernel-only on Gaussian inputs. At a given arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs per byte moved from memory, a kernel cannot exceed the sloped memory roof or the flat arithmetic roofs. The roofs are the empirical HBM bandwidth, the datasheet FP8 peak, and the empirical peak of the 32×32×64 FP8 matrix instruction (MFMA) that the kernels use. The 16×16 shape, which has the higher throughput, reaches 4.60 PFLOP/s (Table V). Each vector roof is the throughput at which all vector instructions of a kernel, packed FP32 included, fill the vector pipe, the unit that runs elementwise arithmetic such as the softmax. The roof of exact P, which evaluates the exponential, comes from a thread trace of an earlier build of the assembly kernel. With FLOPs = BHS2(dqk + dv) the arithmetic intensity is 0.4S FLOP/byte, so every length from 2K up is compute-bound.

Fig. 12: Cycles per launch against the shader clock (SCLK) for ZYFA’s and AITER’s FP8 kernels on Mistral-7B layer 20 at S=16K, at sustained clocks. Kernel time is cycles divided by clock, so a kernel can take less time by needing fewer cycles or by running at a higher clock. Cycles are kernel time multiplied by the SCLK of the slowest chiplet. Filled markers are captured activations, the q, k, and v of the real model, and open markers are Gaussian inputs of the same shape. Points on a dashed line take the same time as the captured-activation point of that kernel.

Fig. 24: Rotating Q and K with a Hadamard matrix before FP8 quantization buys more accuracy per unit of time than running heads or layers in BF16. Each line starts from all-FP8 attention with one input transform (large dot) and moves a growing share of heads or layers to BF16. Time is attention time inside the model relative to all-FP8 ZYFA, including one fused quantization pass. The KL divergence measures how far the next-token distributions move from those of the BF16 model, on 48 PG-19 documents per model. On Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B, only all-BF16 attention reaches the gray BF16 noise band, where a policy (a choice of the heads or layers that run in BF16) is as close to the BF16 model as a second, equally correct BF16 kernel would be.

Fig. 3: The chiplet map helps most at short sequences. The figure gives the throughput of ZYFA with the chiplet map divided by that of the same kernel without it. The map sends consecutive tile pairs of one head to the same chiplet (XCD), so that they share its L2 cache. Multi-head attention, batch size B=1, kernel-only timing on Gaussian inputs as in Table VIII.

Fig. 4: Lean P, which computes each FP8 probability with one multiply-add instead of an exponential, stays within 7.5% of the true probability, against 5.9% for rounding the exact value. The figure gives the relative error of the e4m3 probability with exact P and lean P over one binade (one factor of two) of p, plotted against x = log2 p. Exact P rounds 2x to the nearest e4m3 value. Lean P rounds y from Equation 2 (with shift σ=6 and bias β=0.35) to the nearest integer and uses it as the e4m3 bit pattern, and the dashed line is the error of y before rounding. Over the normal e4m3 range the error depends on the fractional part of x alone, so one binade shows all of it.

Fig. 10: Speed of ZYFA’s FP8 kernels relative to AITER’s default kernel as design decisions are added from left to right, kernel-only on Gaussian inputs, multi-head at B=1. Error bars span the repetitions. At dqk=192 the baseline is Composable Kernel (CK), AITER’s default FP8 kernel for that shape. Step “+Lean P” computes each FP8 probability with a multiply-add instead of an exponential, and step “+Row Sum on MFMA” sums each row of probabilities on the matrix unit. Both steps also turn on per-block scaling, and step “+Assembly Schedule” replaces the HIP kernel with the hand-scheduled assembly kernel. The rightmost point of each line is the final kernel, measured in the same jobs as Table VIII. Section VI-A defines every step, and Figure 11 shows the BF16 kernels.

Fig. 11: Speed of ZYFA’s BF16 kernels relative to AITER’s default kernel as design decisions are added from left to right, kernel-only on Gaussian inputs, multi-head at B=1. At dqk=192 the baseline is AITER’s OPUS kernel, a HIP kernel built with AITER’s C++ template library. Section VI-A defines every step.

Fig. 27: Once its error bound has a cost, an in-kernel two-stage scheme is less accurate (it has a higher KL divergence from the BF16 model) than a static policy that takes the same time. The two-stage scheme runs attention in FP8 with an error bound per block and recomputes the flagged blocks in BF16, at a modeled time of 1 + c+ r w, where c is the cost of the bound, w the share of recomputed blocks, and r the ratio of BF16 to FP8 time. Static policies keep fixed heads or layers in BF16, and their time and KL divergence are measured. The data predate lean P.

Fig. 26: On the NLL, most FP8 policies also differ from the BF16 model, and on Qwen3-8B rotation raises the NLL although it lowers the KL divergence. Each point is the change in negative log-likelihood per token against the BF16 model, with its 95% interval over PG-19 books, for the mixed-precision policies of Figure 24 (choices of the heads or layers that run in BF16), against attention time relative to all-FP8 ZYFA. A lower NLL does not mean that a policy is closer to BF16, as AITER’s FP8 kernel on Qwen3-8B shows.

Fig. 23: Share of the FP8 error energy of the attention outputs that falls in the worst x% of layers, heads, and 128-row blocks, ranked by their own FP8 error, for the median document. The dotted curve is the share if the error were spread evenly, x% of the error energy in x% of the units. The horizontal axis is linear below 1% and logarithmic above.

Fig. 22: Scores that measure the local FP8 error (the error of each unit’s own attention output), such as the error on calibration documents and the quantization error bound, find almost as much of it as ranking by the true error (gray band). ge2 (the gradient-weighted error of a head) and layer KL (how much FP8 attention in one layer alone changes the model output) find little of it, because they rank units by their effect on the model output, which works better end to end (Table XIV). Each line gives the share of the true FP8 error energy in the heads (top) or 128-row blocks (bottom) that a score ranks highest. Static scores are computed in advance on calibration documents and dynamic scores at inference time, and the dotted line ranks the heads or row blocks in random order.

Fig. 19: KL divergence per token from the model with ZYFA’s BF16 attention, KL(BF16 ∥ variant), when every attention call of the model uses one FP8 kernel variant, at 8K, 16K, and 32K tokens on 42 PG-19 documents per model. Lower means closer to the BF16 model. The first two rows are references, attention in fp64 and AITER’s BF16 kernel, which show how far two correct kernels differ through rounding alone, and the gray band covers their range.

Fig. 20: Quantizing the inputs Q, K, and V to FP8 adds most of the error of ZYFA’s FP8 attention, and rounding the probabilities p adds much less. The top row shows the stages of one FP8 attention call. Each bar below is the error that a stage adds on Mistral-7B (12 PG-19 documents, log scale), as the RMS of the change that the stage makes to the attention output O, divided by the RMS of fp64 attention on the BF16 inputs, in percent, pooled over all layers, heads, and rows. papers.abstract: Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{IAPO}, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.
bullets: Existing methods credit orchestration decisions independently, overlooking dependencies between earlier and later choices.
IAPO exactly decomposes policy-performance changes into individual decision effects and higher-order interactions.
It optimizes both components from sampled trajectories and certifies that each update improves performance.
Across long-input reasoning and code benchmarks, IAPO matches the strongest system’s accuracy using fewer tokens.
Ablating interaction modeling reduces code accuracy by 7–17 points, showing its importance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of IAPO. (a) Orchestration decisions depend on one another: a new earlier worker helps only if a later call may read its output, so neither change helps alone. (b) IAPO credits each orchestrator step and every pair of steps in one pass over each training trajectory, and fits one bounded update per step size. (c) With the candidates fixed, IAPO computes two lower bounds on the gain from fresh trajectories, keeps the larger one, and updates the policy only if it is positive.

papers.abstract: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.
bullets: Addresses scattered evidence and subtle distinctions between closely related ATT&CK techniques.
Uses agentic documentation mining to build a shared behavioral representation linking observations, passages, and technique definitions.
Extracts primitive-guided evidence, retrieves aligned technique candidates and confusable alternatives, and validates references and technique requirements.
Evaluated on 610 MITRE ATT&CK-referenced malware reports against 11 baselines; it improves exact-ID F1 by 17.4% over the strongest baseline.
Concept-guided retrieval raises gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%; offline policy refinement further improves performance without parameter updates.

papers.abstract: Enterprise AI agents split requests across subagents, and each handoff can drop, alter or ignore a requirement. A preregistered study on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks compares free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs it and deterministically verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs (S2 -0.4 pp, 95% CI [-14.2, 13.3]). Signing defeats in-transit mutation: unsigned manifests violated 79.2 pp more often than signed ones, which never did; this replicated in gpt-oss-20b and gemma-4-12b. There, without an adversary, signed manifests were descriptively slightly worse than structured handoffs (11.1% vs 2.8%; 16.7% vs 8.3%; not tested) and lost utility overall (gpt-oss-20b, all threats: -28.7 pp). On identical Qwen3-8B trajectories, the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, and an oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits, so the residual risk is in extraction. A preregistered pre-signing injection confirmed this: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest unsafe commits from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 16.7% to 97.2% (gemma-4-12b), and every such commit carried a manifest corrupted before signing. Signing protects transit; extraction is the trust boundary. A testable pre-signing specification (PSE), specified after the injection results and frozen before an offline evaluation, blocked all these injected commits (fixed templates) but refused 45.8%, 11.1% and 22.2% of benign requests, changing completions by -8.3 pp, -2.8 pp and 0.0 pp.
bullets: The study compares free-text, structured JSON, and cryptographically signed requirement-manifest handoffs on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks across five threats.
For Qwen3-8B, signed manifests reduced unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% without detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs.
Signing eliminated in-transit manifest mutation across tested models, while deterministic verification outperformed an LLM checker on detecting violating decisions.
Residual risk lies in requirement extraction: a single pre-signing adversarial line sharply increased unsafe commits across Qwen3-8B, gpt-oss-20b, and gemma-4-12b.
A post hoc frozen pre-signing specification blocked injected attacks but rejected some benign requests, indicating a safety–availability tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.
bullets: Targets unsafe reasoning and answers, inconsistent safety behavior, and failure to identify user intent.
Decomposes safety into four fine-grained verifiable rewards and selects training data based on difficulty.
Uses reasoning-preserving gradient projection to resolve conflicts between safety and reasoning objectives.
Across 1.5B–671B models, reports stronger safety, lower over-refusal, and preserved general reasoning across multiple benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.

papers.selection_reason: Self-scheduling persistent kernels to overlap communication and compute, reducing training latency for transformer models.
papers.title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap
papers.tldr: KOSMOS uses demand-ordered self-scheduling persistent kernels to dynamically overlap communication and computation, accelerating large-model parallel training.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon role-playing dialogue requires consistent character identity, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction. We present a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework that revises original-character memory, stable persona instructions, and a policy for constructing turn-level prompts. Repair outcomes also inform revisions to the updater's diagnostic rules, edit routing, and candidate selection. We specify the updater as a versioned policy with explicit inputs, editable fields, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions. An internal evaluation covers 50 original characters and five models, with two 100-round conversations per character-model pair: 500 conversations per condition. Across the pooled evaluated replies, the bad-response rate decreases from 14.00% (6,973/49,824) to 4.94% (2,459/49,793), a 9.06-percentage-point reduction and a 64.71% relative reduction. In 600 blinded human comparisons, RSI receives 294 wins, 187 ties, and 119 losses, yielding a 71.19% win rate among decisive judgments. The results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution.
bullets: Targets character consistency, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction over extended conversations.
Uses a versioned updater with explicit inputs, editable fields, diagnostic rules, edit routing, candidate selection, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions.
Evaluated on 50 original characters and five models with 100-round conversations in an internal test setting.
Bad-response rate fell from 14.00% to 4.94%, while blinded human comparisons favored RSI in 294 of 600 cases, with 187 ties and 119 losses.
Results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution; broader generalization is not established.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language model responses by spending additional computation at inference time, and the right amount of compute depends on the prompt. Adaptive TTC methods allocate compute based on signals of response quality such as observed rewards, often by stopping once the signal exceeds a fixed threshold, and generally measure cost by the number of generations or tokens. But in online serving, latency is also a cost: it grows with server load, so a method using a fixed threshold spends too little compute when generation is fast and too much when it is slow. For Best-of-$N$ sampling, a widely used TTC method, we propose a two-stage adaptive algorithm that draws an initial batch, then uses the observed rewards and the batch's latency to decide whether to draw a second batch and at what size by comparing expected improvement against predicted cost: it draws one when the first batch's best reward is below a threshold that decreases with the first batch's latency, without explicitly measuring server load. We map each reward to its value under the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the prompt's reward distribution, so the same tradeoff parameters can be reused across tasks; a regression fitted offline on other prompts predicts a distribution for the CDF value of the first batch's best reward, giving the expected improvement in closed form. We evaluate the method by simulation on a preference-based alignment benchmark, measuring generations-equivalent cost: generations plus latency, converted to generations. The method reaches Best-of-$N$'s reward at lower generations-equivalent cost, and conditioning on the measured first-batch latency saves at least as much of that cost as fixed-threshold (latency-unaware) baselines, and more when latency is highly variable, when it grows with batch size, and when the second batch's latency is highly predictable from the first's.
bullets: Targets adaptive test-time compute where latency, not just generation count, is a significant serving cost.
Uses a two-stage strategy: sample an initial batch, then decide whether and how large a second batch should be.
Triggers additional sampling when the first batch’s best reward is below a latency-dependent threshold.
Normalizes rewards via the prompt reward CDF and uses offline regression to estimate expected improvement in closed form.
Simulation results show lower generations-equivalent cost than Best-of-N, with larger savings under variable latency and predictable batch delays.

papers.abstract: Running evaluations of contact-rich robotic manipulation at statistical scale has largely been possible only at well-resourced labs, highlighting the need for affordable and efficient options for broader audiences. We present a reproducible evaluation harness wrapper based on a previous study at 200-rollout scale on serverless commodity GPUs, at a cost of approximately $3.50 USD and 38 minutes of wall-clock per replication (4.4 L4-GPU-hours across eight parallel shards). Using the harness, we report a partially controlled negative result on action chunking with sparse data: three independently trained chunked checkpoints produce zero genuine successes across 780 rollouts, while three single-step checkpoints range from 2.6% to 11.8% success rate. A per-step-replanning control partially isolates chunk prediction, rather than open-loop chunk execution as the mechanism, with the failure localized to the training formulation and multi-step prediction. This work further democratizes physics-based policy development and evaluation through our reusable harness.
bullets: Runs an 800-scale-style evaluation replication for about $3.50 and 38 minutes using eight parallel commodity-GPU shards.
In 780 rollouts, three chunked-policy checkpoints achieve zero genuine successes.
Single-step checkpoints achieve success rates ranging from 2.6% to 11.8%.
Per-step replanning suggests the failure is tied to chunk prediction and training, not simply open-loop chunk execution.
The reusable harness aims to broaden access to physics-based policy development and evaluation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Runtime architecture of one 200-rollout replication. A cloud-resident dispatcher fans out eight containers, each evaluating a disjoint slice of scenario_index; because the harness derives each rollout’s random seed from its index, the union of shards reproduces the unsharded run exactly. Within a container the Drake harness renders headless under Xvfb and queries a co-located gRPC policy server, which keeps the policy implementation outside the harness process. Each shard writes per-episode results to a persistent volume; screening and aggregation read them back afterwards, so no result depends on the dispatching process surviving the run. Model assets and the EGL vendor ICD are baked into the image at build time.

In each scene, the policy instructs the right robotic arm to pick up the red box and place it in the interior of the circular goal marker on the tabletop and the rollout is judged as a success or failure. In scene 125 the arm transports the box onto the goal marker and the rollout is scored successful. In scene 3 the arm reaches toward the box, overshoots, and holds position for the remainder of the episode without relocating it. Red arrows are Drake hydroelastic contactforce vectors. Scene 6 is one of five scenarios whose initial condition places the box directly above the goal; it registers success within 0.3 s with both arms stationary, and is excluded under R1. Camera position varies slightly between recordings.

papers.abstract: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.
bullets: Addresses open-world interactive navigation where obstacles may need to be moved rather than avoided.
Uses explicit VLM affordance reasoning before planning to choose actions such as swiping, picking up, or avoiding objects.
Handles context-dependent cases, such as pushing an empty cart but avoiding one carrying fragile glassware.
Evaluated on a mobile manipulator in real indoor and outdoor environments.
Improves real-robot success by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline, without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MessyNav: A framework for zero-shot open-world interactive navigation. MessyNav consists of an Affordance Reasoner that infers object interactability from an RGB image using a VLM to evaluate both robot-centric physical feasibility and object-centric interaction safety. For example, it will label a cart with a laptop as non-interactive while labeling a wheeled crate with a bin as interactive. Given the object affordance labels, a Task Planner then sequences manipulation and navigation actions from an open-language skill library containing a simple set of motion primitives (pick up, swipe left, swipe right) and a LiDAR-based navigation stack (move to) that we find can tackle a wide range of interactive navigation scenarios. Finally, the generated plan is executed by grounding object references in 3D coordinates using VLM keypoint identification, semantic segmentation, and depth-based deprojection.

Figure 4: Explicit affordance reasoning improves context-dependent task planning. In this scene, a suitcase supporting a stack of books is inherently unstable, while the black cart holding a single book can be safely cleared. [Left] MessyNav reasons about affordances before planning, correctly labeling the suitcase as non-interactive and the cart as interactive, and swiping the cart aside to clear the path. [Middle] vlm-planner-only plans directly from the image without an explicit affordance stage and incorrectly decides to swipe the unstable suitcase. [Right] closed-set-planner assigns fixed category-level affordances that misclassify the suitcase as interactive, leading to an unsafe plan.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results across Environments. We deploy MessyNav in varied settings to test its zero-shot capability. The robot successfully reasons about affordances and executes interactions across different lighting conditions, environments, and object types.
Figure 7: Example Open-Vocabulary Keypoint Detection. We use gemini-2.5-pro [36] to detect keypoints of objects specified by the task planner through language queries.
Figure 6: Hardware: We deploy on the TidyBot++ holonomic mobile manipulator [18] with two cameras and a LiDAR for perception. An onboard laptop runs the autonomy stack.

Figure 9: MessyNav’s failure breakdown compared to the strongest baseline. Sankey diagrams of trial outcomes for MessyNav (left) and vlm-planner-only (right) over 15 real-world trials. MessyNav succeeds on 10/15 trials versus 6/15 for vlm-planner-only. While most of vlm-planner-only’s failures are planning failures in which vlm-planner-only decides to interact with non-interactive objects (7 of 9), MessyNav reduces these to 2, showcasing the importance of explicit affordance reasoning.

Figure 3: MessyNav reasons about context, not just object category. In this cluttered scene, closed-set-oracle assigns affordances by category alone, misclassifying the rolling cart as interactive (ignoring the glassware it carries) and the suitcase as interactive (ignoring its fragile sticker). In contrast, MessyNav reasons at the instance level. It treats the cart and the glass stemware as a single fragile unit and reads the sticker on the suitcase as a contextual cue, correctly labeling both as non-interactive.

Table 3: Scaled-Up Offline Planning Results. We evaluate high-level planning performance across 55 real-world scenes in 5 environments, with 15 repeated trials per scene, assuming perfect low-level execution. MessyNav outperforms the strongest baseline from the real-world evaluation overall and under well-lit conditions, while nighttime remains challenging for both methods.

Table 2: Real-World Interactive Navigation Results. MessyNav achieves the highest success rate across 15 real-world scenes. Success requires reaching the goal without any unsafe interactions. ∗Execution time (excluding VLM queries) averaged across successful trials.
Table 1: Affordance Reasoning Results. MessyNav outperforms geometric and closed-set baselines, highlighting the importance of context-dependent affordance reasoning.

Table 8: Real-World Navigation Scenarios. To evaluate open-world interactive navigation, we test in a bedroom and conference room environments while deliberately varying objects, contexts, and required interactions across trials. The scenes also contain furniture (e.g., couch, bed, drawers, meeting tables) as fixed non-interactive obstacles. Additional objects are listed and marked as interactive (I) or non-interactive (N).
Table 6: Example Context Variations in Affordance Reasoning Evaluation Set. The same object type is marked as interactive (I) or non-interactive (N) depending on context.
Table 5: Composition of the Affordance Reasoning Benchmark. Our benchmark spans diverse environments, lighting, clutter, and obstacle sizes.

Table 7: Affordance Reasoning Comparison. Number of objects with correctly classified interactivity. Simple cases contain objects in their default state, while Complex cases involve contextdependent configurations (e.g., cart with fragile items, table with vase, suitcase with caution tape).

papers.abstract: Panoptic Scene Graph generation (PSG) requires holistic yet fine-grained reasoning over complex relations among objects. However, current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) applied to PSG suffer from a perception bottleneck: they function as static observers limited by fixed-resolution views. As a result, models often overlook critical relations involving small or peripheral objects and struggle to differentiate ambiguous predicates in complex scenes. To address these limitations, we propose PSGAgent, an agentic framework that enhances visual perception for PSG through a think-act-observe loop. PSGAgent allows MLLMs to dynamically refine their visual perception using two tools: a Region Zoom-In Tool for local exploration of small or boundary relations and a Visual Highlight Tool for relation-focused segmentation that filters out irrelevant contextual noise. To optimize decision-making, we construct a two-stage training pipeline. First, we create a high-quality, error-aware Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (M-CoT) dataset that provides robust supervision for cold-start learning. Then, we design a novel hierarchical reward mechanism integrated with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) to enable strategic and adaptive tool usage. Extensive experiments on the PSG benchmark show that PSGAgent achieves SOTA performance, demonstrating strong capability in both holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.
bullets: Addresses the fixed-resolution perception bottleneck that causes MLLMs to miss small, peripheral, or ambiguous object relations.
Uses a think–act–observe loop with Region Zoom-In and Visual Highlight tools for adaptive visual inspection.
Trains the agent with an error-aware multimodal chain-of-thought dataset and hierarchical rewards using GSPO.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on the PSG benchmark, with improved holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PSGAgent.We reformulate PSG as amulti-turn, tool-augmented decision-making process. (Left) Trajectory Construction. We perform error-aware data mining to identify challenging cases caused by saliency bias (relations occupying small regions or located near image boundaries) and semantic ambiguity (long-range contextual interference, high predicate confusion, or tail relations). These identified cases are used to synthesize error-aware Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (M-CoT) trajectories through a structured generation pipeline. (Right) Cold-start SFT and RL-based Enhancement. The agent is first initialized via SFT to learn basic tool usage, and then optimized with GSPO for strategic reasoning. Through a think–act–observe interaction loop guided by a hybrid reward function (𝑅outcome, 𝑅causal, 𝑅highlight, and 𝑅format), the agent learns to autonomously invoke tools (Region Zoom-In Tool and Visual Highlight Tool) to achieve holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of PSGAgent with existing methods. (a) R1-SGG (7B); (b) PSGAgent (3B, ours).

Figure 1: The perception bottleneck in PSG. (a) Saliency bias: static models are biased toward dominant regions, while neglecting small-scale or off-center relations. (b) Semantic ambiguity: long-range contextual interference and fine-grained predicate confusion lead to relational uncertainty.
Figure 4: Analysis of the M-CoT dataset. (a) Classification of error types; (b) Rounds of tool calls.

papers.abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.
bullets: Addresses replay attacks where recorded camera observations remain plausible despite changed physical trajectories.
Adds private Gaussian noise to control inputs and predicts image-derived latent dynamics conditioned on those inputs.
Detects attacks through discrepancies between predicted latent responses and received-image latent representations.
Uses reinforcement learning to adapt watermark covariance based on latent state and detector confidence.
Evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 reaching-and-avoidance task under nominal and replay-attacked observations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. (a) The live observation xt−H is provided to the vision-based controller policy F , which predicts the control input ut−H . In parallel, an encoder maps xt−H to the latent state zt−H . The latent state, together with the detector confidence cj , is provided to the DWM policy to select the covariance Σt−H , from which the private watermark ϕt−H is sampled. The watermark and control input are combined to form the watermarked control input ūt−H , which is applied to the plant. (b) When a replay attack occurs, the encoder maps the received replayed observations to latent states [z′t−H+1, . . . , z ′ t]. These are compared with the predicted latent states [z̃t−H+1|t−H , . . . , z̃t|t−H ] to obtain the residual window rj , defined in (8). The MCUSUM detector processes this window, and the resulting evidence updates the attack confidence cj through (18). When attack evidence persists, the supervisor switches to the damped-stop controller and applies uds t as specified in (7).

Fig. 3. Average (Top) Attack Belief, (Middle) Min Robot-Human separation (m), and (Bottom) End-effector speed (m/s) across 30 episodes. Replay begins at step 60. Blue denotes live observations, red denotes the replayed source observations received by the policy, and green denotes the live trajectory with Simplex stopping.

papers.abstract: Solving visual puzzles requires both accurate interpretation of visual evidence and reliable computation under task-specific rules. Embedding visual assumptions and task constraints directly in solving code makes the represented problem difficult to inspect and revise independently. We introduce Vis2State, a training-free agentic framework that abstracts visual puzzles into explicit, revisable problem states linking visual inspection and execution. Visual inspection guides state construction and refinement, while generated programs solve the represented problem. The model constructs both the state and the program without predefined puzzle schemas or solving procedures. Inspection and execution feedback allow it to revise the problem representation and solving procedure independently. Vis2State achieves the state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks. Cross-model evaluation further demonstrates consistent gains. Ablations, error analyses, and fixed-program state interventions further support the effectiveness of the state-centered design. The code will be made publicly available to facilitate future research.
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly interpreting visual evidence and applying task-specific rules.
Builds explicit problem states and programs without predefined puzzle schemas or solving procedures.
Uses inspection and execution feedback to revise the representation and solving process independently.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks, with consistent gains across models.
Ablations, error analyses, and fixed-program interventions support the state-centered design.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Inspection, State, and Execution in Vis2State. Inspection gathers visual evidence to construct the State, and Execution solves the represented problem. The model refines the state or program through feedback before submitting an answer.

papers.abstract: Recent work in machine learning has demonstrated that transformer-based language model agents can communicate state not only through text, but also directly in latent space via key-value (KV) caches. In this paper, we argue that such cache-to-cache translation can provide utility beyond the original motivating application of real-time agent communication and can instead be utilized for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Building on the Cache-to-Cache (C2C) fusion framework, our proposed system CacheGraft encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache representation between a larger sharer model (4B parameters in our experiments) and a smaller receiver model (0.6B parameters) such that this cache can be injected into the receiver at query time with no need for the larger model. Across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally-run judges, CacheGraft improves answer quality over the text-only receiver baseline in 29 out of 30 comparisons, of which 17 of the 30 are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are zero-shot with respect to the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data. These initial results suggest that latent-space document enrichment may be a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where it is only feasible to deploy a small model at inference time.
bullets: Addresses compute-constrained RAG settings where only a small receiver model can be deployed during inference.
Offline, a larger sharer and smaller receiver model jointly encode each passage into a fused KV-cache representation.
The cache is injected into the receiver at query time, avoiding runtime use of the larger model.
Improved answer quality over a text-only receiver in 29 of 30 comparisons across five QA benchmarks and two judges; 17 improvements were statistically significant.
Results are zero-shot for the fuser, which was not trained on retrieval data; findings are presented as initial evidence rather than a definitive general solution.

papers.abstract: We present \textbf{WeLM-Image}, a unified image foundation model that integrates multimodal understanding into text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference synthesis. Designed for single-GPU deployment in WeChat's large-scale consumer applications, the model processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone combines shared attention with independent understanding and generation parameters to limit optimization interference. Equipping each path with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules provides sparse capacity, with 31.7B stored parameters and approximately 5.4B generation parameters activated per target latent token. A generation-oriented data engine combines a knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary with large-scale visual clustering to balance semantic coverage and editing tasks, while training-time evaluation guides iterative data refinement. Bilingual annotations and verified editing supervision support progressive training up to native 1.5K resolution. We optimize generation and editing separately with rubric- and checklist-based rewards, then consolidate the specialized policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation. In the reported overall comparisons, the 1536-resolution model ranks first among the evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench. MeanFlow-based few-step distillation yields WeLM-Image-Turbo, which generates a $1024\times1024$ image in 4.98\,s on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU using eight guidance-free steps.
bullets: Processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence for multiple visual tasks.
Uses a Mixture-of-Transformers backbone with Mixture-of-Experts modules to separate understanding and generation while enabling sparse capacity.
Builds training data with knowledge-grounded visual concepts, clustering, bilingual annotations, and verified editing supervision, scaling to native 1.5K resolution.
Separately optimizes generation and editing, then merges the resulting policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation.

The reported 1536-resolution model ranks first among evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench; its Turbo variant generates 1024×1024 images in 4.98 seconds using eight guidance-free steps on one NVIDIA H20 GPU.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.
bullets: Addresses test-time scaling when a strong target-problem verifier is unavailable.
Uses asymmetric self-play to generate and improve solutions without verifier dependence.
On a difficulty-calibrated LiveCodeBench v6 subset, it outperforms evaluated baselines across verifier strengths.
In the no-verifier setting, it delivers a 35% absolute improvement in mean@8.
Performance gains largely disappear when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Test-Time Self-Play. Given a target problem x⋆ and previously generated synthetic problems, the proposer policy πϕ generates target-conditioned synthetic problems D consisting of a problem statement, tests, and a reference solution. The solver policy is rewarded for correctly solving the synthetic problems, while the proposer is rewarded for generating synthetic problems near the solver’s current learning frontier (both via GRPO; see the red arrows). The synthetic problem history provides context for the proposer and fills a replay buffer B. After a sufficient number of iterations, the test-time trained solver can then attempt the target problem.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.
bullets: On all 900 long-bucket Video-MME items, no tested frame selector significantly beats uniform sampling; estimated gains remain within ±5 points.
Results from 200-item subsets are unstable: effects can grow by up to 3.8×, reverse sign, and disagree with the full-bucket effect in 35.8% of resamples.
A claimed anomaly-domain “+ASR” gain was partly caused by a development prefix; transcript placement also changes performance substantially and inconsistently across datasets.
Routing to another answering model produces the largest contrast, but most of its gain persists when the soundtrack is silenced, indicating a model-swap effect rather than selection.
The audit releases code, per-item predictions, and scripts for reproducing all statistics.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled audit of long-video QA frame selection and evidence injection; relevant to video understanding and VLMs.
papers.title: Where Do Reported Long-Video QA Gains Come From? A Controlled Audit of Frame Selection, Evidence Injection, and Expert Routing
papers.tldr: A controlled audit finds that reported long-video QA gains mostly come from model routing, prompt/context effects, or small-sample noise—not frame selection itself.

papers.abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.
bullets: Addresses the stability–plasticity trade-off in continual reinforcement learning.
Separates slow, generalizable long-term learning from fast, situation-specific adaptation.
Introduces a novel non-parametric approximation for transient value estimation in complex tasks.
Enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic.
The approach is evaluated empirically and theoretically, with scope focused on the studied task settings.

papers.abstract: Selecting high-quality training data can reduce computation cost for LLM fine-tuning. Prior work on data selection developed a variety of difficulty-based scores, motivated by the intuition that harder examples are more informative. While effective for smaller classification models, we find that such methods often fail to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning. Our analysis reveals that random selection performs better because it is more representative of the underlying input space---i.e., has better coverage. To validate the importance of coverage, we implement a simple clustering-based selection method which selects data that is more representative of the underlying input distribution. On a set of diverse single-domain tasks, this method yields performance at or above that of random selection. On the diverse, multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture, where random sampling no longer guarantees a balanced subset, our method outperforms all methods. Overall, our results indicate that prioritizing coverage over difficulty leads to more effective data selection for LLM fine-tuning.
bullets: Difficulty-based selection often fails to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning.
Random selection works well because it better represents the underlying input space.
A simple clustering-based method selects data to improve coverage of the input distribution.
The method matches or exceeds random selection on diverse single-domain tasks and outperforms all compared methods on the multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture.

papers.abstract: Scientific predictors guide costly experiments, yet returned measurements often reveal errors that matter for subsequent experimental choices. WeightLoop turns this feedback into persistent model updates through a reusable Weight-Space Programming (WSP) editor. We use GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek to construct update programs from the scientific objective, model computation and editable parameters. These programs use accumulated measurements to estimate parameter corrections, validate them on feedback and save accepted changes in the original model. With identical feedback and writable parameters, four pretrained scientific predictors obtain 5.10-18.56% lower primary error. For weather prediction, changing four output-bias parameters reduces root mean squared error by 13.28%. Functional ranking and sequential discovery further connect reusable editing programs to improved experimental choices.
bullets: Addresses the problem of scientific models failing to incorporate newly returned measurements into future choices.
Introduces reusable Weight-Space Programming editors that generate parameter-update programs from the objective, model, and editable weights.
Programs estimate and validate corrections from accumulated feedback, then save accepted updates in the original model.
Across four pretrained scientific predictors, the approach reduced primary error by 5.10–18.56% under identical feedback and writable parameters.
A weather-prediction edit to four output-bias parameters reduced RMSE by 13.28%; ranking and sequential discovery also benefited.
