papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach for improving video generation, but its success depends heavily on reliable reward models. Existing methods either map videos directly to opaque scalar scores or generate free-form rationales that are not explicitly optimized as the basis of the final judgment. We propose ArtiVidRM, a verifiable, artifact-as-rubrics video reward model that follows an observe-then-score paradigm. It first identifies visible generation artifacts and organizes them into a structured artifact list, then uses these artifacts as explicit rubrics for quality assessment. This intermediate representation grounds each score in concrete video-level evidence, making the reward more interpretable and informative for optimization. We further introduce a multi-reward reinforcement learning strategy to jointly optimize artifact prediction and quality assessment. The reward decomposes into complementary objectives that evaluate artifact prediction quality, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency, together with a pairwise preference objective that supervises quality ranking through score differences. By jointly optimizing the intermediate artifact representation and the downstream preference prediction, the model learns to produce informative artifact lists while improving the accuracy of video quality assessment. Experiments show that ArtiVidRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks, provides effective signals for video diffusion optimization, and enables artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.
bullets: Addresses opaque scalar rewards and ungrounded free-form rationales in video-generation reinforcement learning.
Uses an observe-then-score pipeline: predict a structured list of visible artifacts, then assess quality based on those artifacts.
Jointly optimizes artifact prediction and pairwise quality ranking through multiple reward objectives, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks and useful signals for video diffusion optimization.
Supports artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise's i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location's channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7x speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that channel-space Householder transformations offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of precise motion control in video diffusion models.
Uses a sequence of Householder reflections as an orthogonal channel-space transformation guided by user motion.
Preserves each frame’s spatial i.i.d. Gaussian noise structure while creating cross-frame temporal correlations.
Architecture-agnostic and directly compatible with standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines.
Reportedly matches or outperforms prior methods across scenarios and runs 2.7× faster than noise warping.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a robotic harvesting method that combines RGB-D fruit localization, GA-based harvest ordering, and waypoint-based robot motion in dense and unstructured crop environments. The global RGB-D camera provides 3D fruit positions for ordering, while the end-effector-mounted camera provides close-range observation during execution. The GA determines the harvesting sequence, and static or dynamic waypoints define the intermediate robot motion. The method was evaluated in a controlled laboratory testbed and in four-, five-, and six-fruit field conditions. GA solutions were compared with exhaustive enumeration, and both waypoint offsets were examined by parameter sensitivity analysis. Continuous execution reduced unnecessary Home-return motion, while the dynamic waypoint changed with the remaining fruit distribution without changing the GA sequence. In the field evaluation, the dynamic-waypoint continuous strategy produced 40 collision events and a 70.7% target-approach success rate, compared with 55 collision events and 65.3% for the static-waypoint continuous strategy.
bullets: Uses a global RGB-D camera for 3D fruit positions and an end-effector camera for close-range observation.
The genetic algorithm selects harvest sequences, while static or dynamic waypoints guide intermediate robot motion.
Evaluated in a laboratory testbed and field scenarios containing four, five, and six fruits, with comparisons against exhaustive ordering.

papers.abstract: One of the remarkable abilities of Transformer-based neural networks is in-context learning. This motivates us to think about "in-context" control. Can we control a system knowing only (1) that it belongs to a particular family of systems and (2) some data on system evolution (provided as the context trajectory) but no specific parameter information? Specifically, we investigate the ability of Transformer-models to perform "in-context" control of unstable, nonlinear dynamical systems, where context consists only of the unforced system dynamics. We leverage a multi-head, GPT-2-style architecture, and we evaluate performance for two classical nonlinear systems -- the cartpole system and the two-link acrobot system, where the system parameters are unknown to the Transformer. We consider a setting where trajectories from an expert controller are available at training time but not at inference time. Here, we identify training techniques that are essential to train Transformers to perform low-level control. Through an analysis over checkpoints, we show that in-context control is possible, and the learned policy performance generally improves as context increases. Furthermore, the Transformer models can generalize to stabilize systems that are out-of-distribution.
bullets: Studies in-context low-level control when system parameters are unavailable and only unforced dynamics are provided as context.
Uses a multi-head, GPT-2-style Transformer trained with expert trajectories that are unavailable during inference.
Evaluates control on the nonlinear cartpole and two-link acrobot systems.
Finds that specific training techniques are essential for learning effective control policies.
Shows that in-context control is feasible, performance generally improves with more context, and some out-of-distribution systems can be stabilized.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. As such, SAEs may provide insight into an LLM's knowledge representation and internal ``mental'' grammar - topics of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior and of theoretical interest for the study of in silico representations of human language. Language models with fewer than 100M parameters, trained on small corpora, nonetheless exhibit strong grammatical competence and discourse coherence, despite producing content of limited reliability. We use SAEs that we trained on one such model (Pythia-70M) to conduct an in-depth examination of how a single grammatical phenomenon, number agreement, is represented and processed in an LLM. We demonstrate the mechanism and the methodology by which SAEs can be used to find and propagate ``plural noun'', ``plural matrix subject'', and ``generate a plural verb'' features which cause the LLM to produce plural verb forms such as ``are'', ``do'', or ``have'' instead of ``is'', ``does'', and ``has'' in response to prompts such as ``the men in the park''. We show that intervening to remove these features from the hidden states of plural subject noun tokens causes the model to produce singular verbs instead, and vice versa. We also show that corresponding ``singular noun'' and ``generate a singular verb'' features are not as effective for this task. This asymmetry suggests that Pythia-70m makes use of a privative representation of grammatical number in English. These findings replicated with larger LLMs Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b yielded similar results. Our main contribution is a novel approach to the use of SAEs to understanding how LLMs encode human language that addresses a number of technical and methodological challenges.
bullets: Studies number agreement in Pythia-70M using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extending the analysis to Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b.
Identifies features for plural nouns, plural subjects, and generating plural verbs that influence forms such as “are,” “do,” and “have.”
Removing plural features from plural-subject representations causes singular verb outputs, while adding or propagating them promotes plural agreement.
Singular-related features are less effective, suggesting grammatical number may be represented primarily through plural features rather than a balanced singular/plural code.
Demonstrates an SAE-based methodology for probing and intervening on language representations while addressing associated technical and methodological challenges.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained diffusion and flow policies have emerged as powerful backbones for robotics, yet adapting them to novel data via reinforcement learning (RL) remains computationally expensive, sample inefficient and lacks theoretical guarantees. Prior approaches that fine-tune the initial noise bypass costly backpropagation through time but struggle with the "noise aliasing" problem: there does not exista natural link between the noise space value and the action space value. This paper resolves these challenges by introducing the Latent Noise Linear Markov Decision Process (LNL-MDP). We derive the Bridge Equation for LNL-MDPs which eliminates the noise aliasing problem by aligning values with a shared representation between the noise and the action space. Furthermore, our LNL-MDP fine tuning framework falls under the FineTuneRL theory with near-optimal guarantee. Leveraging these insights, we propose Latent Representation Bridging for Diffusion (LARBRID), an algorithm that efficiently learns the representation to optimize the initial distribution that steers the pre-trained model to act optimally in the environment. It yields up to 2-3$\times$ performance increases on challenging control problems across a diverse suite of robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks. Code can be found at: github.com/Maincode-Research/LARBRID.git.
bullets: Pretrained diffusion policies are costly and sample-inefficient to adapt to new tasks with RL.
The proposed Latent Noise Linear MDP (LNL-MDP) establishes a shared representation between initial noise and actions.
A derived Bridge Equation removes the noise-aliasing problem and supports FineTuneRL guarantees.
LARBRID learns a latent representation that optimizes the policy’s initial noise distribution without costly backpropagation through time.
The method improves performance by up to 2–3× on diverse robotic locomotion and manipulation control tasks.

papers.abstract: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.
bullets: Uses a PICO 4 Ultra headset with on-device head/hand tracking and stereo object localisation for tabletop demonstrations.
Adapts preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes.
Evaluated two tabletop tasks in simulation using demonstrations from one operator; cube-placement performance varied across training seeds and headsets.
A baseline struggled with two-stage stacking due to replanning and gripper–object interactions observed in diagnostic replays.
After task-specific trajectory and execution adaptations, the stacking policy met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four noise seeds.

papers.tldr: VREgo uses consumer-VR egocentric demonstrations to train robot manipulation policies, achieving reliable cube placement and stacking after trajectory and execution-rule adaptations.

papers.abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
bullets: The study defines and evaluates calendar-based time-context—the lookback period before prediction—rather than token-context alone.
A decoder-only EHR transformer was pretrained on coded primary-care events and evaluated across 15 nested windows spanning 2–30 years.
AUROC increased from 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued; roughly 80% of the gain occurred within 10 years.
An XGBoost baseline reached a similar peak AUROC, while simulations indicated potential RoPE time aliasing beyond about 20 years.
The findings support reporting time-context as a distinct design axis for clinical prediction models.

papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the volume of data generated at the network edge, where many devices operate under severe memory, processing, and energy constraints. In this context, Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables machine learning (ML) tasks to be executed on microcontrollers, smart sensors, and other resource-constrained platforms. However, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding the algorithms evaluated, energy-measurement methods, reported metrics, influencing factors, and optimization strategies. This study presents a systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research. It identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines the technical factors affecting energy consumption, and organizes the reported optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. The findings highlight the frequent use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, direct measurements and analytical estimations, and factors related to model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision, and input characteristics. The optimization strategies were grouped into model compression, hardware-aware design, system and communication optimization, and data and processing optimization. The results also reveal limited standardization in experimental platforms, measurement procedures, and reporting practices, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison across studies. This mapping provides an updated overview of the field and guidance for developing and evaluating more energy-efficient TinyML solutions.
bullets: Reviews energy-aware TinyML research for highly resource-constrained edge and embedded devices.
Classifies models, learning approaches, energy-measurement methods, metrics, and energy-influencing factors.
Identifies common use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, alongside direct measurement and analytical estimation.
Groups optimization techniques into model compression, hardware-aware, system/communication, and data/processing strategies.
Highlights inconsistent platforms, procedures, and reporting practices across studies.

papers.abstract: Parallel block drafting accelerates speculative decoding by predicting multiple future positions in a single backbone pass, but on-device deployment constrains both drafter capacity and context storage. Under tight memory budgets, drafters must model long-range dependencies and fine-grained draft-position interactions without the growing KV-cache overhead of full-context attention. We propose HyFlash, a compact parallel drafter that introduces a prefix-memory prior to separate long-range context modeling from fine-grained draft-position interactions with limited capacity. Local attention captures recent context and draft-position interactions, while recurrent memory compresses historical target features into fixed-size states. This inductive bias enables effective local and long-range modeling with bounded draft-side memory. Experiments show that HyFlash achieves higher acceptance than full-context attention with substantially less KV storage and with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.
bullets: Targets on-device speculative decoding under limited drafter capacity and context-storage budgets.
Uses local attention for recent context and draft-position interactions, plus recurrent memory for compressed long-range target features.
Maintains bounded draft-side memory through a fixed-size prefix-memory state instead of growing full-context KV storage.
Experiments report higher acceptance than full-context attention, with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.

papers.abstract: Deformable linear object (DLO) manipulation is challenging because high-dimensional configurations, nonlinear contact dynamics, and diverse material and geometric properties produce a broad range of object responses that are both difficult to model and data-intensive to learn. This work studies reinforcement learning for planar manipulation of a one-end-grasped DLO, focusing on training efficiency, observation design, robustness, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. We compare three Proximal Policy Optimization training stacks and find that the GPU-parallel MuJoCo Playground stack enables faster convergence and more consistent performance than CPU-based alternatives under the same wall-clock budget. Relative keypoint observations and an asymmetric actor-critic formulation further improve learning efficiency. Policies trained with observation noise, delay, domain randomization, and disturbances achieve simulation success rates of 96.4% for single-point tracking, 98.0% for disturbance recovery, and 88.8% for two-point tracking. Using markerless RGB-D keypoint estimation, the policies transfer without real-world fine-tuning, succeeding in 9/10, 10/10, and 8/10 physical trials, respectively.
bullets: Studies planar manipulation of a one-end-grasped deformable linear object under challenging dynamics and varied properties.
GPU-parallel MuJoCo Playground training converges faster and more consistently than CPU-based PPO alternatives at the same wall-clock budget.

Training with observation noise, delays, domain randomization, and disturbances supports robust tracking and recovery.

papers.abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.
bullets: Targets the differing precision and retention sensitivities of query-key interactions in long-context attention.
Uses two diagonal-distance boundaries per head to compactly define skipped, 4-bit, and 8-bit computation regions.
Calibrates boundary choices with projected-output error and tile execution cost, then allocates policies across heads under a shared budget.
Employs a fused prefill kernel and reuses quantized keys and values in a compressed KV cache during decoding.
Reports up to 7.88× speedup over Torch attention and 2.65× over BF16, with quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TriAttention, a unified sparse mixed-precision attention mechanism for long-context LLM inference. It optimizes computation by assigning different precision levels (4-bit vs 8-bit) to different tiles based on sensitivity.
papers.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TriAttention accelerates long-context LLM inference by jointly skipping attention tiles and assigning retained tiles 4-bit or 8-bit precision while preserving model quality.

papers.abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
bullets: Addresses compounding representation and dynamics-prediction errors in imagined pixel-based trajectories.
Learns latent representations through prediction and control objectives rather than visual reconstruction.
Uses action chunking to reduce the number of recursive model predictions during value expansion.
Performs strongly across visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10 against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines.
Analyses indicate that long-horizon expansion, action chunking, and latent learning objectives are all important for reliable performance.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.
bullets: Existing extrapolative OPD couples the direction and magnitude of target shifts, which can lead to poorly controlled targets.
D²-OPD uses a per-prefix hard KL constraint to bound the target’s distance from the teacher.
It adaptively determines extrapolation direction from the teacher’s post-training shift and the initial student–teacher gap.
Forward-KL optimization preserves learning signals for low-probability tokens.
Across three settings, it outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points; ablations support each component’s contribution.

papers.abstract: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.
bullets: Token waste is measured by normalizing full agent trajectories, identifying removable spans with an LLM judge, and mapping them to token-level costs.
The framework validates waste through interventions that remove marked spans and observe task outcomes and subsequent actions.
Online pruning removes 41–46% of model reasoning while largely preserving performance across two agent benchmarks.
Waste varies more by task and agent setting than by model, with distinct patterns in reasoning, execution, and harnesses.
The framework turns token waste into an actionable signal for improving models, reasoning strategies, and agent harnesses.

papers.abstract: Robotic automation of laboratory tasks has become a growing interest to remove researchers from hazardous environments and repetitive procedures. However, even equipment as simple as squeeze bottles poses a challenging manipulation problem due to its deformability. This paper presents an adaptive hybrid vision-force controller for robotic grippers to effectively manipulate laboratory squeeze bottles to dispense liquid. This approach integrates force and vision feedback according to the interaction state, enabling effective squeezing while accounting for bottle deformation and recovery. The proposed controller is validated by comparing its performance with a pure force controller on 12 combinations of conditions consisting of 2 target dispense volumes, 2 plastic squeeze bottles, and 1 to 3 squeezes used to dispense. Human demonstrations of these operating conditions were collected using electromyography (EMG) sensing mapped to a desired grip force, which was then used as the force reference for the controllers to squeeze the bottles. Results demonstrated that the proposed adaptive hybrid vision-force controller achieved more accurate liquid dispensing with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 6.54 mL compared to a MAE of 15.92 mL from the pure force controller, while also replicating the human action recorded from the EMG signal more closely.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate dispensing caused by bottle deformation and recovery.
Combines force and vision feedback based on the interaction state.
Uses human EMG demonstrations to derive desired grip-force references.
Validated across 12 conditions involving two volumes, two bottles, and one to three squeezes.
Reduced mean absolute dispensing error to 6.54 mL versus 15.92 mL for a pure force controller, while more closely matching human actions.

papers.abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
bullets: Archetypal contexts—such as “tipping point” or “winner takes all”—are represented separately from the topics and languages in which they appear.
In Qwen3.8-27B, neuron silencing selectively removes recognition of an archetype, topic, or language while preserving the others.
Mapped layers form a “sandwich”: languages in outer layers, topics in intermediate layers, and archetypes near the center.
This organization reportedly emerges during pretraining and appears across all models examined.
The released neurons, texts, and code provide a reproduction package, though the proposed role in intelligence remains a strong interpretation of the findings.

papers.tldr: The study argues that language models encode reusable cross-domain relational patterns in distinct neuron groups, forming a layered architecture that supports analogy and possibly intelligence.

papers.abstract: Neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function, but deployment typically stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce. We show that this representational freedom can itself be used for compression. Rather than redesigning the codec, we search over exact function-preserving transformations and controlled functional perturbations, using the unchanged physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations. Exact gauge families provide a zero-distortion reference under the strict audit; allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains. Across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, our method reduces Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4\%, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN, establishing trained-network representational freedom as a practical storage resource.
bullets: Neural networks can represent the same function with different parameter vectors, creating untapped storage flexibility.
The method searches exact gauges and controlled functional perturbations, then uses the existing compressor to select cheaper representations.
Exact transformations provide zero-distortion compression under strict functional auditing.
Small functional changes yield larger rate-distortion gains across SmolLM2 and Qwen3.
Checkpoint sizes decrease by up to 23.4% with Zstandard, with similar relative reductions for gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN.

papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
bullets: Builds a hierarchical KV-cache tree whose nodes summarize subtrees with pooled keys and values.
Selects at most k candidates per level, reducing per-query selection and reads to O(log L).
Uses shared, dense-attention-distilled poolers and level-relative RoPE positions to support length extrapolation.
Outperforms reported baselines from 131K to 2M tokens; at 1M, scores 60.5 versus 40.0 for Dense + DCA on RULER.
With optimized kernels, achieves 3.2× prefill and 3.8× decoding speedups at 524K on one H200 GPU.

papers.abstract: The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable demonstration collection independently of a specific robot. However, its moving, close-range gripper cameras entangle camera and object motion without a stable external view, leaving the metric geometry needed for precise manipulation implicit in RGB. We introduce Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B spatial World Action Model (WAM) pretrained on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data through two-stage training -- world-only adaptation followed by joint world-action learning -- to jointly predict future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and actions. Stereo-derived depth makes scene scale and spatial relationships explicit within a unified dual-gripper RGB-D representation. Furthermore, evaluating UMI policies requires testing whether UMI's robot-independent demonstration collection translates into policy generalization across robot embodiments, alongside robustness to environmental changes. We introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a twenty-task simulation benchmark built on RoboTwin with UMI wrist-mounted fisheye observations, enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation of UMI policies under environment and embodiment changes separately and jointly without additional fine-tuning. On RoboTwin-UMI, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined embodiment and environment shifts, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline in each setting by 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points, respectively. It also exhibits the smallest success-rate drop under embodiment transfer among the evaluated policies. In a matched pretraining ablation, RGB-only pretraining leads to a 5.75-percentage-point decrease in in-domain success compared with RGB-D pretraining. Across six real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 85.0% average success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 24.2 percentage points. Project page: https://weiduoyuan.com/spatial-umi-dream/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit metric geometry in UMI’s close-range, moving-camera observations.
Pretrains a 5B model on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, first for world modeling and then jointly for world-action prediction.
Introduces RoboTwin-UMI, a 20-task benchmark for separately and jointly evaluating environment and embodiment shifts without fine-tuning.
Achieves 79.10% in-domain and 72.15% under combined shifts, with the smallest embodiment-transfer drop among evaluated policies.
Across six real-world tasks, reaches 85.0% average success; RGB-only pretraining reduces in-domain success by 5.75 percentage points versus RGB-D.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Model architecture and two-stage training of Spatial-UMI-Dream. In both stages, dual-gripper RGB and metric depth (Fig. 3) form a unified RGB-D canvas. The Wan VAE encodes observation history and current RGB-D inputs into visual tokens, while a text encoder supplies language tokens through cross-attention. The shared world-action transformer uses block-causal attention to condition prediction on preceding visual history. Stage 1: world-only adaptation predicts future RGB-D observations, decoded through the Wan VAE and supervised by Lworld. Stage 2: the transformer backbone is initialized from the Stage 1 world-only adaptation checkpoint. Joint world-action training additionally encodes UMI state and noisy actions, and jointly predicts future RGB-D observations and actions through the Wan VAE and action decoder, optimized with Lworld + λaLaction.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.
bullets: Looped Transformers share blocks to reduce parameters, but their effectiveness depends on how repeated outputs are reused.
The method reads individual block updates while keeping the shared stack’s input on a separate path.
Geometric decay controls total update weight and provides a recency prior; attention allocates weight across updates.
On ClimbMix, Loopback achieves lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines using 40–75% of their Transformer parameters, with matched training tokens and executed depth.
It also obtains the highest thirteen-task mean accuracy at 191M, 374M, 778M, 1.4B, and 3B reference scales among the compared designs.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant
bullets: Addresses uneven within-column weight sensitivity and the decoding overhead of runtime outlier detection.
Uses training-free, offline calibration with activation-aware or gradient-informed tile scoring.
Retains top-scoring tiles at 16-bit within a budget and quantizes the rest to 8-bit.
Employs compact weight buffers and local accumulation for efficient mixed-precision execution.
Reports 2.66× original-model generation throughput while preserving or improving quality across several task types.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TileQuant framework for calibration-driven mixed-precision linear layers. The input-activation-aware route (top left) combines forward activation statistics with weight magnitudes, while the gradient-informed route (bottom left) accumulates weight-gradient importance over calibration batches. Per-layer top-k selection converts either tile-score map into a 16-bit/8-bit decision map. Retained tile IDs and grid metadata guide load-time reconstruction (right). The reconstructed layer supplies the selected weights to two arithmetic paths, whose tile products are combined through output-local 32-bit floating-point accumulation.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning has given rise to vision foundation models that learn general-purpose image representations transferable across downstream tasks, yet representation learning for 3D scenes has not achieved comparable success. Motivated by this, we identify key limitations of current 3D representation learning approaches and revisit their core design choices. We first replace the commonly used hierarchical PTv3 backbone with the Volume Transformer, a ViT-like architecture for 3D scenes. We then redesign two core objectives of modern approaches built around student-teacher networks: matching representations across views and predicting masked content from visible context. For the first objective, we separate the roles of teacher and student: the teacher provides clean, consistent targets while the student learns invariance to stronger perturbations. For the second objective, we prevent the student from accessing the masked geometry and instead require it to infer missing representations from visible context only. Finally, we redesign 2D-to-3D knowledge distillation, replacing direct regression of view-dependent image features with view-consistent supervision. Together, these changes form VINO, a framework that learns semantic representations of 3D scenes without labels. VINO substantially improves dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks and transfers strongly to out-of-domain settings.
bullets: Targets the gap between successful 2D vision foundation models and less effective 3D scene representation learning.
Replaces the hierarchical PTv3 backbone with a ViT-like Volume Transformer for 3D scenes.
Separates teacher and student roles for view matching, using clean teacher targets and stronger student perturbations.
Enforces masked-content prediction from visible geometry only and introduces view-consistent 2D-to-3D distillation.
Achieves substantial gains in dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, with strong out-of-domain transfer.

figures.caption: Figure 3: VINO Overview. Overlapping global and local views are sampled from a 3D scene. The EMA teacher encodes clean global views and softly assigns their tokens to learned prototypes, producing balanced targets. The prototypes are optimized independently by encouraging balanced and consistent assignments across global views. The student encodes strongly augmented local views and masked global views. Local-view embeddings, through a projection head, predict the targets of corresponding global-view tokens. Masked view embeddings provide context to a cross-attention-only predictor that predicts the targets at masked locations.

Figure 1: Self-supervised 3D Representations. We propose VINO, a framework for learning semantic representations of 3D scenes with no labels. Trained on 3D data only, VINO captures semantic similarity better than Sonata (Wu et al., 2025), as shown in PCA projections (top) and cosine-similarity maps (bottom). Sonata yields qualitatively similar representations across backbones, whereas VINO better distinguishes semantically different but geometrically similar regions, for example, chair and table legs, and captures semantic similarity across geometrically different instances, as illustrated by one plant strongly activating the other.

Figure 8: Qualitative results on Replica. VINO features of a large indoor scene from Replica (Straub et al., 2019). We visualize PCA on the bottom left and cosine similarity maps between tokens marked with a red cross and the other 3D tokens.

Figure 2: Comparison of Training Views. Sonata (Wu et al., 2025) geometrically corrupts all views and retains masked tokens in the student encoder. In contrast, VINO keeps the teacher’s global views clean, removes masked tokens from the student encoder, and applies geometric corruptions only to local views.

Figure 4: Representation Artifacts. We observe high-norm token artifacts in the representations (left). Register tokens largely eliminate these artifacts, but early in training, the learned representations still strongly reflect local voxel occupancy. Averaging voxel features within each patch removes this residual artifact (right).

Figure 5: Consistent 2D Targets. VFM (Oquab et al., 2024) features of the same 3D region vary across views. We learn prototypes in the frozen VFM feature space, optimized such that corresponding tokens across views produce matching soft assignments. These serve as our targets for 2D–3D distillation.

papers.abstract: We study a two-stage online optimization problem: at each round, a meta-learner first selects an agent-environment pair, then the chosen agent interacts with the environment, and receives a reward. We introduce Meta-Frieren, a general framework for maximizing cumulative reward in this setting. Our analysis yields a simple UCB-style criterion for meta-level selection and recovers prior guarantees as special cases while extending them to broader settings. We instantiate Meta-Frieren with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions. We also derive, to our knowledge, the first high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling, specialize it to finite and parametric function classes, and integrate it into Meta-Frieren. Experiments support our theoretical results and demonstrate that Meta-Frieren can be successfully applied to hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.
bullets: Addresses two-stage online learning, where a meta-learner chooses an agent–environment pair before interaction.
Introduces a UCB-style meta-level selection criterion that recovers prior guarantees and extends them to broader settings.
Instantiates the framework with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions.
Derives a high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling and incorporates it into Meta-Frieren.
Experiments support the theory and demonstrate hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.

papers.abstract: Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) separates attention from the experts of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model and has been reported to raise decode throughput over colocated serving. Whether this advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72 remains unclear: prior results were obtained on other hardware, against narrower colocated baselines, or with analytical models, whereas production engines serve large MoE models on these systems with wide expert parallelism (wide EP). We build and tune FastAFD, an AFD engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other, and compare it against the best vLLM wide EP setting. Experiments show that AFD has a throughput advantage of up to 1.17x over wide EP on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5, and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5. We derive an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only profiles of colocated vLLM, telling whether switching to AFD would pay off before deploying it. The model yields a concise insight: AFD's speedup factors into a batch gain (larger batches, since attention GPUs hold no expert weights), an overlap gain (shorter steps, since the MoE runs on the expert GPUs behind attention), and a disaggregation cost (the GPUs given to experts). AFD has the advantage when the two gains outweigh the cost. This view explains which models benefit from AFD, and shows that speculative decoding helps light-expert models most, where the enlarged overlap gain outweighs the larger disaggregation cost and adds a further 8% to AFD's advantage over wide EP. Looking ahead, serving the experts on accelerators that keep their weights in on-chip SRAM, such as the Groq LPX accelerators paired with Vera Rubin NVL72, would remove most of the disaggregation cost, raising the ideal speedup to 2.48x with speculative decoding. FastAFD is open source at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/FastAFD.
bullets: Evaluated on GB200 NVL72 against the best vLLM wide-EP configuration for Qwen3, Qwen3.5, and MiniMax-M2.5.
Achieves up to 1.17× throughput on Qwen3, 1.16× on Qwen3.5, and matches wide EP on MiniMax-M2.5.
An analytical model predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only colocated-vLLM profiles.
Speculative decoding benefits light-expert models most, adding up to 8% to AFD’s advantage in the reported setting.
The projected 2.48× speedup with SRAM-based expert accelerators is an ideal forward-looking estimate, not a demonstrated result.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.
bullets: Targets the reward-decoding burden in complex reinforcement-learning tasks, where agents must infer desired behavior from noisy scalar feedback.
Uses selected key quantities and reference values to indicate at each step whether behavioral principles are being followed and to what degree.
Agents can learn without a conventional reward, using only simple heuristic principles such as maintaining balance or landing smoothly.
Experiments report fewer samples, strong generalization, and direct transfer to harder settings compared with reward-based methods.
The approach relies on rough behavioral knowledge and does not require accurately modeled system dynamics.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous client data and resource constraints in federated Mixture-of-Experts training.
Estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments via exploit–explore selection.
Provides relevance-estimation error bounds and exact Top-K recovery guarantees.
On a CNN-based CIFAR-100 MoE, loading 5 experts per client improves mean final accuracy by 1.31 percentage points over Full-20 FedAvg with 20 available experts.
Reduces conflicts from correlated expert selection across clients.

papers.title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
papers.tldr: S³-MoE assigns each federated client a small, personalized subset of experts using partial observations, improving accuracy while reducing expert-loading costs.

papers.abstract: Multi-perspective-camera systems are widely adopted since they provide broad visual coverage for autonomous driving, motivating the synthesis of a unified wide view from spatially separated observations. In this work, we formulate wide view synthesis (WVS), which aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent wide view at a specified virtual viewpoint from multiple perspective cameras. Unlike conventional image stitching, WVS requires reasoning about 3D geometry and visibility to handle depth-dependent parallax and occlusions arising from spatially separated camera centers. While vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity view synthesis, its reliance on per-scene optimization limits its applicability to driving scenes. Furthermore, WVS introduces additional challenges, *e.g.*, peripheral stretching under perspective projection and photometric inconsistencies across cameras. To address these challenges, we propose **Wide-View Gaussian Splatting (WV-GS)**, a feed-forward Gaussian-splatting framework that synthesizes wide views without per-scene optimization. Specifically, we introduce Piecewise Perspective Rendering (PPR) to mitigate peripheral stretching through local perspective projections sharing a common camera center, and Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling (SAPM) to account for camera-dependent photometric variations during training. We further introduce **WideDrive**, a synthetic benchmark providing dense ground-truth wide views and adapt a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol to real-world datasets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS for WVS. Dataset and code will be publicly released.
bullets: Wide-view synthesis must handle depth-dependent parallax, occlusions, peripheral stretching, and cross-camera photometric differences.
WV-GS uses Piecewise Perspective Rendering to reduce peripheral distortion with local projections sharing one camera center.
Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling addresses camera-dependent appearance inconsistencies during training.
The authors introduce WideDrive, a synthetic benchmark with dense ground-truth wide views, and a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol for real data.
Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS; code and data are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models must balance two competing goals: learning fine-grained visual distinctions from very limited supervision and preserving the efficiency that makes frozen CLIP-like models attractive for deployment. Existing lightweight adaptation methods, including prompt tuning, LoRA, and cache-based adapters, typically supervise global image embeddings and therefore underuse token-level structure. Conversely, structure-aware methods exploit local evidence but often introduce additional inference-time computation. We propose SD-LoRA, a structural distillation framework that uses token-level graph reasoning only during training and transfers its effects into a lightweight LoRA-adapted CLIP model. During training, a heterogeneous graph teacher models patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relations over high-resolution ViT tokens. Rather than retaining this graph at test time, SD-LoRA transfers its structural bias into the shared CLIP-LoRA backbone through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment, which aligns graph-conditioned representations with support-derived class prototypes. At inference, the graph teacher is discarded; prediction requires only a single CLIP-LoRA forward pass and a cache-based classifier. Across 11 few-shot benchmarks, SD-LoRA improves over a strong CLIP-LoRA baseline by 2.4/1.8/3.0/2.4/2.0 percentage points in the 1/2/4/8/16-shot settings, respectively, without additional graph computation at test time. Results on base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset transfer, out-of-distribution robustness, and calibration further show that training-time structural supervision improves both accuracy and transfer reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/SD-LoRA.git.
bullets: Addresses the tension between fine-grained few-shot visual learning and efficient frozen-CLIP deployment.
Uses a heterogeneous graph teacher during training to model patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relationships.
Transfers the teacher’s structural bias into CLIP-LoRA through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment.
At inference, discards the graph and uses one CLIP-LoRA pass with a cache-based classifier.

Across 11 benchmarks, improves over CLIP-LoRA by 2.4, 1.8, 3.0, 2.4, and 2.0 percentage points for 1-, 2-, 4-, 8-, and 16-shot settings, respectively; also improves transfer, robustness, and calibration.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Few-shot accuracy trends across 11 benchmarks. Each panel shows top-1 accuracy for K ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} shots on one dataset; the first panel reports the macro-average over all 11 benchmarks. SD-LoRA is compared to recent CLIP adaptation methods. Positive values mean structural distillation improves the deployed LoRA+cache model, with especially strong gains in low-shot and fine-grained scenarios.

Figure 2: SD-LoRA framework. It trains a deployable CLIP-LoRA+cache student sθ,η using an auxiliary structural teacher gθ,ψ present only during adaptation. Teacher and student share the LoRA backbone, but the teacher reasons over high-resolution ViT tokens and class-text embeddings with a relation-aware graph transformer. Structural supervision from the graph branch plus Prototype Predictive Alignment updates the shared LoRA parameters θ. At inference, the teacher parameters ψ and graph computation are discarded, and only the lightweight student sθ,η makes predictions.

Figure 1: Structural distillation sharpens token-level evidence. We visualize patch-level attention maps for frozen CLIP and SD-LoRA using cosine similarity between the final [CLS] token and patch tokens. Frozen CLIP attends strongly to background foliage and misclassifies the image as clematis, while SD-LoRA shifts focus toward discriminative flower regions and correctly predicts balloon flower. The graph teacher is used only during training; the visualization is produced from the deployed LoRA backbone without test-time graph computation.

Figure 4: Effect of LoRA placement. We compare fixed LoRA placement and adaptive layer selection under 1/4/16-shot settings. SD-LoRA outperforms both fixed CLIP-LoRA and adaptive CLIP-AST, indicating that adaptive placement complements SD-LoRA: layer selection optimizes where LoRA is inserted, while structural distillation improves how its parameters are trained.

Figure 6: Computational and deployment analysis of our method. A shows the one-time wallclock overhead associated with the additional high-resolution training and re-encoding passes. B reports the computational overhead relative to the CLIP-LoRA training system, showing that the added graph branch increases computation by only 0.61 GFLOPs (+1.31%) while keeping parameter growth modest (+8.0%). C summarizes practical deployment-time metrics on ViT-B/16, including training time, memory footprint, and inference latency. D shows that the method remains well behaved across backbone choices: ViT-B/32 retains competitive average few-shot accuracy, while the higher cost of ViT-L/14 is primarily attributable to the larger backbone rather than to additional method-specific steps.

Figure 5: Effect of cross-modal interaction frequency. We ablate where semantic text–visual interaction is applied across graph layers on Aircraft under 1/4/16-shot settings. Each marker reports the peak accuracy, while the text label indicates the number of epochs required to reach 95% of the peak. Applying interaction in all layers consistently achieves the best peak accuracy across shot regimes and also converges efficiently in the 16-shot setting, reaching 95% of peak in 13 epochs compared with 18 epochs for last only and 22 epochs for none. This suggests that frequent crossmodal interaction improves both final adaptation quality and optimization efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SD-LoRA, a structural distillation framework for few-shot vision-language adaptation, contributing to Multimodal Large Language Models.
papers.title: SD-LoRA: Training-Time Structural Distillation into LoRA for Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation
papers.tldr: SD-LoRA distills token-level structural reasoning into a lightweight LoRA-adapted CLIP model, improving few-shot vision-language adaptation without extra test-time computation.

papers.abstract: Flow matching (FM) generators often face a quality-coverage tradeoff. Inference-time techniques such as classifier-free guidance raise quality, but at the cost of coverage. We revisit a basic property of FM -- an intermediate noisy image corresponds to multiple valid targets, which is collapsed into a single mean velocity by design. This can cover multiple modes of the distribution under ideal conditions, but is it optimal in practice? We instead investigate if directly modeling the modes of intermediate states better covers the modes of the full distribution. To do so, we augment the predictor with a randomly drawn low-dimensional code $z$, sampling $K$ candidate velocities for each training sample. We then apply the loss only to the best-matching candidate. This winner-take-all objective enables different codes to specialize and collectively cover different modes. Furthermore, this term naturally enables a new form of guidance, auxiliary conditioning scaling, which complements traditional guidance methods. Together, these two guidance mechanisms show that our method substantially improves the quality--coverage frontier. We validate on ImageNet-256, using two different testbeds, SiT and RAEv2. Given less than 3% of the original SiT pretraining compute for post-training, at the 67% Recall point, our method reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 19.22 to 5.91. On RAEv2, at the 70% Recall point, it reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 16.83 to 3.18.
bullets: Flow matching can collapse multiple valid targets for a noisy intermediate image into a single mean velocity, limiting coverage.
The method adds a random low-dimensional code to predict multiple candidate velocities and uses a winner-take-all loss so candidates specialize in different modes.
This enables auxiliary conditioning scaling, a new guidance mechanism that complements classifier-free guidance.
On ImageNet-256, the method substantially improves quality–coverage metrics on both SiT and RAEv2 testbeds, with less than 3% of SiT pretraining compute for post-training.

Thick orange curves show the resulting Pareto frontiers. (a) In FDr,6–Recall space, stronger guidance improves quality while largely preserving Recall for our model, unlike SiT, which loses coverage. (b) In FDr,6–DreamSim space, stronger guidance increases within-class diversity for our model while reducing it for SiT.

papers.abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).
bullets: Addresses the limits of one-off benchmarks and holistic scores for deployed agents.
Evaluates span, trace, conversation, and engagement levels across Execution, Substance, Trajectory, and Results, with Conduct as a constraint.
Uses provenance, adjudication, versioned rules, and atomic evidence to handle biased raters and censored outcomes.
An inner loop audits evidence, rules, and metrics; an outer loop drives improvement through per-component regression checks.
Case studies suggest evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring, with reported ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81 and kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63.

papers.abstract: Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian rendering combines compact textured surfaces with flexible 3D Gaussian primitives, offering an efficient alternative to purely Gaussian scene representations for structured environments. Existing scene-reconstruction hybrids commonly follow an additive formulation, where Gaussian residuals compensate for errors left by the mesh. However, not every Mesh-Gaussian conflict is caused by missing content: residual geometry errors, occlusion mismatch, texture-projection artifacts, and view-dependent appearance can make the same mesh content consistent in one view but inconsistent in another. We therefore formulate hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem and present Gaussolve, a subtract-and-refill framework that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content before residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. We introduce a lightweight Neural Dissolve Field, parameterized by scalar spherical-harmonic Gaussians, to learn where and from which viewing directions mesh content should be dissolved. A continuous transmittance fusion rule progressively exposes residual Gaussians behind the dissolved mesh, preserving their reconstruction gradients and avoiding hard visibility discontinuities. Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes demonstrate higher visual fidelity with fewer Gaussian primitives and faster rendering. Project page: https://ooosn.github.io/gaussians-can-subtract/
bullets: Frames hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem rather than purely additive mesh-error correction.
Uses a Neural Dissolve Field to predict which mesh regions should be dissolved and from which viewing directions.
Applies continuous transmittance fusion to reveal residual Gaussians smoothly while preserving reconstruction gradients.
Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes report higher visual fidelity, fewer Gaussian primitives, and faster rendering.

Compared with existing methods, Gaussolve achieves a more favorable quality–compactness trade-off by allowing meshes and Gaussians to cooperate rather than compete.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth, which limits context length, batch size, and decoding throughput.
Amortises values using lightweight per-head predictors, storing residuals only for poorly reconstructed tokens; this provides 4× near-lossless value compression.
Combines value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression in an asymmetric pipeline.
Reconstructs only selected KV pairs during decoding, achieving up to 5× higher peak decode throughput at 4× compression.
Composes with quantisation and eviction to reach 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.

papers.abstract: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.
authors: Sihang Chen, Chen Ye, Wei Chen, Xiaohan Lei, Zhipeng Tang, Sha Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Zixuan Chen, Jiajun Deng, Houqiang Li, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Introduces nine tasks requiring interaction history at key decision points.
Covers environment memory—locations, attributes, and relationships—and process memory for task progress and scheduling.
Uses Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation to derive later constraints from the robot’s own earlier actions, reducing fixed-target shortcuts.
Provides 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training and an HMAP baseline with structured memory and subgoal-conditioned control.
Scope: evaluates memory-dependent behavior in mobile manipulation rather than general-purpose memory.
