papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object's location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System 2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy (System 1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System 1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13% of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals.
authors: Bingao Chen, Haoquan Fang, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to remember occluded object locations and demonstrated action order without invoking a large planner before every action chunk.
Astra (System 2) selects grounded subtasks from visual history; π0.5 executes them; a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor detects subtask completion.
The system retains instructions until completion or a task-specific event, while the policy acts continuously on new observations.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have achieved strong performance on single-task robotic manipulation. However, a single model trained jointly on multiple tasks consistently underperforms the per-task specialists trained on the same demonstrations. We focus on two challenges. First, the convolutional encoders commonly used in diffusion-based policies produce visual conditions that are not discriminative enough. Second, gradients from incompatible action modes update the shared denoiser's dense parameters along the same directions, causing destructive interference during joint training. To address both, we propose SR-DP (Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy). A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens, a task-discriminative visual condition for tasks that share a workspace. We first train the denoiser as a standard diffusion policy, then decompose selected linear layers by SVD into a frozen basis of orthogonal rank-one experts, adapted through spectral routing and Householder input rotations. On six RoboTwin tasks, SR-DP averages a 68.4% success rate, surpassing multi-task VO-DP by 21.8 points and the strongest per-task baseline by 3.8 points. On four real-world bimanual tasks, Stage 2 reaches a 43.0% average success rate and improves over Stage 1 by 19.0 points.
bullets: Multi-task diffusion policies can underperform task-specific specialists because visual conditions are insufficiently discriminative and shared gradients interfere.
A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact, multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens.
Selected denoiser layers are decomposed into frozen orthogonal rank-one experts and adapted using spectral routing and Householder input rotations.
SR-DP achieves 68.4% average success across six RoboTwin tasks and 43.0% across four real-world bimanual tasks; Stage 2 improves 19.0 points over Stage 1.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accepted operations or immediate reads and deadline-bound observable outcomes in asynchronous services.
Uses an independent control plane to monitor service-state predicates, admit or reject completion, and direct recovery.
Evaluated placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and injected transfer delay.
Some accepted tasks missed deadlines, while some rejected tasks met them, showing agent reports were unreliable.
Enforcement kept accepted completions consistent with later observations and terminated unresolved faulted tasks as unverified.

papers.abstract: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. We propose PACT, a training-free commit rule that draws the tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces the positions of each step apart. This certificate holds at every temperature, and we show that no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four models of the LLaDA and Dream families and HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval benchmarks. PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step, yet it usually lowers the total cost because later steps then write more tokens. At the same speed, published decoders also write a word twice in a row far more often than PACT. These results suggest that commit rules should certify the tokens they write. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PACT.
bullets: Existing commit rules assess predicted distributions rather than the tokens actually sampled during decoding.
PACT samples tokens first, certifies the set to write, and spaces selected positions apart; its guarantee holds at every temperature.
The paper decomposes answer log probability into written-token reliability and within-step dependence, motivating certification of actual writes.
Across LLaDA and Dream models on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500, and IFEval, PACT matches published quality with fewer forward passes.
Spacing generally lowers total decoding cost and reduces repeated word writes compared with published decoders.

papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
bullets: Structural memorization records internal expert pathways alongside training data, even when fine-tuning uses few samples.
The strength of these routing fingerprints depends on which model modules are trainable.
Attackers can recover pathways from unconditional generation using only routing information and output logits, without training data or procedure knowledge.
Distributed systems amplify exposure across federated aggregation, edge-cloud, and multi-tenant monitoring boundaries.
Composite metrics using reference-model tail likelihood and complexity-aware normalization improve detection beyond standard membership-inference measures.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/STAR.
bullets: Addresses a late-layer grounding gap in vision-language-action models, where action representations may lose task-relevant visual information.
Applies an exponential moving average to late-layer residual updates so later representations inherit object-aware directions from earlier layers.
Adapts the mixing strength using recent proprioceptive states, applying more conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly.
Improves late-layer object awareness and raises average task success by 4.0 percentage points on robot manipulation benchmarks.
Requires no model updates or architectural changes; its scope is pre-trained VLAs and the evaluated manipulation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.
bullets: Long responses can cause student prefixes to drift from the teacher, weakening later feedback and destabilizing training.
The method replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher-generated segment, then resumes student reasoning.
Persistently divergent suffixes are excluded from the distillation loss while preserving useful student continuation.
Diagnostics show reduced disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses.
Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher–student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models now grade robot videos, and text placed beside the frames can change their verdicts. On clips where the robot is losing progress, we add one log line saying the robot is making progress. Across Gemini, Qwen and GPT judges, this flips correct verdicts to progress 10 to 35 percentage points more often than a neutral line does. A one-line warning that the log may be wrong removes most of this effect. Selected fake "task complete" claims flip half of Qwen's correct verdicts, against a tenth for unrelated log lines. They have no detectable effect on Gemini.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the influence of execution logs on VLM judgments of robot progress, relevant to the evaluation of vision-language models in robotics.
papers.title: Execution Logs Sway VLM Judges of Robot Progress
papers.tldr: Robot-progress judgments by VLMs can be strongly swayed by misleading execution logs, though warnings reduce the effect and susceptibility varies by model.

papers.abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Introduces a dual-timeline benchmark for localized manipulations in open-scene, long-form audio-visual videos.
Includes 16,650 pristine–manipulated twin pairs spanning 998 hours and 27 editing configurations.
Zero-shot AV-LLM prompting performs near chance for detection and poorly for temporal localization.
NFSR uses separate audio and visual temporal decoders over frozen AV-LLM features, achieving the best localization in-domain and across three out-of-distribution settings.
The benchmark exposes errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation and is intended for public release with code and model weights.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.
bullets: Targets outdated scene knowledge caused by changes between robot visits.
Uses probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view selection near the path and uncertain or changing objects.
Integrates perception with hierarchical-task model predictive control, using arm redundancy while prioritizing base-trajectory tracking.
Real-world tests report improved map consistency, lower task-dependent map entropy, and reduced navigation risk versus passive and non-task-aware baselines.
Validated in simulation and real-world sequences with controlled semi-static scene changes.

papers.abstract: The diagnostic capability of WSI agents relies on effective slide navigation to identify diagnostically relevant regions and efficiently integrate evidence across the slide. While in clinical practice, pathologists dynamically examine slides across multiple scales, integrating global and cellular evidence in a sequential manner, existing AI navigation approaches mostly operate at a single fixed magnification or rely on predefined magnification traversal. This mismatch prevents existing methods from modeling cross-magnification interactions and adaptive magnification selection inherent to real diagnostic workflows. We propose PathPilot, a clinically consistent multi-magnification WSI navigation agent that explicitly models cross-magnification localization and evidence-adaptive exploration. Specifically, we introduce a CrossMagLoc that learns magnification-specific diagnostic localization from pathologist viewing behavior and integrates information from adjacent magnifications to identify the diagnostically most relevant region within the current ROI, thereby providing a diagnostically informed starting point for subsequent question-conditioned exploration. We further introduce an EviRegionSearch that starts question-conditioned exploration from this region, progressively accumulating question-relevant evidence and adaptively determining the next navigation action according to the remaining evidence requirement. Their iterative interaction enables PathPilot to sequentially explore across ROIs and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired. Extensive QA evaluations across five cohorts demonstrate consistent superiority over competing SOTA methods on inter/external cohorts, respectively, validating question-conditioned evidence acquisition across regions and magnifications that mirrors the sequential, knowledge-driven navigation of pathologists.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed-magnification and predefined-traversal WSI navigation agents.
CrossMagLoc uses pathologist viewing behavior and adjacent magnifications to localize diagnostically relevant regions.
EviRegionSearch begins from the localized region and selects subsequent actions based on remaining question-relevant evidence.
The two components iteratively explore regions and magnifications until sufficient evidence is acquired.
Evaluations across five cohorts report consistent superiority over competing methods on inter- and external-cohort QA tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the datasets and evaluation cohorts used in this study. Top: Three navigation datasets provide pathologist viewing supervision for CrossMagLoc, including the Skin Eye-Tracking dataset and the TUM Liver and TUM Uterine Viewpoint datasets. The Skin dataset additionally provides pixel-level tumor annotations for region-level localization evaluation. Bottom: Five open-ended QA cohorts are used for end-to-end PathPilot evaluation, comprising the internal TUM Liver and TUM-Uteria cohorts and the external TUM Skin, WSI-Bench TCGA-SKCM, and WSI-Bench TCGA-LIHC cohorts. For the TUM cohorts, the circular plots summarize the predefined H&E-visible findings grouped into tissue-level, architectural, and cellular categories; for the WSI-Bench cohorts, they summarize the distributions of question categories.

Fig. 2: Overview of PathPilot and its two complementary navigation components. Given a WSI and pathology question, PathPilot starts from the thumbnail and iteratively alternates between CrossMagLoc and EviRegionSearch until sufficient evidence has been accumulated for answering the question. CrossMagLoc performs question-agnostic localization of diagnostically relevant candidate ROIs at each magnification by combining magnification-specific representations with spatially aligned information from adjacent scales. EviRegionSearch performs question-conditioned exploration over the ROI identified by CrossMagLoc, integrates morphological observations from the selected ROI with the accumulated evidence, identifies the remaining evidence requirement, and adaptively determines the next navigation action (Move, Zoom In, Zoom Out, or Stop) to select the next region.

Fig. 1: Overview of PathPilot for adaptive WSI exploration. Their iterative interaction enables sequential movement across ROIs and magnifications until evidence is sufficient (e.g., Step t + N), where Stop is selected and the final answer is generated.

Fig. 5: Pathologist-in-the-loop interpretation of CrossMagLoc across five magnifications (thumbnail, 1.25×, 2.5×, 5×, and 10×; top to bottom). The columns show the pathology images (column 1), CrossMagLoc predictions (column 2), test-set navigation annotations (column 3), and independent annotations with morphological explanations from pathologists trained in Europe (column 4) and Asia (column 5). Across magnifications, CrossMagLoc consistently prioritizes diagnostically relevant regions identified by the pathologists while deprioritizing non-primary or artifact-limited areas. At 2.5×, it assigns higher attention to well-preserved tumor regions than to the crush-artifact region, while at higher magnifications it continues to emphasize morphologically informative tumor regions. Overall, its localization broadly agrees with pathologist viewing behavior while additionally highlighting clinically relevant regions identified during independent review.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can generate scientific code, but authoring a scientific simulator (an executable program encoding hypotheses about how mechanisms generate observable signals) requires iterative refinement. Scientific adequacy rarely admits a unique implementation or exact test, so simulators must instead be judged against limited real observations. We study this setting as scientific simulator authoring under weak empirical feedback, where distributional comparisons between simulated and real signals guide revision, and the target is the simulator itself rather than only its generated samples. We introduce SimAuthor, a persistent authoring harness that retains and revises executable simulators, separates scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback, and accumulates reusable implementation mechanisms. We evaluate SimAuthor on six biomedical tasks spanning cardiac and respiratory audio, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiography (ECG). Under a fixed 100-attempt budget, SimAuthor outperforms PUCT score search on all six tasks, generally outperforms textual-strategy optimization, and achieves the highest endpoint score on five of six. The authored simulators also improve on unseen recordings, transfer to independent pretrained representations, and yield substantial out-of-distribution gains in downstream ECG classification. Finally, 111 of 138 audited revisions alter program structure and account for 86.1% of the signed score improvement. These results suggest that persistent revision can progressively convert foundation-model knowledge into better executable scientific simulators from limited empirical evidence.
bullets: Addresses simulator authoring when scientific adequacy lacks a unique implementation or exact test.
Maintains and revises executable simulators, separating scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback and reusing implementation mechanisms.
Evaluated on cardiac and respiratory audio, PPG, and ECG tasks under a fixed 100-attempt budget.
Outperformed PUCT score search on all six tasks and achieved the best endpoint score on five; it also generalized to unseen recordings and downstream ECG classification.
Most audited revisions changed program structure, accounting for 86.1% of signed score improvement.

papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of the daily evolution of sea ice concentration (SIC) is central to improving the credibility and operational forecasting capability of deep learning-based sea ice prediction. However, existing deep learning methods often couple the underlying sea ice evolution relationships and data errors within high-dimensional nonlinear mappings, making it difficult to construct a stable and verifiable evolution core and apply it reliably to practical forecasting. To address this issue, this study proposes a reanalysis-forecast dual-domain decoupled framework for learning sea ice evolution operators. The framework builds upon a lightweight physical baseline to generate daily evolution trajectories, employs a temporally constrained joint multi-lead compensation network to com?pensate for unresolved processes, and introduces an ice-mass?aware transport mechanism to suppress numerical dissipation. In the forecasting stage, the parameters of the base evolution core are fixed, while a lightweight variable-semantic adaptation mechanism calibrates inter-domain distributions and evolution responses, thereby separating forecast-domain errors from base evolution errors. Experiments show that the constructed base evolution core can accurately and stably simulate daily sea ice evolution at both short-term and annual scales under reanal?ysis forcing, and can be effectively transferred to the forecast domain through lightweight adaptation, achieving stable prac?tical forecasting capability while preserving the base evolution structure. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/zhangmaqun65535/SNM upon acceptance of this manuscript.
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of sea-ice dynamics and data errors in existing deep-learning forecasting methods.
Uses a lightweight physical baseline, a temporally constrained multi-lead compensation network, and ice-mass-aware transport to model unresolved processes and reduce numerical dissipation.
Freezes the base evolution core during forecasting and applies lightweight variable-semantic adaptation to correct domain shifts.
Experiments indicate stable evolution simulation from short-term to annual scales under reanalysis forcing and effective transfer to the forecast domain.
The approach is scoped to Arctic sea-ice concentration evolution and forecast-domain adaptation; specific quantitative results are not reported in the abstract.

During forecasting, the evolution core remains frozen. Variable-Specific Input Adaptation (VSIA) calibrates the observed initial condition and forecast forcings, while Response-Domain Semantic Correction (RDSC) further refines the output. The model thereby establishes a structured separation among physical propagation, multi-lead residual learning, and forecast-domain adaptation.

papers.abstract: Success conditioning is a strategy for improving decision-making policies in stochastic environments; it updates a policy by increasing the probability of taking actions that yield successful outcomes. Success conditioning is common to many reinforcement learning applications, yet its limiting behavior and convergence rates are not well understood. In this work, we demonstrate that success conditioning converges to an optimal policy on a broad class of Markov decision processes (MDPs). We also derive convergence rates in some common settings. For discounted MDPs, we prove convergence within $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^p)$ iterations to an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy, where the exponent $p$ depends on problem data. For single-period MDPs, such a policy is obtained within $\mathcal{O}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations.
bullets: Analyzes the limiting behavior of success conditioning, a policy-improvement strategy based on favoring successful actions.
Proves convergence to an optimal policy for a broad class of Markov decision processes.
For discounted MDPs, reaches an ε-optimal policy in O(1/ε^p) iterations, with p determined by problem data.
For single-period MDPs, reaches an ε-optimal policy in O(log(1/ε)) iterations.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Success Conditioning for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: The paper proves that success conditioning converges to optimal policies for broad classes of MDPs and establishes iteration-rate guarantees.

papers.abstract: Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student's trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to $32\times$ fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.
bullets: Targets expensive iterative sampling and intractable sequence-level KL regularization in masked discrete diffusion.
Replaces the sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization and proves an upper bound under an optimal auxiliary denoiser.
Optimizes a trajectory-based, clipped policy-gradient objective over the student’s own few-step sampler.
Across DNA, image, and text generation, achieves high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have reached expert-level performance on competition mathematics largely through the volume of search placed around them: candidate solutions are sampled in quantity and retained only when an external criterion accepts them. Such a procedure improves the outcome that survives it while leaving untouched what the model represents. We examine that question where no external criterion exists: translating statements between the dialects of neighbouring subfields, where fidelity turns on the level of generality at which content is asserted. The source leaves that level implicit in its vocabulary, so a faithful translation must recover it from the relation between the theories. We introduce an instrument that codes truth, content and scope in separate blind queues, with a judge-free measure of whether a rewrite states the hypothesis implicit in its source, and establish its sensitivity with a planted-positive control. Across seven models from four families, translating towards the general framing widens the domain of quantification in 60.6% of rewrites and narrows it in none; translating towards the concrete framing narrows it in 28.3% and widens it in 0.3%. The hypothesis that would prevent it is stated in 21.6% of model rewrites and 4.2% of human statements. Capability does not govern the asymmetry: it appears in every model tested, and the most capable widens least. It replicates on the half of the benchmark held out by a pre-registered rule, and on statements written by mathematicians. Instructing a model to state every hypothesis it requires raises that rate but not its sensitivity to direction. We argue that these systems have acquired an object-level correspondence between subfield vocabularies without the constraint under which a translation between theories carries hypotheses to hypotheses.
bullets: The study tests translation between neighboring mathematical subfields, where implicit scope and assumptions determine fidelity.
It introduces a judge-free instrument that separately codes truth, content, and scope, validated with planted-positive controls.
Across seven models, translations toward general frameworks widened quantification in 60.6% of cases and never narrowed it; concrete-directed translations narrowed it in 28.3% and widened it in 0.3%.
Models stated the hypotheses required by their rewrites in 21.6% of cases, versus 4.2% for human statements; the asymmetry appeared across all models.
Explicitly prompting models to state every required hypothesis increased disclosure but did not improve directional sensitivity.

papers.abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) capture reusable knowledge from large-scale EEG data, while many EEG recordings also include companion physiological signals that provide complementary information beyond the EEG-only interface. The challenge is to preserve this pretrained knowledge while extending the EFM to heterogeneous multimodal recordings through an adaptation inferred from unlabeled target data. We introduce ZeroMAG, a zero-shot multimodal adapter generation framework that extends a frozen EEG encoder and prediction head using unlabeled target recordings, without target labels or target-side optimization. The target datasets are held out from all model training and selection in the ZeroMAG pipeline. ZeroMAG organizes companion modalities around a configuration-invariant adapter, constructs a modality-subject-task condition from unlabeled recordings and task context, and generates adapter weights in a function-constrained latent space learned from source adapters. Across six held-out target datasets and three EFM backbones, ZeroMAG improves balanced accuracy by 7.22 percentage points over EEG-only inference and 4.89 points over direct weight regression, while coming within 0.50 points of supervised multimodal adaptation on average. Ablations further show that removing functional supervision from either representation learning or conditional generation degrades generated-adapter performance, confirming the contribution of both components.
bullets: Addresses how to extend EEG-only foundation models to heterogeneous physiological modalities while preserving pretrained knowledge.
Generates configuration-invariant adapter weights from unlabeled target recordings and task context in a function-constrained latent space.
Evaluated on six held-out target datasets and three EEG foundation model backbones.

papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.
bullets: Targets stateful environments where repeated rollouts are impractical and long trajectories are sparsely verified.
Applies an ordinal filter from the cross-entropy method to replay-buffer samples.
Uses a control-as-inference formulation that connects FTW with GRPO and DPO.
Controls the bounded risk-seeking effect introduced by ordinal filtering.
Matches GRPO and PPO baselines on Sokoban and Search-R1 while trading value models or group rollouts for CPU memory.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation requires high-quality expert data that is expensive to obtain. This makes learning a sample-efficient policy a key issue. To address this, we propose VISTA, a workspace-level equivariant visuotactile diffusion policy for data-efficient contact-rich imitation learning. VISTA projects visual and tactile observations into spherical tokens, injects tactile contact cues into visual spherical directions through permutation-equivariant spherical fusion, and rotates the fused harmonic representation using the end-effector orientation. The resulting representation conditions an equivariant diffusion policy to predict spatially consistent actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings show that VISTA substantially improves data efficiency over strong visuotactile imitation learning baselines. Project website: https://vista-paper.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting expert demonstrations for contact-rich imitation learning.
Projects visual and tactile inputs into spherical tokens and fuses tactile contact cues with visual directions.
Uses end-effector orientation to rotate the fused harmonic representation, preserving spatial consistency.
Conditions an equivariant diffusion policy to predict manipulation actions.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots show improved data efficiency over strong visuotactile imitation-learning baselines.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used where small syntactic errors matter, yet character-level reasoning is still evaluated mostly through isolated probes and aggregate accuracy. We introduce SyntaxBench, a diagnostic benchmark and statistical evaluation framework for character-level reasoning. It contains five core tasks, character counting, letter containment, palindrome detection, edit distance, and longest-string selection, plus index_to_span, a harder substring-extraction stress test. The five core tasks use paired English and character-length-matched random-string inputs. index_to_span documents share a 200-500 word band and are not character-length matched. All six tasks use zero-, one-, and four-shot prompts. We evaluate eight open-weight models from 2B to 32B parameters across 11 reasoning-mode configurations. The framework reports exact-match and relaxed accuracy, Cohen's kappa, paired McNemar tests with odds ratios, bootstrap confidence intervals, Kendall's tau, class-conditional metrics, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison-corrected tests. Three findings stand out. First, tokenization shapes accuracy: random strings are more character-visible than English strings (1.892 vs. 3.169 characters per token), and character-counting accuracy falls as English words occupy more tokens. Second, reasoning mode is not uniformly helpful: Gemma4-31B is nearly unchanged across modes on the near-saturated tasks, while Qwen3.6-27B is worse with thinking on palindrome detection (0.952 non-thinking vs. 0.886 thinking at four-shot). Third, index_to_span remains largely unsolved; the best four-shot exact-match accuracy is 6.75%. Character-level evaluation needs controlled inputs, paired tests, and analyses of tokenization and reasoning mode rather than aggregate accuracy alone.
bullets: Introduces six diagnostic tasks covering counting, containment, palindromes, edit distance, string selection, and substring extraction.
Pairs English and character-length-matched random-string inputs to isolate tokenization effects, with zero-, one-, and four-shot settings.
Evaluates eight open-weight models using exact and relaxed accuracy, paired statistical tests, confidence intervals, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison correction.
Random strings are more character-visible than English, and English counting accuracy declines as words use more tokens.
Reasoning mode is task- and model-dependent; index_to_span achieves only 6.75% best four-shot exact-match accuracy.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Pedicle screw placement is technically demanding in scoliosis treatment. High precision is required due to limited visibility, anatomical variability, and the risk of complications. Although robotic systems assist CT-based planning and execution, they still rely on ionizing intraoperative imaging and complex registration. This study proposes robotic pedicle drilling with real-time preventive breach detection using electrical bioimpedance sensing. Methods: We developed a robotic approach combined with a pedicle-drilling tool equipped with a proprioceptive electrical bioimpedance sensor developed by SpineGuard. A real-time detection algorithm was designed to analyze the electrical bioimpedance signal during drilling and identify abrupt changes in conductivity associated with potential breaches towards the spinal canal. The method operates without external devices or sensors. Results: The ex vivo experiments showed that the proposed method prevented breaches in 100 of the 51 drilling cases. These findings demonstrate the system's ability to detect potentially hazardous events during drilling and to stop the procedure before. The ex vivo experiments demonstrated that the proposed method prevented breaches in all 51 drilling cases. Conclusions: This work demonstrates the feasibility of robotic pedicle drilling with electrical bioimpedance sensing for real-time breach prevention. Using only the tool signal, the method eliminates the need for external sensing systems and supports safer pedicle screw placement.
bullets: Addresses the safety challenges of pedicle screw placement in scoliosis, including limited visibility and anatomical variability.
Combines robotic drilling with a proprioceptive electrical bioimpedance sensor and an algorithm that detects abrupt conductivity changes linked to potential breaches.
Operates using only the drilling tool’s signal, avoiding external sensing systems and intraoperative imaging for breach detection.
In ex vivo testing, the system prevented breaches in all 51 drilling cases.
The findings demonstrate feasibility for real-time breach prevention, but are limited to ex vivo experiments.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) provide a compact and stable formulation for trajectory representation and generalization in robot skill learning. However, their predefined basis layout limits the allocation of approximation capacity according to stage-dependent precision requirements. To address this issue, this article proposes Stage-Criticality-Guided Dynamic Movement Primitives (SC-DMPs) with adaptive basis allocation for precision-critical skill learning. Operator-robot interaction stiffness and a trajectory-consistency cue derived from cross-demonstration task-space variability are integrated to construct a stage-criticality index. Guided by this index, basis centers are redistributed in normalized time through inverse cumulative criticality and mapped to the canonical phase domain, while their bandwidths are refined to adjust local approximation support. This enables denser and more flexible representation at high-criticality stages while retaining sparser allocation elsewhere. Experiments on handwriting trajectories and three real-robot tasks show that the inferred criticality is concentrated in geometrically demanding and task-constrained regions. Comparisons with DMPs, ProMPs, ProDMP, GP-MP, and KMP demonstrate improved trajectory reproduction, endpoint generalization, and task-critical accuracy while retaining a compact model and the stable structure of classical DMPs.
bullets: Targets the fixed basis layout of standard DMPs, which cannot match stage-dependent precision needs.
Builds a stage-criticality index from interaction stiffness and cross-demonstration trajectory variability.
Redistributes basis centers via inverse cumulative criticality and refines bandwidths for local flexibility.
Evaluated on handwriting and three real-robot tasks, with criticality concentrated in geometrically demanding and constrained regions.
Reports improved reproduction, endpoint generalization, and task-critical accuracy versus several motion-primitives baselines.

papers.abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
bullets: Addresses weak texture, specular highlights, deformable anatomy, and contact-rich interactions that challenge conventional and learning-based navigation.
Uses an RGB-D-E Action Chunking Transformer with RGB, estimated relative depth, and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to emphasize fold ridges and geometric cues.
Predicts overlapping action chunks and fuses them through temporal ensembling for continuous, smooth robot control.
In ex-vivo porcine colons, success rates were 85.4% in straight segments, 72.5% in curved segments, 70% in 90-degree turns, and 60% in double-bend sequences.
Triple-bend experiments further demonstrate feasibility, though performance scope is limited to ex-vivo evaluation.

papers.abstract: Mainstream large language models rely on a tokenizer to encode text into a token sequence. Different tokenizers may yield token sequences of substantially different lengths for the same text. With a fixed model architecture, shorter token sequences correspond to lower inference time. We propose a tokenizer training approach named Counting and Filtering (CNF) and a text encoding algorithm called Min-Cost Encoding (MCE). MCE defines a cost function over a text segment, and determines the best segmentation by globally minimizing the overall segmentation cost. CNF builds a raw vocabulary by directly counting valid substrings, and then constructs the final vocabulary through a filtering step based on actual token usage when segmenting the training corpus with MCE. The CNF-MCE conbination offers several advantages over BPE, including higher token efficiency, greater scalability, and lower dependency. Across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups, CNF-MCE consistently achieves better compression than the evaluated BPE tokenizers. With a 250K vocabulary, CNF-MCE increases compression rate by 26% and 30% on English web text over the o200k_base and qwen250k tokenizers. Experiments scaling the vocabulary to 1M entries on English web text demonstrate sustained improvements over BPE, with a token efficiency improvement of over 60% and vocabulary utilization rising from 52.9% to 96.9%. The MCE algorithm does not depend on a merge list (as in BPE) or token probability (as in UnigramLM), making it applicable to a wide range of vocabularies, including those built from BPE, UnigramLM, CNF, and others. Language models trained from scratch at the 1.8B and 8B scales achieve comparable average performance to models using the BPE tokenizers across 11 benchmarks. These results demonstrate that CNF-MCE can improve token efficiency significantly while maintaining competitive downstream performance.
bullets: Targets inefficient tokenization, where longer sequences increase inference cost.
Uses Min-Cost Encoding (MCE) to find globally optimal text segmentations under a defined cost function.
Trains vocabularies with Counting and Filtering (CNF), combining substring counting with usage-based vocabulary filtering.
Outperforms evaluated BPE tokenizers across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups; gains persist at 1M vocabulary size.
Models trained with CNF-MCE achieve comparable average performance to BPE-based models across 11 benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.
bullets: Targets CoM localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies where visual geometry and tracking are unreliable.
Adapts pretrained V-JEPA features with a temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories.
Introduces HiddenMass Benchmark: 50K simulated MuJoCo trajectories and 63 real-world sequences with calibrated CoM ground truth.
Reduces normalized simulation CoM error from 41.7% to 25.2% and improves real-world physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%.
Zero-shot transfer remains challenging: phase-aware supervision moves predictions toward hidden offsets but can cause overshoot, while phase-agnostic targets may collapse toward centroids.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Qualitative Kinematic Trajectories. A comparison of 2D predicted paths during multiaxis tumbling within a static observation window. (Left) Spatial models (e.g., DINOv2) suffer from visual-kinematic aliasing, tracking high-contrast surface distractors instead of momentum. (Right) STATERA-50K-Crescent successfully isolates the smooth Newtonian parabolic arc of the hidden mass, directionally aligning with the verified Ground Truth despite a Euclidean vector overshoot.

Figure 2: STATERA Architecture. A 16-frame video sequence is processed via a partially-frozen V-JEPA 2.1 backbone. Temporal tubelets are mixed using a 1D Convolution before passing through the Spatial Preservation Decoder. The network bifurcates to output a continuous spatial heatmap (Head A) and a regularizing 1D Z-Depth scalar (Head B).

Figure 6: The Vector Overshoot Artifact. (Left) An architecturally complete model (1K-Anchor) correctly learns to bound the hidden mass phase within realistic 3D physical constraints. (Right) Ablating the absolute 1D Z-Depth regularizer (1K-No-Z-Depth) causes the 2D spatial extractions to lose physical scale constraints, leading to a severe, unregularized Euclidean explosion far beyond the physical boundaries of the rigid body.

Figure 1: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematic Tracking. (Left) The HiddenMass-50K training environment featuring procedurally generated asymmetric masses. (Right) Zero-shot inference on real-world video sequences. While spatial baselines collapse to the visual centroid, STATERA successfully identifies the directional phase of the offset Center of Mass. The prediction pulls away from the visual center along the true kinematic vector (noting an empirical Euclidean overshoot inherent to the 2.5D spatial projection).

Figure 4: Curriculum Label Smoothing. Target probability distributions across training epochs. By mathematical design, at Epoch 0 (κ = 0), both targets initialize as identical broad Gaussian rings (σ = 12.5). Over the curriculum, the phase-agnostic baseline (Sigma) decays into an isotropic impulse (σ = 3.0), omitting phase data. Conversely, the phase-aware SOTA (Crescent) scales its Von Mises angular mask (κ → 50.0), forcing the network to continuously optimize for rotational torque direction.

Figure 5: Visual-Kinematic Aliasing (Bimodal Split). During high-torque rotations where groundtruth phase is highly ambiguous, models trained on static phase-aware targets output high-variance, bimodal probability heatmaps. The network essentially “hedges its bets” between two physically plausible mass locations, resulting in expectation collapse and severe temporal jitter.

Figure 7: HiddenMass Benchmark Profile. The Unified HiddenMass Score (HMS, orange) is calculated as a weighted composite: 25% Kinematic Accuracy, 25% Tracking Stability, and 50% Physics Disentanglement, explicitly penalizing statistical reward-hacking. Low Disentanglement (teal) reveals that DINOv2 and STATERA-50K-Sigma are deceived by visual and heuristic aliasing, defaulting closer to the geometric centroid. STATERA-50K-Crescent actively breaks this heuristic, achieving substantial positive physical disentanglement and securing the highest overall HMS (59.6).

Table 2: Zero-Shot Real-World Transfer (N=63). STATERA-50K-Sigma achieves the lowest spatial and jitter errors. However, unclamped Disentanglement analysis reveals DINOv2 and STATERA50K-Sigma struggle to fully disentangle the offset. STATERA-50K-Crescent remains the only architecture to achieve substantial positive disentanglement toward the hidden mass. Point trackers were evaluated via an idealized Dynamic Surface Centroid Proxy (initializing a uniform point grid around the object’s initial bounding center and gracefully falling back to the geometric center upon track death).

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration demands that robots continuously evaluate candidate viewpoints based on their expected information gain and execution cost. Sampling-based planners estimate this gain by volumetric raycasting and, due to its computational cost, evaluate candidates under an assumption of mutual independence, ignoring the overlap between viewpoints along the same path. This work presents a GPU-accelerated method for computing path-dependent marginal information gain, where instead of storing and merging the observed unknown voxels along each candidate path, previous observations are represented using depth buffers. Candidate rays are projected into the depth buffers of their ancestors to identify observation overlap and exclude regions expected to be observed. The planning tree is evaluated in depth order to maintain the dependency between viewpoints and their optimized yaws, while candidate nodes and rays at each level are processed in parallel on the GPU. The proposed method stays within 5-10% of the exact marginal gain computed using voxel hash maps, with speed-ups of up to 118x on a desktop GPU and 28x on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The method was integrated into two sampling-based exploration planners and evaluated in three simulation environments, where marginal gain reduced the time to 95% coverage in five of the six evaluated planner-environment combinations. Real-world experiments also showed a 30% reduction in the time to 95% coverage, as well as earlier exploration termination times.
bullets: Addresses the cost and inaccuracy of assuming independent information gain between viewpoints on the same path.
Projects candidate rays into ancestor depth buffers to detect overlapping observations without storing voxel sets.
Processes planning-tree levels and candidate rays in parallel on GPUs while preserving viewpoint dependencies and optimized yaw choices.
Achieves gain estimates within 5–10% of exact voxel-hash-map computation, with speedups up to 118× on desktop GPUs and 28× on Jetson Orin NX.
Integrated planners reached 95% coverage faster in most simulation cases and showed a 30% real-world reduction in coverage time.

papers.abstract: We focus on legible robot motion generation in social navigation settings. Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently infer the robot's intent. While mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, social robot navigation presents a new challenge: the robot must clearly convey its intent while ensuring human safety in dynamic pedestrian environments where human attention is often divided. With the goal of enabling robots to generate legible motion in dynamic and constrained spaces, we investigate how the choice of representation and the level of human attention shape navigation performance and human impressions. Focusing on the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, we conduct two controlled user studies involving alternative legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) investigates the role of intent representation, showing that passing-side legibility, particularly when adaptively updated, leads to smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion allows for smooth human motion even under distraction, even if this is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI.
bullets: Legible motion must communicate intent while maintaining safety in dynamic, constrained pedestrian environments.
Two controlled user studies evaluated alternative legibility formulations within a shared model predictive control framework.
Passing-side intent, particularly when adaptively updated, was perceived as more competent and less demanding than destination-based and non-legible motion.
Legible motion enabled smoother human movement under distraction, although subjective ratings did not always show the same effect.
The findings support interaction-level intent representations for coordinating robot–human navigation.

papers.abstract: Video generation models (VGMs) offer strong spatiotemporal priors for embodied observation--action modeling. However, joint-space action vectors lack explicit image-space structure and vary in dimensionality and semantics across embodiments, making it challenging to directly leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors of VGMs. End-effector visualizations provide an alternative but do not specify the full articulated configuration needed for robot execution. We present Dream4ACT, a world model built for joint video-action modeling across embodiments. To unify action representations across embodiments, we introduce a shared visual action interface, called action views, which render target joint configurations from four prescribed virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics. This shared visual representation preserves embodiment-specific articulated geometry while allowing observation and action sequences to share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Through masked flow-matching, our model supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and joint observation--action generation within a single jointly trained model by varying which future sequences are corrupted. To recover executable action sequences from predicted action views, we propose a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview recovery mechanism, without a learned embodiment-specific decoder. Dream4ACT achieves an average success rate of 88.98\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and an overall score of 65.66 on TriWorldBench, supporting effective closed-loop manipulation and competitive action-conditioned multiview prediction through the visual action interface.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between embodiment-specific joint-space actions and video models’ image-space representations.
Renders target joint configurations from four virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics as shared “action views.”

Recovers executable actions with a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview procedure.

papers.abstract: Scaling has become a primary driver of progress in language and vision foundation models, yet its role in precise correspondence matching remains underexplored. In this work, we present Flow Any Scene Transformer (FAST), a scalable correspondence model driven by two key insights. First, we reveal that the query-key projections inside single-view vision foundation models encode a coarse yet reusable prior for cross-view matching. Second, reusing these pretrained projections in cross-attention form yields a highly effective initialization for a ViT-based matcher built from a single-view encoder. Guided by these insights, we build FAST upon a vanilla single-view foundation model, utilizing a zero-parameter rewiring strategy to convert selected self-attention layers into cross-attention for cross-view interaction. This design allows ViT-based matchers to scale with advances in single-view foundation models, bypassing the need for a dedicated pair-centric pretraining stage. To fully unlock the scaling potential of this formulation, we assemble a 6-million-pair training corpus for general-purpose dense 2D displacement estimation across diverse co-visible image pairs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FAST achieves state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks, while scaling favorably with both backbone size and training data.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored role of scaling in precise correspondence matching.
Reuses query-key projections from single-view vision foundation models as a coarse, transferable cross-view matching prior.
Uses zero-parameter rewiring to convert selected self-attention layers into cross-attention, avoiding pair-centric pretraining.
Trains on a 6-million-pair corpus for general-purpose dense 2D displacement estimation across diverse co-visible images.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across many benchmarks, with favorable scaling by backbone size and training data.
